title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
body_text: Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass | Alpine Linux About Downloads Releases Community Sponsors Donate docs wiki git issues packages mirrors security Small. Simple. Secure. Alpine Linux is a security-oriented, lightweight Linux distribution based on musl libc and busybox. 2026-11-05 Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd . Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon. If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd . Either one closes the hole. What is the problem? An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries. The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024 bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without one reachable. Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes . No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing. Who is affected? You are affected if all of the following are true: You run the Alpine openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or you run openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no . ( openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.) PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it). The machine has an account whose password field is * . This includes: root , which ships as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16. OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so root is only reachable if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That does not help if another account that can log in is able to become root, for example through doas . Any key-only user created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*' . Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry. The alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images (see below). At least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ password hash. Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20). Who is not affected? Docker and other container users that do not run sshd in the container. Systems with PasswordAuthentication no . Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes (with UsePAM no you are affected). Locked accounts: those with ! as the password field in /etc/shadow (a line starting user:!: ). They cannot log in with a password or a key. Systems where no account has a $ -style password hash. Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes PasswordAuthentication no . How can I fix it? 1. Update apk upgrade -U -a Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement ). The fixed package versions are: Branch Fixed openssh version edge 10.6_p2-r0 3.24 10.3_p1-r2 3.23 10.2_p1-r1 3.22 10.0_p1-r11 3.21 9.9_p2-r1 3.20 9.7_p1-r6 3.19 9.6_p1-r3 3.18 9.3_p2-r4 3.17 9.1_p1-r7 3.16 9.0_p1-r6 Restart sshd after upgrading ( rc-service sshd restart ). Upgrading the package does not restart a running sshd , so you must do it after. 2. If you cannot update: disable password authentication Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login. Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s default sshd_config reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases ignore it. The sed command changes yes to no on every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config , whatever the spacing, including lines inside a Match block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and saves the original as /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak . The last two commands check the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result: mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \ -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \ /etc/ssh/sshd_config sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication The last command should print passwordauthentication no . To undo, delete /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak back over /etc/ssh/sshd_config . Cloud images (tiny-cloud) The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas . They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd . An attacker then gets a shell as alpine and can use doas to become root. Images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed package. Images from earlier point releases do not, so on every running instance, update openssh or disable password authentication. Releases that are no longer supported (3.21 and older) These releases have the same bug. 3.21 reached its end of support on 2026-11-01, but we have published fixed packages for each release all the way back to 3.16. How do I know if I was attacked? Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password ( alpine , root , or any key-only user). Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised. How could this happen? When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt with crypt() (the C library function that turns a password into its stored hash) and comparing the result to the stored password field. For an account whose stored field is too short to contain a salt (the random prefix of a hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account. musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds. OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. The stable-branch packages above carry a patch for the same problem. Credits Reported by ÃzgÃ¼n KÃ¼ltekin of Wakefield . Thanks to Damien Miller and Darren Tucker of the OpenSSH project for the fix and the 10.6p2 release, to Timo TerÃ¤s for help analyzing the issue, and to Natanael Copa, who built and uploaded the updated packages. © Copyright 2026 Alpine Linux Development Team all rights reserved | Privacy Policy

You can also grab the latest ZIP from Releases , unzip it, and drag Window Sweaters.app into Applications. If macOS blocks it, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway after trying to launch it. The app isn't notarized by Apple yet. Apple's instructions explain this step. Make yourself cosy Click the yarn icon in your menu bar to change the style, pattern, border width, and stitch size. You can also pause the sweaters or quit from there. To leave an app bare, open Apps and untick it. Its windows lose their sweater straight away, everything else stays as it is, and it stays off until you tick it again, even after a restart. Only want sweaters on a few apps? Choose Turn Off for All Apps , then tick the ones you like. Apps you open later start off too. By App gives each app its own sweater. Zigzag gives them all a softer, matching cream zigzag in colours taken from their icons. Try both and see what you like. If macOS asks for Accessibility access, enable Window Sweaters in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility so it can follow which window is focused. The sweaters Custom sweaters for 37 apps, and counting! Almost 40 little colourways, with colours picked by hand. These are just a few of my favourites: Shown above in By App and Zigzag. Here’s everyone we’ve knitted for so far: Apple: Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, Notes, Calendar, Reminders, Apple Music, Photos, Preview, Terminal. Work and notes: Notion, Paper, Granola, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom. Coding and AI: Cursor, VS Code, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok Bot, Ghostty. Design: Figma, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator. Microsoft Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook. More favourites: Spotify, WhatsApp, Google Chrome, Firefox, Telegram, Discord. See every sweater and its close-up stitches in the catalogue , or download the By App PDF . The 37 custom sweaters keep their hand-picked colours and patterns. Other apps borrow colours from their own icons, softened into yarn, and get a two-colour zigzag, picnic or twinkle sweater in By App mode. The pattern stays the same for each app. If an icon has no usable colour, the app keeps a stable colour chosen from its name. Icons are sampled locally in the background when needed. While the colour is being prepared, the border uses its usual fallback. Zigzag uses icon colours for every app, the 37 custom ones included, with a cream zigzag, or a deeper shade of the app’s colour on pale apps. Colours you set in apps.conf always win. Other shared patterns keep their own contrast yarns, with each app’s own base colour. A little work in progress I built this on my Mac and use it myself, but there are still rough edges. Borders hide while you resize a window and return when you're done. The app is built for macOS 13 or later, on Apple Silicon and Intel . I've tested it on Apple Silicon with macOS 26; older macOS versions and Intel Macs haven't had the same hands-on testing. It uses private macOS window APIs, so system updates may affect how it works. If something looks wrong, open an issue and tell me your macOS version, Mac model, and whether you're using another screen. Reproduction steps help a lot. Build it yourself You'll need Apple's Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ) and Python 3. git clone https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters.git cd window-sweaters ./scripts/build-app.sh python3 scripts/install-local.py This builds outputs/Window Sweaters.app , installs it in ~/Applications , and opens it. The installer backs up any previous local installation before replacing it. Your own colourways If you'd like to experiment, edit these files and restart the app: ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/apps.conf ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/charts/ The folder still uses the app's original name so existing settings keep working. For example, an app rule looks like this: Claude = #D58561 atelier-claude Names match app-name prefixes, ignoring capitalisation; the longest match wins. You can also put your own PNG charts in the charts folder to replace built-in patterns. If you like setting things up from the command line, Window Sweaters also runs an optional shell script at startup, if you have one at ~/.config/window-sweaters/sweatersrc or ~/.sweatersrc . Taking it off Quit Window Sweaters from the yarn icon first. Then, if you installed it with Homebrew: brew uninstall --zap --cask window-sweaters --zap also removes your saved colourways. Leave it off to keep them for later. If you installed it by hand, drag Window Sweaters.app to the Trash, then delete these if you want everything gone: ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders ~/Library/Preferences/local.knitborders.app.plist macOS remembers the Accessibility permission separately, so remove Window Sweaters from System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility too. Contributing make test # run the tests make catalogue # render the sweater collection make bench # benchmark the renderer See CONTRIBUTING.md for more details. title: sshole
body_text: *sshole · sshhole.com * ss h ole so openssh on musl linux (alpine, openwrt, buildroot, yocto, and a lot of the docker images you've pulled) has had a little problem since 2016. accounts that should never take a password at all (root, your key-only deploy user, ldap users, the default user on alpine's aws and azure images) take any password longer than 256 characters. yes, any password. yes. i know. yes. 1980 the first star 1990s the password check 1990s the fine print 2012 crypt stops saying NULL 2012 the 256-byte cap 2016 bob's salt 2019 the fix for the fix 2024 ten quiet years 2026 how i ran into it 1980 the first star back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd , right next to your username. in a file everyone could read. in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon . nobody's supposed to ever log in as it. a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today 3bsd · /etc/passwd · 1980 Address github.com/dspinellis/unix-history-repo/blob/BSD-3/etc/passwd the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself" 1990s how sshd checks your password ok so these days the hash lives in /etc/shadow and looks like $6$abc$k2P9… . the $6$ means sha512, abc is the salt, the rest is the actual hash you type your password, sshd hashes it with that same salt and checks if it comes out identical. same = you're in. that's it and if the field is just * ? there's nothing to match. type whatever you want, it's never getting you in 1990s the fine print one more rule. if crypt() can't do its job, it returns NULL. like if the salt asks for some algorithm the system doesn't have, there's nothing to compute, so you get NULL instead of a hash the single unix spec · crypt() · 1997 Address pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xsh/crypt.html pretty clear. except a lot of programs never check for NULL. they just compare whatever crypt() gives back with the stored field, hit the NULL, and crash 2012 crypt stops saying NULL so musl (the libc under alpine) goes ok fine, crypt() just won't return NULL anymore. if it fails, it returns a single character instead. that character can never match a real password, so programs don't crash, they just see a wrong password now guess which character they picked for that " ? " yep. the star. again. musl · b3c4cc12 · aug 2012 Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12 "reportedly." musl · b3c4cc12 · the diff Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12 "should not happen" gone, NULL gone, "*" in 2012 three weeks later then musl adds sha512 crypt. the thing is, sha512crypt gets slower the longer the password is, so someone could send one giant password and keep your server busy for a long time. so musl just caps it at 256 bytes and refuses anything longer musl · 88bf5a8a · aug 29 2012 Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=88bf5a8a twenty days after the "*" commit btw musl · crypt_sha512.c @ 88bf5a8a Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/misc/crypt_sha512.c?id=88bf5a8a KEY_MAX) return 0;" loading="lazy"> so past 256 bytes crypt fails. and when crypt fails… it says "*" . musl · crypt_sha512.c Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha512.c literally in the comment the whole time 2016 sshd borrows bob's salt CVE-2016-6210. ask sshd about a user that doesn't exist and it says no instantly, cause there's nothing to hash. real users take a few ms longer. so just time it and you know who exists the fix is kinda funny. no real hash to check? sshd grabs some other account's salt and hashes your password anyway, just to waste the same amount of time. still a no, just a slower no openssh-commits · jul 2016 Address lists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2016-July/005428.html "for invalid users." and also, it turns out, real users with a * . 2019 → 2022 the fix for the fix 2019. turns out alpine's docker images had no root password. at all. CVE-2019-5021. alpine fixes it by locking root with ! but without pam, ! also kills ssh keys. and cloud images log in with keys. 2022. alpine 3.16 switches root to * . still locked, keys work again alpine aports · fbe926af · shipped in 3.16, 2022 Address gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/commit/fbe926af.patch narrator: it did not. 2016 → 2026 ten quiet years why did nobody notice? well, maybe someone did. maybe someone pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt, half a slack message or a whole ssh key, and it just let them in. you've never pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt?? amazing. a fresh box with no passwords set isn't affected. a * in shadow needs a wrong try first. openssh tests on openbsd and glibc, musl doesn't test sshd, and most distros go through pam, which never even calls crypt for a * . so as far as anyone knows, nobody noticed. as far as anyone knows. some people got really close though libc-alpha · debian #714219 · 2013 Address sourceware.org/legacy-ml/libc-alpha/2013-07/msg00046.html a debian dev asks glibc to copy musl's "*" . six years later debian moves to libxcrypt, which says "*0" , and closes the bug. one character away. musl mailing list · dec 2024 Address openwall.com/lists/musl/2024/12/31/2 this thread is about busybox passwd breaking on a 257 character password. same "*" , same limit. nobody says "sshd" openssh-commits · 30 oct 2026 Address lists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2026-October/013271.html a security review fixes pick_salt() . the bug is four lines below it. four days before i found it. nov 2026 how i ran into it i was messing around with openssh, mostly the boring parts where it talks to libc, like the password code. people don't really look at that stuff, they look at the crypto. so i built sshd every way i could think of (glibc, musl, pam, no pam, shadow, no shadow) and threw like 17,600 weird logins at it. weird hashes, broken accounts, passwords way too long oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it every build agreed on every login. except musl without pam. that one said yes to things it shouldn't tl;dr try it one debian box, one alpine box. type stuff. it all runs right here in your browser, nothing gets sent anywhere ozgun 256 × A 300 × A clear 256 1024 0 bytes debian · glibc crypt(pw, bob's salt) alice's field * alpine · musl crypt(pw, bob's salt) alice's field * are you affected? is your sshd running on musl ? (alpine, openwrt, buildroot, yocto) is it not using pam ? alpine's openssh-server doesn't by default, or maybe you set UsePAM no are password logins still on? they are by default is there an account with just * as its password? key-only users, ldap users, root on alpine and some other account with a real password? then that * account takes any password between 257 and 1024 characters on alpine's official aws and azure images that's the default alpine user, and it has passwordless doas . so it's root on debian, ubuntu, fedora or anything else with glibc? going through pam? dropbear? openbsd? you're fine what now you # update. openssh 10.6p2 fixes it. $ apk upgrade openssh # can't update yet? turn password logins off. $ echo "PasswordAuthentication no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf $ rc-service sshd restart did you get hacked? check. check github.com/oz9un/sshole root@your-box see a line like that? an account with no password just took a password if that's the case… i'm sorry. you got hacked. by an * sshole found by ozgun kultekin at wakefield we're hiring. wakefield.co/careers

title: The Hackintosh Reborn
body_text: The Hackintosh Reborn... with AI Yoon's Blog Organizing my thoughts ABOUT ME November 5, 2026 Â· macos diy opinion The Hackintosh Reborn... with AI Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating back to the late 1980s. At the time KVM and PCI passthrough were relatively new technologies, and this guide provided near-native performance with GPU acceleration. A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away. That day has come and the latest version of macOS 27 (Golden Gate) released this year is no longer compatible with x86... Just a few days ago, I decided to create an iOS app for the first time. It required XCode 26 for development, so I used my spare ThinkPad T490 as my development machine and installed macOS 26 using a posted guide . The installation was smooth and painless. XCode 26 has integrations with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, and this was my first foray into AI-assisted coding. After some initial tinkering with x86 workarounds , I was pleased that I had a functional iOS app within a day, without touching a single line of code! So how does this all tie in? Well, this is exactly what the Hackintosh community could hardly envision five years ago: the rise of AI . Waiting patiently and gently until now, the hackintosh and the hackios community has seen an absolute explosion in development, activity, and success in the past few weeks! As one person aptly wrote, this is the power of Claude Code with Ghidra on steroids. Just to list a few recent developments, we have: macOS 27 running on the Snapdragon Laptop: macOS 27.2 Beta on an ARM SBC RK3588 with Mali drivers: iOS 17 running on the Nintendo Switch OLED: Support for 50-series Nvidia GPUs with nullmoth: I'm barely scratching the surface, with further developments in AirDrop , accelerated video decode , and even running translated macOS 27 on x86 . As much as we lament the cost of AI, there are some glimmers of hope: you just might be able to have your hardware and own it too. Copyright 2026Â |Â Powered by Ghost Â +Â Crisp

Nov 20th, 2025 - Introducing Quick and Research assistants # Kagi Assistant Introducing Quick and Research assistants Today, we are officially introducing Kagi Research assistants (previously known as "KI"). Read our full announcement here . Their main strength is research: identifying what to search for, executing multiple simultaneous searches (in different languages, if needed), and synthesizing the findings into high-quality answers. Simply choose whether to prioritise speed or depth: Quick optimises for speed , providing direct and concise answers. Research focuses on depth and diversity , conducting exhaustive analysis for thorough results. Research is available to Ultimate subscribers only. To achieve this, they employ different base models for specific tasks. We continuously benchmark top-performing models and select the best one for each job, so you don't have to. And on top of web search, weâve added new behavioural layers and a wider toolset, including Python execution and image generation for higher-quality answers. July 31st, 2025 - Kagi Assistant gets tags, bulk actions, and much more # Kagi Assistant This week's release brings several big updates to Kagi Assistant, laying the groundwork to exciting new chapters ahead. Introducing tags Tags let you organise your Kagi Assistant threads. Each thread can have multiple tags. Advanced control for Bangs via Regex We've added an optional "Regex" field to Custom Bangs for more precise control. Instead of $1 always being the first word and $2 the second, you can now define exactly how your query is split to create more powerful shortcuts. For example, to create a custom translator for a query like !tr spanish live long and prosper , you can now separate the language from the text. In your Custom Bang settings, you would use: Template: https://translate.kagi.com/?to=$1&text=$2 Regex: (\w+)\s+(.*) This pattern tells the Bang to use the first word for $1 and the entire rest of the query for $2 . If you leave the Regex field blank, your Bangs will continue to work as they always have. A Lens will focus Kagiâs search on one or more (up to ten) particular sites, date ranges, regions, keywords, or file types. You can also exclude sites or subsites. Kagi has several default Lenses, and you can add your own customized Lenses: Kagi is used as an example for why it's important to pay for what you love , and how it helps align the incentives between the user and the service provider: In order for Kagi to make more money, they have to make search quality better. By Salon Published November 5, 2026 2:28PM (EST) Facebook X Reddit Email Save Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication. Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier. When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing. Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it. The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you. We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us. The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness. Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today. Thank you for being part of our story. title: Download your favourite YouTube videos
body_text: You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos – The Sun and The Air The Sun and The Air Home Blog Cohost Archive About 29 Oct, 2026 What Veilguard tells me about Mass Effect 5 13 Oct, 2026 You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos 27 Sep, 2026 September Basho Wrap-up 01 Sep, 2026 September Basho preview 31 Aug, 2026 The Gameplay Loop - Zero Company You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos 13 Oct, 2026 Signal boosting Laura's post that you should absolutely download and archive the stuff that matters to you. The corporate internet is hostile to art and the things you love do not belong to you unless you claim them for yourself. If you've been around for a while on YouTube, just look at your "liked videos" playlist and see how many of the early ones are no longer available (something you literally have to enable in the playlist settings, it's that endemic). The tools to do this in a basic way are extremely easy to get hold of, and generally have good defaults. I'm also going to talk a little about my own setup, and why it is the weird way it is, but it's definitely overkill for most setups. yt-dlp or one of it's many wrappers 1 will do most of what you need, and a folder on a bulk storage drive or NAS will be plenty sufficient to make sure you always have access to them. For me though, I had a particular need - I have unfortunately programmed myself to be almost entirely unable to fall asleep without a Many a True Nerd Let's Play on a low volume. This comes with a couple of issues. I need to be able to play it on my TV. It has to integrate into my existing NAS infrastructure. I need to be able to organise hundreds of videos across dozens of playlists. This is a bigger sticking point than it sounds. Adding new ones or placing them can't be a manual job. Again, hundreds of videos. My NAS media library is built around Jellyfin, which has a concept of Playlists but they're really not intended as a first-order organisational structure. You're expected to take a few tracks from a bunch of existing albums and place them in a playlist separate from the actual Library . No, Jellyfin has a very rigid concept of either Movies, TV Shows > Seasons > Episodes, or Artists > Albums > Songs. TV Shows is the obvious analogue here, and with some really wild finagling I was able to get a setup together that is good enough to satisfy for now 2 . My setup looks like this: Jellyfin In Jellyfin I have a Library setup in TV Shows mode called YouTube. I've turned off all metadata scrapers and the like, and have it set to prefer file data over file names. ytdl-sub This is the only yt-dlp wrapper that allowed me to properly maintain the Playlist structure to any extent, and is entirely based on a series of .yaml files. In it's self-hosted docker-compose form, it comes with a web-app VSCode IDE which is honestly super handy - bridges the tech-comfort gap nicely. I have a custom genre and list of MATN playlists I want it to collect and set metadata for. You can also see there I have a handful of Folding Ideas videos set as "Documentaries" - this is more in keeping with how ytdl-sub expects to be used. The truth is that 99% of youtubers, and 99.9% of viewers, don't particularly need to structure everything as playlists within a channel. Most have a much higher proportion of one-off to series videos that make my MATN structure utterly pointless. As such, ytdl-sub defaults to tagging videos with a Season field organised by Year, but it stores them in folders named for the Playlist. This leads to Jellyfin putting every one of those playlist videos in 2 places within the channel - a Year Series, and a Playlist Series: I only recently realised how to fix this, which is to assign the Playlist title as the Season Number in my ytdl-sub config file - it seems like it should break, but it doesn't: I could write a script to go in and fix this for all my existing series, but the issue is that once Jellyfin has Imported a video, I can't get it to update the Season Number without fully reimporting the Library, something I'm not really interested in doing for a terabyte of video. Oh, speaking of storage size... Tdarr Tdarr is a service that can automatically run through a library of videos and re-encode it in whatever way you desire - usually to some smaller, more efficient format or codec. I use it to encode everything in my media server to HEVC/H.265 as storage is my main bottleneck - processing power is the tradeoff and I have that in spades. I'm honestly not going to recommend Tdarr unless you are very comfortable looking at a massively complex and poorly designed UI and making the smart decision to do the minimum. Everyone I know who has used it has come in with grand ambitions of brilliant complex workflows and settled on just using the default one because it works fine. It has a tendency to break on anything remotely complex, and I had to manually tweak a script so that it wouldn't cry any time there was a data stream, but once it gets going it just chugs along re-encoding gigabyte after gigabyte. It does seem to cause Jellyfin to lose Thumbnail images for reasons I haven't fully figured out, but it's generally fixable either manually, with a "refresh metadata", or in your media management software of choice. It saved me about 700GB across my 2TB library, though I probably could have avoided some of that cost by just being more picky about my downloads. Again, I don't really recommend it! But if you're in a pinch, it will absolutely do the job. ✉️ Reply via email These are probably rife with vibe-coding, as yt-dlp scripts are well documented online and using the command line is daunting for most. ↩ As with all things homelab - it's never perfect, which keeps the hobby alive forever. ↩ #blog #homelab   rss | contact me Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
body_text: I wish tech companies knew more about me | exotext ← Rakhim's blog I wish tech companies knew more about me 3 November 2026 "Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens... I have never felt anything close to that. I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads: When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern. Using Google Chrome, logged into my Google account, I searched for info about Google AI plan usage limits, got an AI-generated response with a link to the help page, clicked it and ended up, logged out, on a Finnish-language landing page (because I'm located in Finland). My user account, system locale, browser locale, and keyboard settings are all set to English. I am logged into Chrome and all Google services. I travel to Germany every few months, and lots of services that I've been using for years suddenly decide I speak German. The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab. Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland. A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is. I clicked on that ad; now I keep getting other 3D-printing-related ads. Here's an ad for an email/WhatsApp marketing tool. I never needed any marketing tool, nor do I own a WhatsApp business account. Now it's a Helsinki hotel. I live in Helsinki, I haven't searched for local hotels since 2014 when I first arrived here. A fucking asphalt cleaning tractor. I searched YouTube for installation instruction for a specific appliance "AEG CCS84751", watched a couple of relevant videos and the next day saw my homepage populated with more videos about random ovens and stoves. OK, so, let's see, a user searches for installation instructions for a very specific, concrete model. What could we machine-learn from this, what are the options here? The user is into ovens The user is into installing appliances The user needs this one particular instruction for this one particular oven because the user maybe bought that oven and wants to install it, once, maybe? My bank keeps sending me offers for car insurance. I have car insurance with that bank. Have had it for years. An airline, when reminding me of an upcoming trip, send info about visas and border crossing laws which don't apply to my citizenship. They literally have a scan of my passport. Netflix on Apple TV asks me to select a user every time I launch it. I've had this account for 15+ years, and never had more than one user on it. I always select the only option there is to select. There is no setting to disable this screen. My mobile provider keeps sending me discounts for children's products and events from their corporate partners. I don't have children. HBO keeps recommending me foreign movies and shows which I cannot watch as they don't have English subtitles. I have no doubts that a lot of information is being tracked, stored, and sold. Since that's already done, could you guys at least use some of it?.. Powered by Exotext

Working together with the Action Shot feature, it freezes motion while maximizing available light, producing crisp, vibrant images with richer detail and more natural color. The 50MP ultrawide camera³ fits more into every frame, transforming tight spaces into expansive compositions and making it easier to capture sweeping landscapes, large landmarks and group photos without stepping back. And a 50MP front camera delivers sharp, ready-to-share selfies and supports 4K video recording, so selfie videos feature the same bold colors and clarity as still photos. For a more cinematic video experience, the motorola signature 27 features a powerful Video Enhancement Engine that uses AI to intelligently optimize color, contrast and dynamic range in real time. Support for Dolby Vision ® , the same technology used by leading filmmakers, helps enable richer, more immersive video. Combined with the Qualcomm® Electronic Image Stabilization and 3.5° OIS hardware on the main camera, panning, walking, and handheld recording looks more fluid and stable, so users can stay in the moment while the camera does the hard work. the brightest display available in a smartphone 20 Engineered to unlock the full potential of the latest advances in display technology, the motorola signature 27 features a new Extreme AMOLED Duo display, the brightest display available, designed to provide a premium viewing experience in virtually any environment. Built with breakthrough Tandem Technology, it combines two emissive layers into one, producing brighter visuals, richer color and greater efficiency. With up to 12,000 4 nits of peak brightness, users can comfortably view maps, messages, photos and videos virtually anywhere, whether navigating a sunny afternoon, checking directions on the go or capturing content outdoors, without needing to shield the screen or strain to see it. Plus, 1.5K Super HD resolution and Dolby Vision® bring entertainment to life with exceptional sharpness, contrast and precision. This advanced display is also designed to be smarter and more durable, delivering up to 34% greater energy efficiency and up to a 121% longer lifespan than traditional AMOLED panels. 24 Pantone® Validated color calibration ensures colors and skin tones appear true to life 5 , while SGS-certified blue light technology helps reduce eye strain. powering next generation experiences At the heart of the motorola signature 27 is the Snapdragon® 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 Mobile Platform, making it among the first smartphones to feature Qualcomm Technologies’ latest flagship mobile chipset. Engineered to power breakthrough gaming, advanced camera experiences, ultra-fast connectivity and AI, it delivers the performance needed for today’s most demanding mobile experiences and the next wave of AI innovation. To sustain peak performance when it matters most, the motorola signature 27 pairs the platform with Motorola’s ArcticMesh cooling system that uses micro-diamond-infused thermal gel and a thermal chamber that is 40% larger than the previous generation⁶ to keep performance running at its best during extended gaming sessions, AI tasks, video recording and intensive multitasking. With a new 6‑antenna design delivering faster 5G downloads, up to 2x faster Wi‑Fi speeds 6 , Wi‑Fi 8 compatibility, the motorola signature 27 is built to stay fast, capable and ready for next-era AI. And seven years of OS upgrades 23 help ensure the experience stays reliable long into the future. AI that goes beyond assistance The motorola signature 27 is designed for Gemini Intelligence, which brings the best of Gemini to Android’s most advanced devices, alongside out-of-box Google Gemini experiences and Motorola Qira. The motorola signature 27 can understand context, help people create, support decisions and move from intention to action across the apps and services they use every day. As Google rolls out these capabilities to Gemini Intelligence⁷ devices globally in the coming months, motorola signature 27 will be ready to bring them to users around the world: Whether booking a ride or preparing a grocery order from a shopping list on your screen, Gemini helps users go from intention to action with less effort. Gemini can handle complex, multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf , reducing app switching and helping them stay focused on what matters. Users remain in control throughout, with the ability to view progress, jump in, or stop a task. 16 Rambler 17 transforms natural speech into polished messages, letting users think out loud while it refines their words in the background. Rambler removes filler words, edits repetition, and organizes ideas into clear paragraphs or bullet points. Users can correct themselves mid-sentence, switch languages seamlessly, and review everything before sending, ensuring they share exactly what they intend. Afterwards, users can quickly ask Rambler to rewrite, rephrase, translate, or reformat their text. Create My Widget 18 enables users to create personalized widgets by simply describing what they want to see. Whether it’s a tracker to follow your monthly spending, daily recipe inspiration, or a trip countdown with your travel details, your homescreen can be as personalized as you want it to be. Sign-to-Text 19 translates American Sign Language (ASL) into written English in real time using the device’s front-facing camera. Integrated with Gboard and Live Transcribe, it opens new ways for users to communicate across digital and in-person interactions. Right out of the box, the motorola signature 27 also includes powerful Google Gemini⁸ experiences designed to bring new levels of creativity, including Gemini Omni, which enables users to create and edit video through natural conversation, and Lyria which generates custom soundtracks from simple prompts. In addition, the device features Motorola Qira ⁹ , a built-in AI system designed to connect and enhance experiences across supported Motorola and Lenovo devices, helping users get more from their broader ecosystem through a single, seamless hybrid AI experience. the only smartphone with “Audio by Bang & Olufsen” As the only smartphone in-market to feature Audio by Bang & Olufsen, the motorola signature 27 unlocks an elevated audio experience built on Motorola’s recently announced multi-year partnership with Bang & Olufsen. Combining Motorola’s premium mobile innovation with Bang & Olufsen’s renowned expertise in sound and design, the device is engineered to deliver sound that is meant to be felt, not just heard. Featuring dedicated Sound Modes and an all-new speaker architecture, the device is tuned to preserve the character of the original recording, alongside deep bass, clear vocals and greater fidelity across music, movies and games. distinctive design, exceptional durability With the motorola signature 27, Motorola continues the evolution of its signature family design philosophy, that balances aesthetic expression with everyday usability. The device features a sleek aluminum silhouette with contoured edges and a thin profile that feels comfortable in hand, while delivering a distinctly premium look and feel. Complementing the refined design is a seamlessly integrated camera plane, finished in smooth ceramic and brushed aluminum, creating a sophisticated focal point that feels both purposeful and modern. Precisely crafted with a ceramic and glass construction, the motorola signature 27 is available in two unique, elevated finishes: PANTONE Coal Smoke, which features a tactical weave finish inspired by automotive design and performance materials, and PANTONE Capulet Olive, which features a textile-inspired finish influenced by premium fashion and interior design. Premium materials and durability come together in the motorola signature 27, featuring Corning® Gorilla® Glass Ceramic 3 , an aerospace-grade aluminum frame, military-grade durability (MIL-STD-810H) 10 , and IP68 and IP69 ratings for enhanced protection against the elements. 22 power that gives the freedom to do more To back up all this powerful innovation, the motorola signature 27 features a 7000mAh battery 11 , 35% larger than the last generation, so users can stay connected longer, stream and create without interruption, and move through the day without constantly thinking about battery life.
