OpenSSH 2.9.9 fixes a weakness in the key file option handling, including source IP based access control. OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0 implementation and includes sftp client and server support. This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below). We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued support and encouragement. Security Notes: =============== This release fixes weakness in the source IP based access control for SSH protocol v2 public key authentication: Versions of OpenSSH between 2.5 and 2.9.9 are affected if they use the 'from=' key file option in combination with both RSA and DSA keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2. Depending on the order of the user keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 sshd might fail to apply the source IP based access control restriction (e.g. from="10.0.0.1") to the correct key: If a source IP restricted key (e.g. DSA key) is immediately followed by a key of a different type (e.g. RSA key), then key options for the second key are applied to both keys, which includes 'from='. This means that users can circumvent the system policy and login from disallowed source IP addresses. Important Changes: ================== OpenSSH 2.9.9 might have upgrade issues introduced by the long time between releases, which may affect people in unforeseen ways: 1) The files /etc/ssh_known_hosts2 ~/.ssh/known_hosts2 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 are now obsolete, you can use /etc/ssh_known_hosts ~/.ssh/known_hosts ~/.ssh/authorized_keys For backward compatibility ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 is still used for authentication and hostkeys are still read from the known_hosts2. However, old files are considered 'readonly'. Future releases are likely to not read these files. 2) The CheckMail option in sshd_config is deprecated, sshd no longer checks for new mail. 3) X11 cookies are stored in $HOME OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt, Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom. OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH 1.3 & 1.5 protocol implementation and a 99% SSH 2 protocol implementation, including sftp client and server support. OpenSSH 2.5.0p1 was skipped because of interoperability issues with ssh-1.2.18 => ssh-1.2.22. We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued support and encouragement. Important Changes: ================== 1) Features added to the implementation of the SSH 2 protocol: * agent forwarding * support for -R forwarding * RSA host and userkeys * extended support for older SSH 2 protocol implementations OpenSSH still lacks support for rekeying, so you have to turn off rekeying if your server tries to force this feature. The next release of OpenSSH will probably support rekeying. 2) Damien Miller contributed an interactive sftp client. The sftp client works for both SSH protocol versions. 3) David Mazieres' ssh-keyscan has been added to the OpenSSH distribution. 4) Now there are three types of keys in OpenSSH: RSA1 is used by the SSH 1 protocol only, RSA and DSA keys are used by the SSH 2 protocol implementation. You can generate RSA keys for use with SSH 2 protocol with: $ ssh-keygen -t rsa -f /etc/ssh_host_rsa_key To use RSA or DSA keys in SSH 2 protocol, simply add the public keys to the .ssh/authorised_keys2 file. IdentityFile2, HostDsaKey and DSAAuthentication are obsolete: You can use multiple IdentityFile and HostKey options instead, e.g HostKey /etc/ssh_host_key HostKey /etc/ssh_host_dsa_key HostKey /etc/ssh_host_rsa_key in /etc/sshd_config The option DSAAuthentication has been replaced by PubkeyAuthentication. Fingerprinting works for all types of keys: $ ssh-keygen -l -f $HOME/.ssh/{authorized_keys,known_hosts}{,2} 5) Important changes in the implementation of SSH 1 protocol: The OpenSSH server does not require a privileged source port for RhostsRsaAuthentication, since it adds no additional security. Interoperation with SSH 1.4 protocol 6) New option HostKeyAlias This option allows the user to record the host key under a different name. This is useful for tunneling over forwarded connections or if you run multiple sshd's on different ports on the same machine. Alternatively you can use the UserKnownHostsFile or UserKnownHostsFile2 options to specify separate host key files for the connection. 7) The ReverseMappingCheck is now optional in sshd_config. If you combine this with the 'sshd -u0' option the server will not do DNS lookups when a client connects. 8) Stricter Hostkey Checking 9) Option Change Summary: a) New or changed: ChallengeResponseAuthentication MACs PubkeyAuthentication HostkeyAlias (Client only) Banner (Server only) ReverseMappingCheck (Server only) PermitRootLogin {yes,without-password,forced-commands-only,no} {Allow,Deny}Groups now support supplementary groups sshd -D for monitoring scripts or inittab ssh -t multiple -t force tty allocation b) Obsolete: DsaAuthentication (use PubkeyAuthentication instead) HostDsaKey (use HostKey) Identityfile2 (use Identityfile or -i) SkeyAuthentication (use ChallengeResponseAuthentication) TisAuthentication (use ChallengeResponseAuthentication) OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt, Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom. Cloos Jr. <cloos@jhcloos.com> ------------------ OpenSSH 2.1.1p2 (2000-07-01) Announcing the release of portable OpenSSH 2.1.1p2. This release primarily contains fixes to the bugs that have been reported over the last month, in particular: - Invalid time bring written to utmp/wtmp on systems using bash2 - Several lastlog fixes - AIX, SCO, Irix portability fixes - Avoid failures on PAM systems when using PAM authentication modules which require a tty. - Entropy collection fixes for Solaris. - EGD robustness improvements - Fixes and enhancements from the OpenBSD team: - Fixed options processing in authorized_keys2 file - Compatibility with commercial SSH 2.0.13 and 2.2.0 - Numerous minor fixes There are also a couple of new features: - Shadow password expiry support (no password change support yet) - Irix 6.x array sessions, project IDs and system audit trail IDs - Beginnings of Tru64 / OSF SIA (Security Integration Architecture) support - Beginnings of NeXT support Version 2.1.1p2 will be available from the mirrors listed at http://www.openssh.com/portable.html (as soon as they update). This release contains the fix for the "UseLogin yes" vulnerability identified in Markus' release and several other enhancements and bugfixes. Including: - Better login code. Andre Lucas has rewritten the login code to be much more modular and extensible. In the process he has fixed the problems with Solaris utmp[x]. - Revised the entropy collection code to be faster and more reliable. - Fix for RSA host restrictions ("from=" in authorized_keys) It is recommended that all users upgrade to this version. Portable OpenSSH 2.1.1p1 is available from one of the many mirrors listed at: http://www.openssh.com/portable.html Regards, Damien Miller OpenSSH 2.1.0p1 (2000-05-09) This is to announce the release of openssh-2.1.0, the first stable release of portable OpenSSH to incorporate support for the SSH2 protocol. The SSH2 protocol offers a number of advantages over the SSH1 protocol including standards compliance (SSH2 is on the IETF standards track[1]), improved security and operation without RSA (which is patented in some countries). The SSH2 support in OpenSSH has been developed by Markus Friedl, with support from the OpenBSD team. This is also the first version of the portable version of OpenSSH to offer built-in entropy collection. This removes the requirement for EGD on systems that lack a /dev/random driver. As a result, OpenSSH-2.1.0 now requires a recent version of OpenSSL[2] to compile (version 0.9.5 or later). NB. The portable version of OpenSSH is currently in the process of merging its webpages with the official OpenBSD project. Please use http://www.openssh.com/ from now on. Distribution files are also available from the mirrors listed at http://violet.ibs.com.au/openssh/files/MIRRORS.html Please read http://www.openssh.com/report.html before reporting bugs. Patches, bug reports, developer and user queries are welcome on the mailing list ( http://www.openssh.com/list.html) . Regards, Damien Miller [1] http://www.ietf.org/html.charters/secsh-charter.html [2] http://www.openssl.org/ OpenSSH 1.2.3p1 (2000-03-24) The Unix/Linux port of OpenSSH 1.2.3 was released yesterday and should be available from a mirror near you. title: The Lisp curse, now coming to your ecosystem
body_text: The LISP curse, now coming to your ecosystem! - Tim ZÃ¶ller Tim ZÃ¶ller Menu Home About Talks & Sessions Blog (EN) Blog (DE) Book me! The LISP curse, now coming to your ecosystem! Posted by Tim ZÃ¶ller on March 05, 2026 · 4 mins read The LISP curse is often quoted as the reason why so few libraries and reusable components exist for LISP dialects. According to the concept, LISP is so powerful and flexible that it allows developers to create custom solutions easily, leading to them working longer in isolation. This causes them to often reinvent the wheel, because creating code to solve your own problems can be easier / faster than relying on the libraries (and way of thinking) of other people. This leads to a lack of central frameworks and libraries, like many other language ecosystems have. Sometimes itâs also mentioned that this powerful, flexible code which was written in isolation often lacks documentation and can be hard to comprehend by third parties, so other developers prefer to write their own modules â and the curse keeps on. Yes, this post is about LLM-assisted coding I was drawn into several discussions this week where people claimed that with the ease and quality of Large Language Models, it is now easier and cheaper to generate code than to use existing abstractions like frameworks or libraries. If we ignore the fact that established libraries are incredibly stable, tested by hundreds of thousands of developers, included in thousands of CI pipelines and maintained by experts on the topic, if we accept the assumption that it is easier to let an LLM generate functionality than to learn the interfaces of existing libraries and frameworks (or let the LLM integrate these libraries or frameworks), what would the implications for language ecosystems like Javaâs look like? More isolation, more individualism, less collaboration A lot of people contributed to the success of Open Source ecosystems in the last decades through collaboration, collective problem solving and with the goal of solving hard problems. The first effect of the aforementioned scenario would be the decline of people using the open source libraries, reducing feedback to the maintainers. If I could just solve my problems with one or two prompts, 20 minutes of waiting time and a couple of dollars worth of tokens, why should I bother with research? Why should I bother with the API decisions other people made? Why should I bother with reading documentation? As a second effect, the creation of new Open Source libraries would stagnate. The hard part of doing Open Source is maintenance. Structuring your code, hosting infrastructure, publishing to artifact repositories. Versioning, backwards compatibility, keeping the stack up to date. If generating code is that easy, if I can solve my own problems that quickly, why should I bother modularizing the code, sharing it with the world and doing all the project management an Open Source project needs? I have everything I need in my generated module, I can break the API if I need to, adjust everything exactly to my use case, my stack. These two effects might even amplify each other in the long term. If fewer Open Source libraries are provided to integrate new technologies, new approaches into a language ecosystem, people might be even more inclined to just write / generate their own solution and be done with it. A grim outlook As you might have already read between the lines, I donât share the assumption that we can skip adding libraries and frameworks to our code and just generate everything instead. Iâd rather rely on proven libraries with well-defined abstractions than generate hundreds of lines of code which solve a local problem for me. âNot generated hereâ is just a different version of âNot invented hereâ. Still, I think that Large Language Models in coding are here to stay, and that this scenario will arrive in some way. Maybe not as drastically as some thought leaders now proclaim, but by accident. Open Source collaboration will decline to some degree and software development might become a much lonelier task than it is now. ← Previous Post Next Post → Email Mastodon GitHub Twitch LinkedIn RSS Feed (EN) RSS Feed (DE) Copyright © 2026

Awesome repositories are no longer awesome
body_text: Awesome repositories are no longer awesome Erik Gahner Larsen ← Back Awesome repositories are no longer awesome Nov 5, 2026 On GitHub, you will find a lot of repositories with the prefix 'awesome'. They usually contain curated knowledge and resources related to a certain domain, such as awesome-python (see, e.g., this repository for a list of awesome repositories). I used to see these awesome repositories as potential goldmines of good content. However, nowadays I see most of them as irrelevant and useless. There are two reasons for this, and they are both related to AI. First, as many of these awesome lists get older, they contain a lot of outdated material if they are not actively maintained. You are in most cases better off simply asking a decent AI model for inspiration or the material you need. That is, I find it difficult to believe that most of these awesome lists are of interest to people anymore. If they remain useful, it will mostly be for agents looking to find and check relevant resources. I had a quick look at the awesome-R repository. The repository was last updated more than a year ago, and most of the resources included in the overview are either outdated or will not be of general interest to people using R. One of the first links in the repository is an overview of the top 50 downloaded packages - as of 2016! This is simply not a good resource if you want to explore R in any shape or form. Second, a lot of these awesome repositories are being flooded with AI slop. Go to any random awesome repository these days and you will most likely find a lot of pull requests suggesting the most generic tools and resources. For example, take a look at this awesome-free-online-tools repository. It is a small, unknown repository with 13 stars but 91 open pull requests at the time of writing. I did not look at all of these pull requests, but the ones I looked at all suggested generic vibe-coded tools. I found this resource because of a pull request made to one of my repositories, a simple project where I store material I like related to statistics. The suggestion was to add StatOrigin ("a free, open database of industry statistics"), and once I had a quick look at the resource and the other pull requests made by the user, I could easily close the PR. This user alone has created at least six vibe-coded websites (StatOrigin, ScanChess, Sticker Printer Hub, QuizQuip, LiquidityPools, DefiLPKit) and submitted more than 100 pull requests to various awesome lists to add these websites. It did not take me long to find examples where these tools were merged into the relevant repositories (see, e.g., here , here , and here ). However, I also found examples where people did the basic work of checking out the material, such as here , where the PR was closed with the following explanation: "There is not yet sufficient evidence of qualified educator review, independent validation of the educational content, or demonstrated learning outcomes." Good stuff! My point is not that these awesome repositories are now all bad. They can still be awesome. But as a general approach to finding good resources, awesome lists are less awesome than they used to be. As AI gets better at finding and creating resources (and creating pull requests for said resources), these awesome repositories will become less relevant and less useful. CREATE AN ACCOUNT SIGN IN Computing News The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt Dina Genkina 02 Nov 2026 4 min read Dina Genkina is the computing and hardware editor at IEEE Spectrum iStock In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA , Wikipedia , the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server. As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI. “One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.” PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed. “If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University . “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately. Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.” AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible. “There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.” This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever. One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models . “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.” Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.” Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them. Matthew Green , an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.” In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.” One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.” From Your Site Articles Your AI Agent Is Now a Target for Email Phishing › With $1 Cyberattacks on the Rise, Durable Defenses Pay Off › What Anthropic’s Mythos Means for the Future of Cybersecurity › Related Articles Around the Web The PHP Foundation — The PHP Foundation — Supporting, Advancing, and Developing the PHP Language › cybersecurity internet artificial intelligence Dina Genkina Dina Genkina is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum focused on computing and hardware. title: Spreading Liquid with Three.js
body_text: Spreading Liquid with three.js | mofu Spreading Liquid with three.js 11/1/2026 ENGLISH / 日本語 Introduction At Vue Fes Japan 2026, I talked about implementing a liquid foundation effect. In this article, I'll continue from my previous fluid simulation article and explain how I created that effect. I developed this liquid-spreading effect for a Japanese cosmetics brand's liquid foundation promotional project released in 2021. ちょっと前なんですが今年6月にprimavisaシリーズのファンデーション・下地のテクスチャをシミュレーションできるサイトが公開されました。 homunculusさんにお声かけいただいて実装担当しました。 いろんな種類とカラバリをお試しできるのでぜひ見てみてください。 https://t.co/RiK5wff7S9 https://t.co/dyNJNoizSY — Misaki Nakano (@misaki_mofujp) December 18, 2021 Liquid Spreading Demo I chose blue rather than a foundation shade for this demo, even though the original project was about makeup. Try dragging your mouse or finger across the liquid below. Reset Where I Started When I was asked to implement a foundation simulation in January 2021, I had no idea where to begin. I spent about a month repeatedly touching foundation and thinking about what makes it look and behave like foundation, or more generally, like a liquid. I had already thought of using a height map to represent a physical quantity, but I wasn't sure how to move that height around. I wondered if there was a simpler approach. In the end, I decided that a fluid algorithm was probably the best solution. When you drag a finger through liquid, it bulges up on the opposite side, and the surrounding material gets pulled along. To reproduce those movements, I started by implementing a fluid simulation. How It Works First, Some Background This effect uses the results of the fluid simulation I introduced in an earlier article on this blog. It uses the same velocity map to create the liquid-spreading movement. Stable Fluids with three.js mofu-dev.com The raised liquid in the opening demo is rendered in a fragment shader, rather than by deforming the geometry. I prepare another FBO, which I call a height map, to represent the thickness of the liquid. What Is a Height Map? Height maps are often used for terrain, but here I use one to represent liquid thickness. The diagram below illustrates a height map recording the thickness of a liquid. The height value at each position represents how much liquid is present there. Implementation Flow The fluid simulation itself is explained in my previous article, so here I'll focus on updating thickness and opacity, and rendering the result. Use the velocity map to find the source UV and update the thickness. Update opacity in an alpha map using the current height map and the history of where liquid has been applied. Calculate normals from the height map, then render with a Matcap and the alpha map. 1. Moving Thickness with the Velocity Map First, I prepare the initial values for the height map. I create a hemispherical blob, raised at the center, using a fragment shader and store its height in the height map's R channel. initialHeight.frag float calculateHeight ( float value) { return sqrt (( 1.0 - value * value) / 12.0 ); } void main () { vec2 point = (vUv - 0.5 ) * 2.0 * resolution / min (resolution.x, resolution.y); float distanceFromCenter = length (point); float height = calculateHeight ( smoothstep ( 0.0 , 0.3 , distanceFromCenter)); height = smoothstep ( 0.0 , 0.025 , height) * height * 0.66 ; gl_FragColor = vec4 (height, 0.0 , 0.0 , 1.0 ); } I render these initial values into an FBO, then update the thickness using the velocity map. The velocity map produced by the fluid simulation records the direction and magnitude of movement at each position on the screen. First, I sample the thickness and velocity at the current pixel. According to its velocity, I calculate how much thickness should move away and subtract that amount from the original thickness. height.frag float previousHeight = texture2D (heightMap, vUv).r; vec2 flow = texture2D (velocity, vUv).xy; float previousStrength = smoothstep ( velocityThreshold.x, velocityThreshold.y, length (flow) ); float removed = min ( previousHeight, previousStrength * 0.3 * previousHeight ); removed is the amount of thickness subtracted from the current pixel. Next, I use advection , which also appeared in the previous fluid simulation article. I trace the velocity backward from the current pixel and sample the thickness at the source position. Here is the implementation of backtraceUv() , which calculates the source UV from the current UV, velocity, and elapsed time. height.frag vec2 backtraceUv (vec2 uv, vec2 flow, vec2 fboSize, float dt) { vec2 ratio = max (fboSize.x, fboSize.y) / fboSize; vec2 velocityRatio = fboSize / min (fboSize.x, fboSize.y); return uv - flow * velocityRatio * dt * ratio; } height.frag vec2 sourceUv = backtraceUv (vUv, flow, fboSize, dt); float sourceHeight = texture2D (heightMap, sourceUv).r; float sourceStrength = smoothstep ( velocityThreshold.x, velocityThreshold.y, length ( texture2D (velocity, sourceUv).xy) ); float added = min ( sourceHeight, sourceStrength * 0.3 * sourceHeight ); vUv is the current pixel's position. sourceUv is the position found by tracing the velocity backward. The backtraceUv() function uses velocity and the time step dt to calculate that position. added is the thickness brought from the source position to the current pixel. Finally, I subtract removed from the current thickness and add added to update the height map. height.frag float nextHeight = max ( 0.0 , previousHeight - removed + added); gl_FragColor = vec4 (nextHeight, 0.0 , 0.0 , 1.0 ); The result is written to the R channel of gl_FragColor . The G and B channels are 0, and the A channel is 1. The alpha map and rendering shaders later read this value using texture2D(heightMap, vUv).r . In this way, each pixel loses some thickness and gains thickness from its backtraced source position. I also use smoothstep() so that the thickness barely moves when velocity is small. This prevents stationary areas from constantly flowing and focuses movement around the areas affected by dragging. This is not a physically accurate, volume-conserving calculation. I adjusted it to achieve the appearance I wanted. Each frame, I sample the previous height map, render the result into the next one, and alternate between two FBOs. 2. Keeping the Traces with an Alpha Map A height map represents the raised shape of the liquid, but it doesn't fully reproduce the traces left when the liquid is spread thinly. I wanted some color to remain even where the thickness had almost disappeared, so I added a separate alpha map. This alpha map uses both a value derived from the current thickness and the maximum value recorded so far. alpha.frag float previousMaximum = texture2D (alphaMap, vUv).r; float current = smoothstep ( 0.0 , 0.01 / 0.7 , max ( 0.0 , texture2D (heightMap, vUv).r) ); float maximum = max (current, previousMaximum); gl_FragColor = vec4 ( maximum, maximum * 0.5 + current * 0.5 , 0.0 , 0.0 ); current is calculated from the current frame's height map. maximum keeps whichever is larger: the current value or the previous maximum. This records where the liquid has passed. The R channel stores the historical maximum, while the G channel stores an equal blend of that maximum and the current value. The B channel is unused. The final rendering pass samples the G channel. As a result, opacity doesn't immediately fall to zero when the liquid moves away and the thickness decreases. Some color remains where the liquid has passed, making it appear to adhere to the surface. This isn't a physical model of drying or absorption. It is simply a history used to preserve the traces of the liquid . 3. Calculating Normals from the Height Map Finally, I use the height map to add highlights to the liquid's surface. This demo doesn't move actual geometry vertices to form the liquid's bumps and ridges. Instead, I calculate surface normals from the height map inside the fragment shader. For each pixel, I sample its height and the heights of its immediate neighbors in the X and Y directions. These three points form two vectors, whose cross product gives the surface normal. render.frag float height = texture2D (heightMap, vUv).r; vec2 stepSize = 1.0 / resolution; vec2 uvX = vUv + vec2 (stepSize.x, 0.0 ); vec2 uvY = vUv + vec2 ( 0.0 , stepSize.y); float heightScale = 0.2 / 0.66 ; vec2 ratio = resolution / min (resolution.x, resolution.y); vec3 position = vec3 ( (vUv * ratio).x, height * heightScale, (vUv * ratio).y ); vec3 positionX = vec3 ( (uvX * ratio).x, texture2D (heightMap, uvX).r * heightScale, (uvX * ratio).y ); vec3 positionY = vec3 ( (uvY * ratio).x, texture2D (heightMap, uvY).r * heightScale, (uvY * ratio).y ); vec3 normal = - normalize ( cross (positionX - position, positionY - position) ); The normal has a different direction on flat areas and steeply raised areas. This difference lets me render shading and highlights that make the flat surface appear to have raised liquid on it. I use a Matcap texture for the color and highlights. I convert the normal into Matcap UV coordinates, sample its color, and combine it with opacity from the alpha map. render.frag vec3 color = texture2D ( matcap, normal.zx * 0.5 + 0.5 ).rgb + 0.05 ; float alphaValue = texture2D (alphaMap, vUv).g; gl_FragColor = vec4 ( color, step ( 0.1 , alphaValue) * alphaValue ); The actual shader also adjusts the color based on the tilt of the normal. The height map controls the surface shape, the Matcap controls the appearance, and the alpha map determines how the liquid's traces remain on the surface. This Is Not a Physically Accurate Fluid Simulation The thickness calculation described above is not physically accurate. Fragment shaders process pixels in parallel, so a pixel cannot directly write its thickness into another pixel at the destination indicated by its velocity. Instead, each destination pixel traces the velocity backward and samples the height map at the source position. However, multiple pixels can sample approximately the same source region. Because thickness isn't distributed precisely among destinations, the total amounts removed and added don't always match. Therefore, the total liquid volume isn't conserved. As shown above, the thickness remains relatively stable with straight movements. When drawing circles, however, the sampling bias accumulates and the amount of liquid keeps increasing. This method prioritizes visual appearance rather than accurately conserving the amount of liquid. Bonus: Texture Precision I also noticed something interesting during development. The demo below shows grayscale lighting calculated from height-map normals. Use the toggle to switch between 8-bit and 32-bit float textures. Reset 8 bit 32 bit float A 32-bit floating-point texture can store height values with finer precision, producing smoother contours and shading. An 8-bit texture, on the other hand, stores only 256 levels per channel. This quantizes the height map and produces visible steps in the normals and shading. I found it interesting that the limitations of 8-bit precision, which I usually associate with color gradients, showed up here as visible steps in the shading. Bonus: Mixing Three Colored Liquids I also tried another experiment for fun. I prepared three hemispherical blobs like the one in the first demo and gave each a different color. You can drag your mouse or finger to spread the liquids and mix their colors. Reset Each liquid has its own height map and alpha history, while all three share the same velocity map. Thickness and opacity are updated using the same calculations as in the first demo. Finally, I mix the colors according to each liquid's thickness using a simplified Kubelka–Munk model, and calculate surface normals from their combined height. Where the thickness is almost zero, I use the remaining alpha history of each color to determine the mixing ratios. A Final Note I decided to write about this implementation now because I don't think I'll have many opportunities to use this method again, and because I wanted to document the method I worked out myself before AI becomes even more capable. Over the past year alone, I feel AI has become much better at understanding coordinates and space, and at connecting the visuals I want to create with the calculations and implementation needed to achieve them. Publishing this may mean the method is no longer something special. Even so, I thought I could leave a trace of what I was thinking and how I arrived at this visual effect. Table of Contents Introduction Liquid Spreading Demo Where I Started How It Works mofu BLOG ABOUT

title: Nasdaq plummets 4% into correction territory
body_text: Stock market news for Nov. 5, 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Daily Stock Market Live Updated Thu, Nov 5 2026 4:18 PM EST Share Share Article via Facebook Share Article via Twitter Share Article via LinkedIn Share Article via Email Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates Sean Conlon Davis Giangiulio Hugh Leask Lee Ying Shan Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026. Jeenah Moon | Reuters Stocks plummeted on Thursday, erasing the sharp gains from the rally seen in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections , as investors accelerated their move away from technology stocks on fears of a data-center buildout slowdown. The Nasdaq Composite declined 5.52% to close at 24,315.00. The tech-heavy index slid into correction territory, falling more than 10% below a record set last month. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to end at 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and settled at 51,523.06. The Dow more than wiped out its advance from Wednesday's massive postelection rally. All three major averages posted their worst day since April 2025. The small-cap Russell 2000 index decreased 4.45% and also entered a correction. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Nasdaq Composite, 5-day Stocks related to the artificial intelligence trade, particularly those linked to the chips industry and data centers, slid for a second day. Investors fear that a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress as well as victories in key gubernatorial races could decelerate the data center buildout . For instance, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont — who caucuses with Democrats — has called for a national data center moratorium. In a post on X Wednesday evening, Sanders wrote that "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." Chipmakers Broadcom and Nvidia respectively fell 10% and 9% Thursday, while software stock Oracle moved lower by almost 7%. Another chip stock, Qualcomm , reported earnings that beat estimates , but the stock dropped 9% on a weaker-than-expected earnings outlook. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down more than 12% for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020. Shares of neocloud companies also retreated, with CoreWeave losing almost 10%. Nebius and Iren slid about 15% and almost 17%, amid worries about a backlash to the industry in light of the election results in various states. Investors are "stepping away until they get a better sense of the implications of the midterms around the AI capex cycle in particular, which is the biggest economic tailwind we've had going for us for the last, call it, three years," said Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion. "It's about tone and tenor from the party that did really well, incredibly well, at the federal level and at the state level." Thursday's selling pressure was so intense that it spread to other parts of the market. Shares of industrial giant Caterpillar declined 6%, while financial stock JPMorgan fell 4%. Aerospace name Boeing and athletic apparel giant Nike pulled back 2%. "Unlike yesterday, you're just seeing that the sell-off in tech, the size of it, is now feeding itself into the broader market," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Wealth. "The rubber band is becoming increasingly stretched." On Wednesday, the Dow jumped more than 1,500 points to notch its best day since April 2025 after a decisive midterm win for Democrats. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also popped more than 1% each. Areas related to AI were under pressure, however, while economically-sensitive stocks rose. 6 Hours Ago Stocks plummet on Thursday The Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images U.S. equities sold off significantly during Thursday's session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to settle at 51,523.06. The S&P 500 shed 4.36% to 7,353.73, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.52% to 24,315.00. — Sean Conlon 6 Hours Ago Mag7 was losing close to $900 billion in aggregate market value heading into final hour Magnificent 7 tech stocks on display at the Nasdaq. Adam Jeffery | CNBC The Mag7 stocks were losing close to an aggregate $900 billion heading into the final hour of trading Thursday. Nvidia alone was worth some $374 billion less than at Wednesday's close; Tesla was down $161 billion; and Microsoft $117 billion. Apple shed nearly $59 billion in market value, Meta Platforms almost $58 billion, Amazon was lower by about $55 billion and Alphabet by more than $42 billion. — Scott Schnipper and Nick Wells 6 Hours Ago Loop downgrades Dollar Tree, says buy Ollie’s instead Loop Capital downgraded Dollar Tree to Hold from Buy on Thursday, maintaining its $140 price target after shares rallied more than 20% since early October. “We believe our bullish fundamental outlook on Dollar Tree is largely priced in at current levels,” Loop Capital’s analyst Anthony Chukumba said. The downgrade reflects valuation concerns rather than weakening fundamentals. Chukumba said Ollie's Bargain Outlet ("Ollie's") provides a more compelling long opportunity for investors seeking exposure to the deep discount retailing space heading into the fast-approaching holiday selling season. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Dollar Tree and Ollie's price chart The analyst said high gas prices and tighter household budgets will push more shoppers toward Dollar Tree ahead of the holidays. The retailer’s growing range of products at different prices also continues to lift sales at existing stores. “All that said,” Chukumba said, “with Dollar Tree stock trading above its historical average next fiscal year P/E multiple, we believe upside potential and downside risk are fairly balanced at current levels.” — Deena Zaidi 7 Hours Ago Truist Securities downgrades Nike Thursday Nike stock caught a downgrade from Truist Securities Thursday. The firm re-rated the sportswear retailer lower to hold from sell while keeping its $29 price target. Analyst Joseph Civello said the stock's gain over the past month is due to "positive sector rotations rather than an improvement in underlying fundamentals." Over that period, shares have risen 16%. The rise has resulted in a stretched stock valuation that "prices in an overly optimistic turnaround," the analyst wrote. Analysts also called out pressures across Nike's portfolio including weak product launches and a deteriorating outlook in its key China market. Truist lowered its full year 2028 earnings per share estimate to $1.30, below the Wall Street consensus of $1.50 and the firm's prior estimate of $1.40, the firm said. Nike shares are down 38% year-to-date, however. — Paulina Likos 7 Hours Ago Wall Street is positive on Arm Holdings Rene Haas, CEO of chip tech provider Arm Holdings, holds a replica of a chip with his company's logo on it on March 5, 2025. Hasnoor Hussain | Reuters Several investment banks are positive on chip designer Arm Holdings on Thursday after the company reported strong licensing and weak royalties in its latest beat-and-raise quarter. "Licensing is a leading indicator of future Royalties (12-24 months) [and] suggests continued strong customer interest in custom silicon solutions," Vivek Arya at Bank of America said in a Thursday note. He cautioned that "Arm's increasing dependence on SoftBank for Licensing revenue could pose circular financing concerns." — Tobias Burns 7 Hours Ago Things have to get a lot worse before NYSE circuit breakers kick in As bad as Thursday's stock market washout is, conditions have to get a lot worse before the New York Stock Exchange circuit breakers would kick in and pause trading. At the Thursday low, the S&P bottomed out with a loss of 4.23% before recovering somewhat. Level 1 and Level 2 Market-Wide Circuit Breakers that halt trading for a minimum of 15 minutes only come into effect between 9:30 am ET and 3:25 pm ET if the S&P 500 drops by 7% or more (Level 1) and 13% (Level 2). A Level 3 decline of 20% or more can come into effect at any time and halts trading for the rest of the day. When were the circuit breakers last used? Four times in March 2020 , twice before the major Covid lockdowns began to be put in to place on March 15, and twice after. The only other time that the circuit breakers, first introduced in the aftermath of the 1987 stock market crash, were used was once in October, 1997 during the Asian financial crisis. — Scott Schnipper 7 Hours Ago Wells Fargo raises outlook for McDonald’s People enter a McDonald's restaurant in Times Square, Manhattan, on Sept. 29, 2026, in New York City. KHemaz | GVN | Getty Images McDonald's jumped more than 6% on Wednesday after reporting better-than-expected earnings . Wells Fargo liked the numbers too. The bank reiterated its overweight rating on the fast food company's stock in a Wednesday note, and raised its price target to $300. That indicates a 7% gain from Wednesday's close. Analyst Zachary Fadem said the company's financial report showed numbers that were encouraging. "Q3 cleared a low bar, shares were washed out & MCD cited notable progress on value w/ new steps in '27," he wrote in the note. "Skepticism likely persists… but [Wednesday's] print is a step in the right direction." In afternoon trading Thursday, shares were pulling back by more than 1%. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon McDonald's 5-day. — Davis Giangiulio 8 Hours Ago Tech sell-off drags Nasdaq Composite below its 200-day moving average Market information at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 5% on Thursday afternoon, sending the index below its 200-day moving average for the first time since April. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Nasdaq Composite in the past day The S&P 500 is also near its 200-day moving average, trading less than 1% from that level. If the broad market index were to slip below that threshold, that would mark its first time doing so since April. Big tech players dipping below their respective 200-day moving averages include Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Marvell Technology, Micron Technology, Sandisk and Cisco. The sell-off in the tech sector comes as a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections is now raising fears that the data center build-out could be in for a slowdown. When an asset or an index trades below its 200-day moving average, it suggests that a longer-term downtrend may be unfolding. This is especially the case if it closes below the 200-day moving average. — Darla Mercado and Nick Wells 8 Hours Ago All S&P 500 sectors suffer losses All 11 S&P 500 sectors were trading in negative territory on Thursday afternoon as selling across the U.S. equity market picked up steam. Information technology was the biggest laggard, dropping 6.6%. The group's declines were then followed by a fall in consumer discretionary stocks as well as industrials. Those two sectors were down 4.1% and 4%, respectively. Most stocks in the broad market index were also trading lower, as the S&P 500 recorded 419 losers and 84 gainers. The index was last down 3.9%. — Sean Conlon 8 Hours Ago Wall Street’s fear gauge jumps to highest level since March The Cboe Volatility Index briefly climbed to 28.09 Thursday, its highest level since March 31, when it touched 29.64. Currently, the VIX is at 26.26. The VIX, which measures expected stock-market volatility and is often called Wall Street's "fear gauge," last traded above 30 on March 30, when it reached 31.52. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon VIX — Deena Zaidi and Gina Francolla 9 Hours Ago Chip stocks plunge for worst day since March 2020 Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 2, 2026. NYSE Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF falling close to 11%. A closing decline greater than 10.44% marks its worst day since March 2020 with every component down more than 6%. After a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress , which could spell more regulation of the AI buildout, stocks tied to the AI trade, particularly those linked to the chips industry and data centers slid for a second day. Astera Labs and MACOM Technology Solutions fell roughly 17% and 18%, respectively. AMD and Micron dropped 15% each, while Arm slid about 12%. The SOXX was down 15% for the week. — Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells 9 Hours Ago Stock market wipeout is lessening pressure on the Fed to hike rates in December The equity market sell-off is easing pressure on the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates at its last meeting of the year, on Dec. 9. Odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates a quarter percentage point from their current 3.75%-4.00% range have fallen to 70.1%, down from 82.7% on Wednesday and 79.9% a week ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool , which is based on 30-day fed funds futures prices. Conversely, the chance that the Kevin Warsh-led central bank will be able to keep rates where they are in December stands at 29.9% at midday Thursday, up from 17.3% on Wednesday and 20.1% a week ago — Scott Schnipper 9 Hours Ago Global Payments trades higher despite lack of an immediate buyout Piotr Swat | Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty Images Global Payments didn't use its third-quarter earnings report to confirm speculation that the company is working out a deal to go private , but it did show that it is continuing to integrate its Worldpay acquisition, which CNBC expects will support its stock in the future . Shares are trading higher despite the broader market pullback. The payments company earned $3.58 per share after adjustments, in line with the FactSet consensus estimate and an increase of 10% year-on-year. It reaffirmed its full year 2026 outlook. Adjusted operating margin rose 220 basis points to 42.5%, powered by the successful capture of operational efficiencies and synergies from the Worldpay integration. The company now expects Worldpay synergies of $650 million, up from $600 million previously, by the end of 2028. Global Payments all-in-one Genius point-of-sale and business management platform saw strong growth in the quarter with bookings more than doubling year-on-year. Performance in the Middle East continues to be hurt by the war, but was "generally in line with our expectations," CFO Josh Whipple said on the earnings call. He categorized the recovery as "very uneven and inconsistent." Management declined to comment on reported buyout talks with Clayton Dubilier & Rice and shareholder GTCR, saying it doesn't "comment on market rumors or speculation." On the call, CEO Cameron Bready said he is "not really going to be able to get into the reporting or any of the specifics around it." — Justin Zacks 10 Hours Ago AI declines are just getting started, Macro Research Board warns Declines for the super intelligence, or artificial intelligence, trade still have a long way to go, investment strategists at the Macro Research Board are warning on Thursday. "The shakeout in A.I.-related stocks has much further to run," the firm said in a Thursday note. Researchers said that "investors are beginning to question excessive forward profit estimates." They recommend diversifying away from tech stocks amid general sensitivities in equities. "In this environment, our bet has been a churn in the aggregate U.S. and global stocks indexes (at least for now), but with a meaningful rotation underneath the surface (including divergences in the absolute price of stocks/sectors)," they said, adding that monetary and fiscal policy are not currently restrictive. — Tobias Burns 11 Hours Ago Tech stocks are selling off hard, entering vicious correction The Micron Technology offices in San Jose, California, Dec. 16, 2025. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Tech stocks are getting pummeled on Thursday. Chip stocks central to the AI trade in particular are getting walloped. Micron and AMD are down 16% and GPU powerhouse Nvidia is down 8%. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon MU, 1-day — Tobias Burns 11 Hours Ago Analysts are meh on Qualcomm after weak earnings forecast Thomas Fuller | Lightrocket | Getty Images Wall Street is measured on the outlook for Qualcomm after the company delivered a weak earnings forecast on Wednesday. Analyst Stacey Rasgon at Bernstein has a market-perform rating on the stock and a price target of $155; Joseph Moore at Morgan Stanley has an equal-weight rating and a price target of $197. Customer diversification is the buzzword on the Street for Qualcomm, as mentioned in multiple research notes. "The debate has shifted to diversification: ambitious data center targets of $5B in FY27 and $15B+ in FY29, and continued strength in autos," Morgan Stanley's Moore said on Thursday. — Tobias Burns 12 Hours Ago Gold and silver extend post-election rally, head for best week since August Gold and silver bars of various sizes at the precious metals dealer Pro Aurum in Munich. Sven Hoppe | Picture Alliance | Getty Images Gold and silver futures climbed Thursday as a weaker U.S. dollar and lower Treasury yields supported a rally following the U.S. midterm elections. Falling oil prices eased inflation concerns. December gold futures touched $4,155.80 an ounce, their highest since October 22, while December silver reached $53.49, its highest since October 29. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Gold stock price The yellow metal is up more than 5% this week as silver has gained more than 6%. Gold was on pace for its strongest weekly advance since the week ended Aug. 7, while silver was heading for its best week since Aug. 21. Gold miners joined the rally, with the VanEck Gold Miners ETF up about 1% on Thursday and more than 10% this week. Harmony Gold and IAMGOLD are among the leaders, each gaining more than 13% this week. Equinox Gold has risen more than 15% on the week. — Deena Zaidi and Gina Francolla 12 Hours Ago Nasdaq dips into correction territory The Nasdaq Composite tumbled into correction territory on Thursday, trading 10% below a record close set last month. The benchmark was down 3.9% on the day as chipmakers sold off. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Nasdaq Composite dips into correction — Fred Imbert 12 Hours Ago VIX moves above 22 The CBOE Volatility Index rose on Thursday as equity sell-off picked up steam, with Wall Street's so-called fear gauge last up 22.59. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon .VIX, 1-day — Sean Conlon 12 Hours Ago Dow opens higher The Dow Jones Industrial Average began Thursday's session in the green. The blue-chip Dow added 334 points, or 0.6%, just after the opening bell. The S&P 500 dipped 0.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7%. — Sean Conlon 13 Hours Ago Jobless claims drop again as layoffs near lowest since 1969 Jobseekers wait to speak with recruiters during the Catalyst Career Group Dallas Job Fair in Dallas, Texas, US, on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Dylan Hollingsworth | Bloomberg | Getty Images Jobless claims slipped further last week, hovering around levels not seen since the late 1960s, the Labor Department reported Thursday. Initial filings for unemployment claims totaled a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended Oct. 31, down 6,000 from the prior period and below the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 197,000. The total tied for the lowest since July, which was the bottom going back to September 1969. Continuing claims, which run a week behind, rose 23,000 to 1.72 million. — Jeff Cox 13 Hours Ago Productivity spikes, labor costs slide Productivity posted a stronger-than-expected jump in the third quarter while the portion of output that showed up in worker pay hit a record low, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday. Nonfarm business sector productivity surged 3.6% for the period, up from 2.1% in the second quarter and well ahead of the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 2.9%. Compensation less productivity, a metric known as unit labor costs, contracted 0.7%. At the the same, the percentage of output that goes to workers in the form of compensation, known as the labor share, slipped further to 53%, the lowest in a data series that dates back to 1947. — Jeff Cox 14 Hours Ago Shake Shack, Peloton and Wendy's among the stocks making the biggest moves premarket Check out the companies making headlines before the bell: Shake Shack — Shares rose 3.8% after the fast-food chain published its third-quarter results. Adjusted earnings per share of 40 cents topped an LSEG estimate of 35 cents per share. Revenue of $423 million was just below the $426 million consensus. Management also reaffirmed the company's full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $1.6 billion to $1.7 billion. Peloton Interactive — The maker of fitness equipment jumped 7% after Peloton Interactive posted fiscal first-quarter revenue of $559 million, besting the LSEG consensus estimate of $554 million. However, earnings of 19 cents per share missed the 21 cents expected. Wendy's — Shares were little changed after the fast food chain rejected a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a Trian Fund Management-led group. The group late last month offered $7.35 per share in cash to take Wendy's private. Read the full list here . — Sarah Min 14 Hours Ago Why Trump's reaction to Democratic victory in the midterms aided Wednesday’s rally US President Donald Trump speaks at the White House ballroom construction site in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty Images The stock market skyrocketed on Wednesday on the heels of a decisive sweep for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections . But that was not necessarily the only driver of the climb. "President Trump's acknowledgement of the Democrats' victory in the midterms and his expressed openness to collaborating with the opposition have helped markets to rally on hopes that contestation of the results and more adverse polarization can be avoided," said Thomas Hempell, Generali Investments senior economist. Trump told The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal overnight Tuesday that he accepted the results and would work with Democrats. Those headlines coincided with a rebound in stock market futures. Read the full story here . — Sean Conlon 15 Hours Ago Wendy's rejects Trian takeover bid Wendy's shares were down slightly after the fast food chain on Thursday rejected a a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a Trian Fund Management-led group. The group late last month offered $7.35 per share in cash to take Wendy's private. — Fred Imbert 16 Hours Ago The midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade The U.S. midterms could widen the AI divide: tighter data center rules may reward tech giants with capacity in hand and squeeze debt-funded companies trying to catch up. Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races raised the prospect of tougher scrutiny for data center projects, adding to investor concerns about how quickly new capacity can be built and financed. How the midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade 16 Hours Ago OpenAI pledges to pay for data center power after election highlights AI concerns Sam Altman, chief executive officer and co-founder of OpenAI Inc., speaks during a Bloomberg Television interview at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty Images OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI. OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke 18 Hours Ago U.K.'s FTSE 100 hits three-month high The FTSE 100 touched a three-month high on Thursday morning. The U.K.'s blue-chip index rose as much as 119 points to 10,948, up more than 1.1% in early trading and reaching its highest level since Aug 7. The index was last seen 0.86% higher. The rise comes as traders await the Bank of England's latest interest rate decision, due later Thursday. The market expects the central bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee to raise rates by 25 basis points to 4% from 3.75% — its first hike in more than three years. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon FTSE 100. Shares in British lenders moved higher ahead of the BoE's decision, due at 12:00 p.m. in London (7:00 a.m. E.T.). title: Lemmings CSS Animation
body_text: Walker Playground Star Fork Walker playground Add walkers with the button below or __walker.add() . Drag one to carry it, flick it to throw it. Resize the window and walkers ride the surface they're standing on, so a fast resize launches them. Add a walker Stairs Stairs too tall to climb Floating platforms Pit Walls Cards These wrap onto new rows as the window narrows, which shoves anyone standing on them. Card one Borders are solid. Walk the top edge or get trapped inside. Button Card two Buttons and form fields are solid too. Card three Text is a floor you can land on but walk through. Card four Throw a walker up here. Another Cage Reading Columns of text reflow a lot when the window changes size, so this is a good place to try a resize launch. Each line of text is its own floor. Walkers can drop from line to line, fall off the end of a short line, and land on whatever is below. Lines sit closer together than a walker is tall, so text never blocks them. Only borders, boxes, buttons, images and fields do. That keeps walkers from getting stuck between two lines of a paragraph. Near the bottom of the page there is one long floor to catch anything that falls all the way down.

Uses the official v11 release , with Kimi K3 as judge. K3.1 Pro uses Kimi Code; GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 use Claude Code; GPT-6 Astra uses Codex. Claude scores are from official system cards. Agents' Last Exam. Uses the official v1.1 release , comprising 122 tasks, including 86 CLI tasks. Runs that bypass stated requirements receive zero. DeepSeek and Kimi are evaluated with Claude Code and Kimi Code, respectively; other results are from the official benchmark website. OfficeQA Pro and OfficeQA Pro v2. GPT-6 Astra uses Codex; other models use Claude Code. Each task provides the complete PDF corpus as page images without machine-readable text. External-model trajectories that retrieve reference answers online receive zero for those tasks. Frontier Finance. Evaluated with the official Finance Agent v2 harness. HANDBOOK.md. Evaluated with the official OpenHands-based harness, using tasks from the benchmark's early open-source v1 release. Harvey Legal Agent. Evaluated on 1,251 public tasks with Artificial Analysis's Stirrup harness. The reported score is the all-pass rate: the percentage of tasks passing every rubric criterion. OSWorld V2.1. Kimi models use the Kimi Agent harness in the official OSWorld v2 repository. GPT-6 Astra's score is taken from Muse Wonder's technical report. DECK-Arena and Design Bench. DECK-Arena evaluates presentation generation on real-world queries; Design Bench covers graphic design through direct and reference-image few-shot prompting. Both evaluate python-pptx, pptxjs, and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with integrated search and image generation. The automated grader is calibrated on more than 10,000 human judgments. BrowseComp. Uses context compaction triggered at 200K tokens and a 500-step maximum. If the limit is reached, the agent is forced to answer before judging. All runs use temperature = 1.0 and top-p = 1.0 . GDPval-AA v2.1, AA-Briefcase v1.1, and AutomationBench-AA. Scores are cited from Artificial Analysis . APEX-Agents. Scores are cited from the official leaderboard . Tool-augmented multimodal evaluations. GDP.pdf w/ python, ZeroBench w/ python, and ChartoGraphy w/ python are averaged over five runs; other multimodal benchmarks with Python are averaged over four. For GDP.pdf w/ python, each original PDF is sent to a sandbox for IPython processing. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash at medium reasoning effort and the official judging prompt. The reported score is the task-macro mean rubric pass rate. Reasoning, knowledge, and multimodal benchmarks GDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. The table reports the strict pass rate among fully scored responses. GLM-5.3 Max and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max scores are cited from Artificial Analysis . HLE-Full and HLE-Diamond. The full evaluation sets contain 2,500 and 1,000 questions, respectively. For scores marked * , accuracy is reported on the text-only subset. Run counts. GDP.pdf, ZeroBench, and ChartoGraphy are averaged over five runs; other multimodal benchmarks are averaged over four. MMMU-Pro. Evaluated using the official protocol, preserving the original input order and prepending images to the text input. PerceptionBench. An in-house benchmark focused on atomic visual perception capabilities. Kimi Hallucination Benchmark. Evaluates factual accuracy on an internal set of challenging, de-identified prompts drawn from practical work tasks. The table reports claim-level hallucination rates assessed by fact-checking agents. Cybersecurity benchmarks ExploitBench. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the official harness under a 300-turn budget. The table reports the pass@5 maximum-capability score: for each environment, the best of five seeds is scored by capability flags reached out of 16; arbitrary code execution counts as all 16 capabilities. Comparison scores are from OpenAI , Anthropic , and GLM-5.3 . ExploitGym. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Kimi Code under a six-hour wall-clock budget per task. GPT-6 Astra, Claude, and GLM comparison scores are taken from their respective official reports, with Claude results using the same six-hour budget. xdev-bench-hard. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Kimi Code; GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 use Claude Code. The internal benchmark contains expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks. The final model is evaluated at pass@3 over a random subset of runs, without hard timeouts or output-token limits. 4. Deployment and Availability You can access Kimi K3.1 Pro's API on https://platform.kimi.ai by selecting kimi-k3.1-pro , and we provide OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API for you. Currently, Kimi K3.1 Pro is recommended to run on the following inference engines: vLLM — see recipes SGLang — see cookbook TokenSpeed — see recipes 5. Model Usage The thinking effort of Kimi K3.1 Pro is configured with the top-level reasoning_effort request field, which supports "low" , "high" , and "max" (default "max" ). For multi-turn conversations and tool calls, Kimi K3.1 Pro requires the complete assistant message returned by the API to be passed back to messages as-is — including reasoning_content and tool_calls , not just content : import openai def chat_with_preserved_thinking ( client: openai.OpenAI, model_name: str ): messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Tell me three random numbers." }, { "role" : "assistant" , "reasoning_content" : "I'll start by listing five numbers: 473, 921, 235, 215, 222, and I'll tell you the first three." , "content" : "473, 921, 235" }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What are the other two numbers you have in mind?" } ] response = client.chat.completions.create( model=model_name, messages=messages, stream= False , max_tokens= 4096 , reasoning_effort= "max" , ) # the assistant should mention 215 and 222 that appear in the prior reasoning content print ( f"response: {response.choices[ 0 ].message.reasoning} " ) return response.choices[ 0 ].message.content For full guides and examples (vision input, structured output, partial mode, tool choice, dynamic tool loading, context caching), see the Kimi K3.1 Pro Quickstart and Thinking Effort . 6. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours. I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.
