title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
body_text: Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model | Ricursive Intelligence Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model. To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains. Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4). Rippleâs dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The modelâs small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , OpenRouter , and Fireworks . Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million . In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone. In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding , as estimated to the best of our knowledge. Â¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run. Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.  Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling , score centering , and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved. The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA. A Co-Designed Model Architecture Ripple-65B Previewâs architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization. Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping , gated attention , global NoPE , and value residuals . Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements We optimized Rippleâs pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.  Our starting point was Olmo 3âs model ladder , from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention . Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC ) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals . In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.  Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale. Conclusion We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier. We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.  At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If youâre interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers . Â¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain. Â© 2026 Ricursive Intelligence, Inc.

title: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
body_text: Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works | MindStudio Skip to main content Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Blog / Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works RTX Spark Linux Nvidia DGX Spark Linux dual boot laptop Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works A hands-on look at dual-booting Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop, the GPU clock throttling bug found, and why WSL still wins. Edited by Luis Chavez-Mattos , Director of Product · November 1, 2026 · RSS Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop? Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read. TL;DR Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly. A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown. GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in , compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it. Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly : Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9. Memory allocation is a separate headache , since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM. WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today , since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM. A real fix depends on Nvidia , specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark. Self-host Remy. On-prem or in your private cloud. Remy and every app you build stay inside your walls. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC? The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM. That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place. Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance. How do you actually install Linux on it? The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot. Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel. Going back to Omarchy solved the driver problem, since its kernel already bundled Nvidia’s open-source driver. At that point Linux booted properly, but could only see 28GB of the laptop’s 128GB of unified memory. That’s because the laptop’s firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use, and that split is only adjustable from Windows. Dropping the Windows-side GPU memory reservation down to 4GB freed up 120GB for Linux to see once booted. After that adjustment, the laptop ran a full desktop at 4K and 120Hz, with working audio, touchpad, keyboard, and CUDA acceleration. Getting video output over HDMI during the install process was its own obstacle. Early in the process, the laptop would only display video on its own internal screen, not over HDMI, which required pointing an external camera at the laptop’s screen just to see what was happening during remote-controlled installation steps. How does Linux performance compare to Windows and WSL? This is where the story turns. With GPT-OSS-120B running on the GPU, Windows produced 65.4 tokens per second. WSL, which runs a Linux environment inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical. The DGX Spark desktop unit, running Nvidia’s native Linux build, came in at 61 tokens per second. Native Linux on the laptop, however, dropped to 13.9 tokens per second, roughly five times slower. Every team builds with AI. Nothing gets lost. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today The gap showed up again with vLLM running eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second while native Linux reached 39.5. A longer benchmark run told the same story in time rather than throughput. Windows finished in about 8 minutes while holding the GPU near 2.2 GHz. Linux took 37 minutes, with the GPU parked around 790 MHz the entire time. Temperatures stayed low, between 40 and 47°C, so this isn’t a thermal throttling issue. The GPU simply isn’t being allowed to run at full speed. Oddly, the direction of the problem flips depending on power source. Unplugged, Linux hit around 61 to 67 tokens per second on LM Studio, comparable to Windows. Plugged in, that same test dropped to about 15 tokens per second. Clock speed told the same story: around 1,800 MHz unplugged under load, and down to roughly 780 MHz when connected to wall power. Why does plugging in the laptop slow Linux down? The cause traces back to a component visible in Windows Device Manager called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework. This piece of firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, since a laptop (unlike the desktop DGX Spark) has to balance power delivery between both chips rather than feeding the GPU on its own line. Disabling that controller in Windows reproduced the slowdown directly: tokens per second dropped from around 83 to about 31, and clock speed fell from roughly 2 GHz down to the same 786 MHz seen on Linux when plugged in. Re-enabling the controller restored normal speed immediately. That confirms the controller, not the kernel, the distribution, or the Nvidia GPU driver itself, is what’s holding Linux back. The deeper issue is that the firmware hands this controller a table of power settings that is encrypted. Windows has the key to decrypt it. Linux currently does not, and no software fix attempted during testing could enable it, including one attempt that triggered a kernel panic. Extracting the decryption key from the Windows driver was floated as a theoretical workaround, but that would amount to a fragile, single-machine hack rather than something that works broadly. A real fix needs to come from Nvidia shipping equivalent power management logic in its Linux driver. Is WSL a good substitute for native Linux right now? For most developers, yes, at least for now. WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, so it inherits Windows’ full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. It also runs Linux-first AI tools like vLLM and SGLang without the clock throttling problem that affects native Linux installs. The one adjustment needed is memory. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, which isn’t enough for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory machine, so that allocation needs to be increased manually. Once that’s done, WSL benchmarks land close to native Windows performance, making it the more practical choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly. Frequently Asked Questions Can the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop dual-boot Windows and Linux? Yes. Dual-booting was demonstrated on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop using Omarchy, a Linux distribution that already included Nvidia’s open kernel driver for this chip, after an initial attempt with Debian required manual driver and networking workarounds. Why is Linux so much slower than Windows on this laptop when plugged in? Developers have their tools. Enterprises have Remy. Without a Linux equivalent, the GPU’s clock speed gets locked around 780 MHz when the laptop is connected to power, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows. Does unplugging the laptop fix the Linux performance problem? It helps significantly. On battery power, Linux GPU clocks and token throughput come much closer to Windows levels. The severe slowdown specifically appears when the laptop is plugged into wall power, which is the opposite of what most users would expect. Is WSL the same as running native Linux on the RTX Spark? Not exactly, but it’s close in practice. WSL runs a Linux environment on top of the Windows kernel and driver stack, so it retains Windows’ GPU clock boost behavior and avoids the throttling issue, while still supporting Linux-native AI tools like vLLM. Will Nvidia fix Linux GPU performance on RTX Spark laptops? That depends on Nvidia shipping the platform controller’s power management logic in its Linux driver. The encrypted firmware power table currently can only be decrypted by Windows, and no workaround found so far restores full clock speed on Linux without it. (Image credit: AMD) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 19 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds. As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history. Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: AMD) (Image credit: AMD) Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year. Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%. (Image credit: AMD) The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft , OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems. You may like Intel shifts production capacity from consumer to server CPUs in face of 'unprecedented' AI demand Desktop CPU shipments crater 20% amid high component costs, but AMD gains record share despite 'ugly' desktop processor market Nvidia revenue tops $96 billion as memory commitments soar to $160 billion AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025. "We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth." Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter. (Image credit: AMD) Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago. Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%. What to read next AMD beats Intel to the trillion-dollar club as stock price soars Intel reportedly set to hike CPU prices by 10% ahead of 'major annual product' launch in March 2027 Nvidia expects to sell $20 billion worth of Vera Rubin hardware this quarter "In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint." AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027. Embedded business strong, set to accelerate As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers. (Image credit: AMD) AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years. "Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year." Beating Intel For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint. In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints. (Image credit: AMD) If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead. The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages. title: A new Go API for JSON
body_text: A new Go API for JSON - The Go Programming Language Skip to Main Content Why Go arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Case Studies Common problems companies solve with Go Use Cases Stories about how and why companies use Go Security How Go can help keep you secure by default Learn Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Docs arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Go Spec The official Go language specification Go User Manual A complete introduction to building software with Go Standard library Reference documentation for Go's standard library Release Notes Learn what's new in each Go release Effective Go Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code Packages Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Community arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Recorded Talks Videos from prior events Meetups open_in_new Meet other local Go developers Conferences open_in_new Learn and network with Go developers from around the world Go blog The Go project's official blog. Go project Get help and stay informed from Go Get connected Why Go navigate_next navigate_before Why Go Case Studies Use Cases Security Learn Docs navigate_next navigate_before Docs Go Spec Go User Manual Standard library Release Notes Effective Go Packages Community navigate_next navigate_before Community Recorded Talks Meetups open_in_new Conferences open_in_new Go blog Go project Get connected The Go Blog A new Go API for JSON Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026 Introduction JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago! Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes. After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json and introducing the new packages. Problems with encoding/json Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings. Behavior flaws There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json : Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream. encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names. Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default. Case-insensitive unmarshaling : When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation. Inconsistent calling of methods : Due to an implementation detail, MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by encoding/json . While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior. API deficiencies The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive: It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader . Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v) , which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input. Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types, but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions. Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method. The Compact , Indent , and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer . This limits the usability of those functions. Performance limitations Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations: MarshalJSON : The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned []byte . Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation. UnmarshalJSON : The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON . Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again. Lack of streaming : Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader , they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens. Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function, then the performance becomes quadratic. Trying to fix encoding/json directly Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package. While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise . We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2 , but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package. This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2 ), where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1 ). Building on encoding/json/jsontext Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the encoding/json/jsontext package that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go. JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components: syntactic functionality that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and semantic functionality that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values. We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling. This diagram provides an overview of this separation. Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods. The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data. The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package, contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax, while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package, contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data handled by the bottom half. The basic API of jsontext is the following: package jsontext type Encoder struct { ... } func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error type Decoder struct { ... } func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error) func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error) type Kind byte type Value []byte func (Value) Kind() Kind type Token struct { ... } func (Token) Kind() Kind The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON at a syntactic level and derives its name from RFC 8259, section 2 where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text . Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level, it does not depend on Go reflection. The Encoder and Decoder provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens. The constructors accept variadic options that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding. Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1 , the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner. A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as a named []byte . It is identical to RawMessage in v1 , which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value . A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens. A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type with constructors and accessor methods. It is analogous to Token in v1 but is designed to represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation. To resolve the fundamental performance problems with the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods, we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON as a streaming sequence of tokens and values. In v2 , we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods that operate on an Encoder or Decoder , allowing the methods’ implementations to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON , nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value provided to UnmarshalJSON . These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder . Introducing encoding/json/v2 Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the encoding/json/v2 package. It is designed to fix the problems in v1 , while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package. Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2 . Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2 . For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to study the examples in the v2 package , the “ Working with JSON ” tutorial, or read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic . The basic API of v2 is the following: package json func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error) func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error The Marshal and Unmarshal functions have a signature similar to v1 , but accept options to configure their behavior. The MarshalWrite and UnmarshalRead functions directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader , avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder just to write or read from such types. The MarshalEncode and UnmarshalDecode functions operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and are actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions. Unlike v1 , options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions, greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2 . There are several options available in v2 which are not covered by this article. Type-specified customization Similar to v1 , v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation by satisfying particular interfaces. type Marshaler interface { MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) } type MarshalerTo interface { MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error } type Unmarshaler interface { UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error } type UnmarshalerFrom interface { UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error } The Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces are identical to those in v1 . The new MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder . This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder . See the OrderedObject example for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members. Caller-specified customization In v2 , the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type, where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods or the default representation for a particular type. func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options type Marshalers struct { ... } func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options type Unmarshalers struct { ... } func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers MarshalFunc and MarshalToFunc construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types. Similarly, UnmarshalFunc and UnmarshalFromFunc support similar customization for Unmarshal . The ProtoJSON example demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all proto.Message types to be handled by the protojson package. Behavior differences While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1 , its behavior has changed in some ways to address problems in v1 , most notably: v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8. v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name. v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively. v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name. v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null , "" , [] , and {} ). v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration , which currently has no default representation , but provides options to let the caller decide. For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics, or even other caller-determined behavior. See “ Migrating to v2 ” for more information. Performance optimizations The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1 . Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower. The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1 , with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x. In order to obtain greater performance gains, existing implementations of Marshaler and Unmarshaler should migrate to also implement MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom , so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner. For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes (see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315 ), while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude. For more benchmark details, see the go-json-experiment/jsonbench repository. On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1 . You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28. Compatibility The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go. The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise. Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2 . That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported. We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together. Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies. For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package. That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior. No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected. Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct. The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance. No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2 ’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood. We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2 . As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options . Each behavior difference is controlled by one of these options. Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options. With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo ) or new struct tags (e.g., embed ) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users. Migration Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites. encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2 , and which option controls those behaviors. Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on. For example, we can select all v2 behavior except that duplicate names are allowed: json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(true)) Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except that duplicate names are disallowed: json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(false)) The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2 . More information For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see: The “ Working with JSON ” tutorial, The encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext package documentation, The encoding/json package’s v2 comparison documentation, and the encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide . A long time coming The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years. In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package, Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json ) first drafted his thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like . Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers , Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the Protocol Buffer specification required, nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner. Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable, Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and started to build a prototype (with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module). Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt) joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing. Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our recorded meetings and meeting notes . Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes . This work has been public since the beginning, and we increasingly involved the wider Go community, first with a GopherCon talk and discussion posted in late 2023 , formal proposal posted in early 2025 , and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25 for wider-scale testing by all Go users. The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point, incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable empirical experience from use in production settings. It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem. Thank you to everyone that contributed! title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
body_text: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup? 508 points by eggbrain 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 636 comments I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI. 1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc) - Which tiers? - Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)? 2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models. - Which models and providers? 3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses? - What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)? 4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools? - For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom. 5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse? - If you are using them, what are your main use cases? ----- I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.   help Animats 18 hours ago | next [–] Embarrassingly, I don't have one yet. I'm mostly still writing code one keystroke at a time. I've used Github Copilot to translate between languages and look things up, but haven't trusted it to write new code or fix anything. Claude Fable is now good enough that I should be using it. The latest Claude version is said to be comparable to a mid-career graphics programmer, which is about what I need. Six months ago it wasn't good enough to use for such work, and probably would have made a hash of my code. There's been progress. But Anthropic's business practices are scary. They have a reputation for cancelling accounts for random reasons, offer rather bad terms, and have no customer support. I have a strong aversion to services with a reputation for cancelling services arbitrarily. They will apparently cancel based on their system's guesses as to what you're working on. Sometimes they guess wrong. What I'm doing (metaverse clients) is so far out of the mainstream they may guess wrong. I'm currently stalled signing up for Claude because their verification email system can't get to my inbox. (Some problem with their using Constant Contact, a spam system, to send transactional emails to my own domain, which, long ago, I had blocked at the Constant Contact end. I think. The verification email never touches the inbound mail server.) It's very important to Anthropic that you sign up with the "right" email address, and it may not be possible to change it, so using some disposable address is not a good idea. Suggestions? reply creativeSlumber 14 hours ago | parent | next [–] > But Anthropic's business practices are scary. They have a reputation for cancelling accounts for random reasons, offer rather bad terms, and have no customer support. I have a strong aversion to services with a reputation for cancelling services arbitrarily. They will apparently cancel based on their system's guesses as to what you're working on. Sometimes they guess wrong. What I'm doing (metaverse clients) is so far out of the mainstream they may guess wrong. Then use open alternatives as much as possible. Something like Opencode with OpenRouter with Deepseek 4.1 from ZDR provider works very well and costs like 1/20th. reply bloppe 5 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I also think OAI is much better than Anthropic in this regard. They don't try to gatekeep nearly as much. But I agree that open alternatives are sort of a theoretical ideal. Just a lot harder to get those mega-subsidized. reply scosman 11 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] It costs 1/20th the price at token pricing, but an Ultra subscription is still amazing value. reply jpardoe 11 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] In practice all of these open models are more expensive than a Claude subscription. reply ggregoire 10 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Are they? (genuine question, i've got no experience with Claude) This month I used 1 billion tokens (including cache) with DS4.1 flash and it cost me 7% of my $10 opencode go sub. If you meant in developer time, then I don't know but it seems very fast to me (rarely thinks more than ~10sec, never more than ~30sec) and usually oneshots what I prompt it to do. I use opencode tui as harness. reply jeffyaw 6 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] i found they were until recently. mimo 2.6 flash and glm 5.3 flash seem to finally be cheaper. i find ds4.1 flash still on the high side. reply ChrisRR 16 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] You don't even need to start off with Fable. Give Opus 5.5 a try first and then then try Fable if you feel like you need to push it further reply nedt 13 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I have a longer history of agents sessions and used those to benchmark the different models. Sonnet 5.5 is already pretty strong, but not always as careful (leaked secrets into the session). Opus 5.5 is already able to solve everything I'm doing. You might not need Fable for anything. Biggest different between Opus and Fable in my benchmarks was price. Also Opus 5.5 is cheaper now then previous Opus so you might also not need Sonnet as much for cost savings. reply nycdatasci 12 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Based on blended benchmarks from Artificial Analysis, Opus 5.5 is stronger than Fable 5.1. Are you finding use cases where Fable is superior? reply felixgallo 11 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Fable can go deeper than Opus in my experience. Opus is incredible for relatively now-simple things like coding, but Fable has delivered improved results for me in data analysis on relatively obscure topics. That said one gets much more Opus for a subscription than one does Fable, so obviously benchmark your own cases and come up with your own cost benefit analysis. reply computomatic 17 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] You can access Claude models through any number of providers - OpenRouter, AWS Bedrock, etc. and as far as I know, Claude Code can be used with any of them. The only real benefit to going direct through Anthropic is the subscriptions. It’s worth the risk for the discount, but if you get locked out, there’s other (pricy) options to get unblocked. reply Fervicus 9 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] It's crazy to me that this is considered embarrassing now. People should stay up to date with current tech, but we shouldn't be ashamed of not using LLMs. Let's re-normalize coding by hand. reply martin82 52 minutes ago | root | parent | next [–] Coding by hand, sure! But let the LLM at least auto-complete your thoughts. They are still your thoughts, but it's just 100x faster than coding by hand. reply Animats 5 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I did, for a long time, but we're past that point now. Someone else got something done in three months that took me years of hand coding. reply bloppe 5 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] If something took 3 months, then there must have been a good deal of manual attention involved, even if it wasn't typing each character by hand. I still find that it's often faster to combine manual coding with generation. I often start by setting up a skeleton with a bunch of TODOs, then tell my agent to fix each TODO. If my agents can't seem to stop coming up with insanely massive diffs for what should be small changes, it's often much faster to just code it properly by hand. reply steve1977 5 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] And thinking by brain. reply olmo23 18 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Just use a random gmail address, it works. reply fidelramos 3 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Or use SimpleLogin. reply Forgeties79 12 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] If the concern is business practices, privacy, etc. adding Google to the mix doesn’t seem great reply walrus01 17 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] I would suggest that based on your current level of "trust" in these things (justifiably very low, I use zero openai or anthropic products myself) that you look into self hosting locally something reasonably capable and smart on your own hardware, on llama-server or something functionally equivalent to it. And running it in something like the opencode harness, using zero of the opencode API or online services. Qwen 3.8-flash-next will run on a lot of different hardware setups that are within the reach of normal people, or possibly deepseek v4 flash 1017, glm5.3-flash, things in that general category. reply sampullman 13 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Qwen 3.8-flash-next is great, but if they say SOTA models from 6 months ago weren't good enough for the kind of code they write, Qwen isn't going to cut it yet. reply Animats 6 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I'm not doing enough to rent my own GPU farm. reply thefourthchime 1 day ago | prev | next [–] It used to be more interesting and elaborate, switching between different models. I used to use Cursor, then Codex, but since Opus 5.5 came out, I just use the Claude IDE. I got rid of all my skills and just set it to medium. Then I vaguely talk to it about very high-end things that I want, and it comes back with magic. Rinse and repeat. I'd say the biggest trick is just to tell it what complete looks like. Be very specific about what you want it to come back with once it's done. That gives it a good idea what the goal is. It'll automatically create subagents and all that stuff. Although if you have money to burn and you're doing something large, you can tell it to just go wide or boil the ocean. Also, make sure you're working on at least five different things. Otherwise, you're sitting around for one agent. reply fhub 1 day ago | parent | next [–] I can do 5 things concurrently for about a day max. 3 things concurrently all week and my weekends are spent untangling my brain. 3 things per day on Mondays and Tuesdays and 2 things per day concurrently on Wed-Fri and I feel ok but crave holidays. reply thefourthchime 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I probably have some kind of pysccosis. I've had a personal $200 plan from one of the AI providers since March 2026. I'm never not making things now, I haven't rebooted my laptop for weeks because there is always an agent building something. I cycle between 4-5 work projects and 2-3 personal projects. Every night I tell me agents I'll be going to bed and to not ask questions and keep going. I've always loved building things, but this feels more like an addiction than healthy sometimes. They're not all done, and half the projects I bench, but this is where my personal projects live. https://wooten-labs.com reply fishtoaster 5 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] > I haven't rebooted my laptop for weeks because there is always an agent building something. I'm pretty pilled on cloud agents these days. If I've got 5 agents going at once, each is in their own dedicated, isolated cloud environment. There are a bazillion services for this now ampcode, hoplite.sh, cursor's cloud agents, devin.ai cloud, and more. I haven't had an agent do anything from my laptop in a month or two. reply networkbug 16 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] not gonna lie, you don't need to be doing these projects. they're not really worth it. instead of building an app to help you meet up with your friends somewhere central just go meet up with them and explore together. reply vidarh 10 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I don't need to be doing all of these projects, but I enjoy doing all of these projects, much more than I enjoy going somewhere to hang out with people. setup windows 11 with Rufus boot to disable online MS account creation https://rufus.ie/en/ - [download window 11 x64 iso from here ]( https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/software-download/windows11 ) - then download vmware workstation pro (you ll need to create a free account to get the download link on their website) - install vmware workstation pro - turn internet off - plug your pendrive in with the rufus w11 x64 iso on it (mind ya, this pen drive ll first need full formatting before burning a w11 image to it) - press f2 to reach bios in vmware settings and make it boot from pendrive - turn internet off on your machine (DO NOT keep it on) - install w11 (keep a 100gb for vmware) - without updates it ll load real fast and you wont need an MS account (rufus takes care of it) - while it installs, download revo uninstaller pro on a separate machine https://onefiles.net/9d170d01078634b5 (latest version 5.4.x) and put it inside a second pendrive / portable hdd - once w11 loads, it ll ask you to enter a password, keep existing password blank and enter literally anything for a new password - voila you are done with w11 setup inside vmware - now connect the 2nd pendrive with revo and install it (need to clean uninstall many tools, hence we need this one) - now go to search bar and type check for updates and update everything on w11 inside vmware - next stop get unigetui from ms app store or from here https://devolutions.net/unigetui/ (it is a package manager responsible for installing just about everything else with auto updation of all packages) - the open unigetui and search for the following packages vlc, winrar, winhance - winhance is the fully customizable debloater you ll need to turn off all telemetry (we ll debloat after installing all the other requirements) - next go to ms app store and install python or open powershell and type python - the open unigetui and search for the following packages vlc, winrar, winhance - winhance is the fully customizable debloater you ll need to turn off all telemetry (we ll debloat after installing all the other requirements) - next go to ms app store and install python or open powershell and type python - mind you this installs a python version manager that lets you install and uninstall multiple python versions - after this python version manager is setup, install a specific version of python like ``` py install 3.13 ``` - next we need a node.js version manager, use fnm for it https://github.com/Schniz/fnm - once installed, it may need to be added to environment variables manually - once again choose a specific version of node.js and install it using ``` fnm install 23.12.0 ``` check fnm --help for commands - next we need a java version manager, use jvms for it https://github.com/ystyle/jvms - pretty self explanatory - now install git and again it ll give you some trouble over environment variables, command not recognized etc, fixable with some gpt help - at this point, we got git, node version manager, java version manager and python version manager and are ready to rumble - install vscode/ visual studio whatever - install codex - install claude - install opencode (both cli via npx and desktop app) and check their plans out https://opencode.ai/console/go - install ghidra , ghidra-mcp (mind you open ghidra-mcp first because it only works with specific versions of ghidra and java) this is the reason we installed a java version manager - check out setup for rea https://github.com/morluto/rea requires npx setup for rea and ghidra both, read documentation - run winhance, check recommended settings under optimize and every other tab and restart the vm a few times for full debloat with 0 telemetry services - congrats you have a full blown agentic environment at this point (if I missed anything i ll come back and update) reply guhcampos 1 day ago | prev | next [–] 1.a) At work: I can choose between Cursor and Claude on a meter. Been using Cursor for a long time and happy with it until they started to force Grok down our throats. I was happy with Composer 2. Recently switched to Claude Code. The company also runs some open weight models in-house and I have been using them through Claude Code itself, with VSCodium as my Code Viewer. I almost never need anything stronger than Sonnet at work - 80% of which is YAML and Terraform these days (or rather markdown, if you really think about it). 1.b) For personal stuff I maintain an Opencode GO subscription, USD40 tier. I also have a Google One subscription which is supposed to have some AI capabilities, haven't tested it yet. 2) Besides my Opencode GO subscription, I sometimes add a few bucks to use Zen. It's rare: my USD40 is usually fine for the month. I've recently started using Nvivia NIM free tier models for some time insensitive tasks too. I have a Qwen model available on my Mac (M1 PRO 64GB) but haven't found it to be useful, as I need my laptop for everything else I'm doing beyond inference. GLM 5.3 Flash and Deepseek 4.1 Flash do most of the work for my personal stuff. Nemotron does the time insensitive stuff, which is mostly summarizing text. I've been using GPT Luna 6 a lot because it's currently cheap as hell, so I'll often talk to GPT Luna and hand off coding to GLM or Deepseek. I find that Luna communicates MUCH better than the Chinese models - I assume because it does not go through the extra language barrier step between English and Chinese. GLM, Qwen and Deepseek are incredible tool callers, but their prose is insufferable. 3.a) At work I'm using Claude Code for the Anthropic models and Opencode for the self-hosted ones. Ditched Cursor recently. I've been meaning to try to integrate the self-hosted models into Claude Code but haven't yet, so hand-offs between the two harnesses involve a lot of markdown. I've switched out of Cursor because A. they've been bullying us into using grok for everything and B. The company setup would not support the use case of mixing the self-hosted and closed models in the same harness - this limitation is on our side. 3.b) For my personal stuff I've been using mostly Hermes. Some actual coding goes into Opencode, often piloted by Hermes itself. I'm using Zed as my code editor, but with the AI features disabled. My opencode subscription is actually configured in Zed, but I prefer the UI without them. 4) No. I don't really need them. I run 5-6 parallel sessions at most, otherwise I can't keep track of what's being done anyway. Each parallel session is on a different task, so I generally don't need them to spit enormous amounts of code. I rarely have to wait more than a few minutes for a task to finish, and I'm always thinking or writing or managing something else in between anyway - not looking at the screen waiting. 5) Hermes. Generally happy with it - despite it being extremely unstable between updates, with frequent regressions, weird UI bugs and half assed features (bot mode, anyone?). I have 3 distinct instances (laptop, home server, VPS) doing different things - all hooked up to the same memory provider (honcho) under a single user profile, and a handful AI profiles on each. All have limited access to my Obsidian Vault, which is synced between them using Obsidian Sync. I generally use the laptop instance for day-to-day use: planning work, assigning tasks to myself and to the other agents, capturing ideas, light coding, etc. The homeserver instance manages a limited set of features on the server itself, from upgrades, documentation and more devopsy stuff to organizing files, managing transcoding queues, etc. The cloud hosted version automates is not very used yet. I plan to have it pilot an n8n instance I keep to automate some boring stuff, like filing weekly tax records and automatically forwarding bureaucratic e-mails, nothing fancy. reply Scrounger 1 day ago | parent | next [–] > 5) Hermes. Generally happy with it - despite it being extremely unstable between updates, with frequent regressions, weird UI bugs and half assed features (bot mode, anyone?). I have 3 distinct instances (laptop, home server, VPS) doing different things - all hooked up to the same memory provider (honcho) under a single user profile, and a handful AI profiles on each. All have limited access to my Obsidian Vault, which is synced between them using Obsidian Sync. I am just getting into setting up Hermes on a VPS. If you have any high ROI tips/tricks/advice on how to make this work well, please let me know! Appreciate it! reply pmarreck 1 day ago | prev | next [–] herdr, opus 5.5 (max), codex (max), and I am still refining how they all communicate, currently codex became unwakable at some point while claude can be woken with a message just fine. reply sparklingmango 1 day ago | prev | next [–] Right now, it's Claude Code on Opus 5.5 w/ herdr to manage multiple sessions at a time. reply jkelleyrtp 1 day ago | prev | next [–] devin reply ibrahimsayar96 13 hours ago | prev | next [–] test reply teekert 19 hours ago | prev | next [–] Ok I don't understand how people can deal with the information coming from a fleet of agents burning 100s-1000s of €/$ as month. I have a Claude Code pro subscription, and mostly have Opus as a thinking buddy, we have thoroughly designed a data model together, we have implemented it in Django. Then we designed the RBAC system and now we are making views per role. It is so intense! Constant decisions, walls of text with pros and cons to decisions. I mean the speed is amazing, the code quality is also amazing, but the amount of information I get to process is just insane, and I enjoy it less than the flow-state writing of code. I think I'll get used to it, and the speed is motivating, but man. I can not picture keeping 10's of agents on tasks. What am I doing wrong? Should I trust the system more? Or am I just mostly working on decisions now and the 1000$ token burners are not bothered with that because they have a full backlog, where I need to fill it myself? I deal with the overload by making abstractions (a visual of the data model/db schema with color coded relations etc, a table for RBAC, think about permissions in "Axes"... I'm always looking for smart tricks to "think better", to be able to hold more information and reason about it. What must exist in me, what can I outsource? Btw, as a FOSS person I so hate that I am not owning my means of production anymore, I have a home battery for all my infra, very proud of what I build, but I can't run my agents :( I really hope that will change soon (for privacy and for control reasons.) I pisses me off that I can't get nice hardware, meanwhile I can get a Muse or Dot, which is an LLM with a VM with up to 12 GBs of RAM, for free, paid for by their borrowed money. This whole idea makes me die a bit inside. For the company I do all IT for we have a Mistral Team subscription, I find it hard to work with anything other than Claude Opus, I really force myself to do it but I often think: Pff, Opus would have gotten this right. But I remember feeling the same when I switched from Google to DDG (3000 years ago) and I never switched back. So it's probably just familiarity. I also have HermesAgent on a nuc here in front of me, it makes small automations: Scans for positions or projects for my company, parses RSS feeds for relevant cybersecurity news, researches things when I ask, stores notes and articles with I can interrogate as a "body of work" <- love that btw, it's like an external memory where the faintest glimmer of a memory can help you dig up that one nugget of knowledge. Or you can find trends in TFAs you love. You can really get to know yourself a bit better. Most things it makes are LLMs out of the loop, just automations build from simple Unix-style tools that I could have made myself but never took the time for. It's also nice that it solves edge cases itself. It burns less then €3 a month on deepseek or so (just processing public data for me). I keep it on a separate vlan and away from important stuff. reply laurasg 19 hours ago | parent | next [–] I don't think you are doing anything wrong; it is overwhelming. But I also don't think "trusting" the system more would help. IMO, now coding is a bit more like maintaining critical infrastructure; it may be built quickly, but you need to keep an eye out for random decisions agents are taking that will cost you (money, security...) in the future. I have seen Claude making many sneaky decisions and (maybe) coincidentally burning more tokens by doing so reply Kwpolska 19 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] You use Claude as a "thinking buddy", meanwhile those who spend $500+ on LLMs have shut their brains off, and have delegated all thinking to the LLM, producing tons of slop. reply luisgvv 11 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] This is what I've been thinking lately. I've watched people showing up their setups and it's "cool" to fully automate and watch everything get done while sipping tea, but I bet you if something breaks or a product manager asks them they'll still rely on being a meat proxy. No idea if this is the future lol reply teekert 10 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] The meat proxy is very easy to just remove, no need to pay for the tea sipping. We much find where we bring value. As did all generation before us when automation influenced their work. reply Uptrenda 13 hours ago | prev [–] VS code with claude plugin. Basic private git repos per project on github, nothing special, I keep everything simple. 1. subscription: claude max 20x 2. other subscription: nope 3. harness: vs code with claude plugin 4. orchestration: no 5. broader agents: grok for outreach. my development setup is a high-end local esxi server (multiple internet cons and a graphics card). The server has about 30 different OSes on it (static ips / ssh setups for all vms.) I use a VM on that machine to run my IDE with full access to the other VMs. I have good snapshots for all the VMs so if anything breaks they are easily restored. This setup makes it easy to develop software for any OS and also test complex software interactions. For hosted internet services: I use a single OVH debian machine. I pre-pay everything over a large period so the bills are always paid. That keeps it reliable as I can say that even if I go broke in the future I'll have paid it for quite a while (useful in this economy, lol.) Session notes: I feel like the best approach is for us all to just maintain a personal wiki for our projects. But I must admit I've been lazy in that respect. All my attempts to manage my notes never works because im such a messy, chaotic person. My natural state is disorder. So I'll just (1) destroy it by accident (2) forget to back it up (3) forget to use it (4) get tired of using it. I envy those super organised people. Backup: my services are backed up locally. My local repos are backed up to github, email, and remotely. Agents deleting anything by accident isn't something i have to worry about. They have ruined VMs before. I can easily restore them. So far I've only ever lost notes because of laziness. Security: my security setup could be vastly improved by using discrete key pairs with restricted permissions for github. What I worry about most is just things like prompt injection and the agent accidentally downloading malware. Lateral traversal out of vms is hard but not impossible. I'd wager there's still lots of private stuff on the vms too. I monitor everything closely at least and can restore a snapshot if i get paranoid. reply Guidelines | FAQ | Lists | API | Security | Legal | Apply to YC | Contact Search:

title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
body_text: Residential Proxies Detected on White House Network LAYER 3 INTEL Tripwire Intel API IP Intel Pricing Blog Docs Contact Sign in Get started Tripwire Intel API IP Intel Pricing Blog Docs Contact Sign in Residential Proxies Detected on White House Network Layer3 Intel Team · November 4, 2026 Our Residential Proxy Observatory , launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity. While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650 . AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network. Confirmed residential proxy activity observed from the White House network, October 5 to November 3, 2026. What we observed From October 5 to November 3: Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times . Those exits came from 6 addresses , on 26 of the 30 days . 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network. To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits. This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services. Why this is concerning Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them. Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets , the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems. No place is too remote The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet. Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena. We also recorded three observations from Antarctica . All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station. Other remote places with activity: Pitcairn : 1 Starlink address, 1 observation. Norfolk Island : 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations. Svalbard : 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations. Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7). Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide. For relevant agencies: We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page .
