Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Search Sign in AI Security Software Microsoft Developer Open Source BOFH Who, Me? On Call Anthropic REG AD security North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist 'It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,' exchange says Jessica Lyons Jessica Lyons Cybersecurity Editor Published tue 3 Nov 2026 // 22:04 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers 3 days ago Google says Asian advertisers spending less due to Europe's customs changes 4 days ago In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security 6 days ago Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour 7 days ago China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B 8 days ago North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist . In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” REG AD Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group , known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists . The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers , who are then hired by Western companies , and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices . REG AD With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation . While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened.  In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.”  The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities. According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware. Here’s the script: CREATE  /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_   REG AD MODIFY  pyenv_ → 3,414 B   DELETE  .../libexec/pyenv  (3,344 B)      ← remove the valid pyenv RENAME  pyenv_ → pyenv  (3,414 B)  ← replace it with a malicious version DELETE  /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv  (3,414 B) ln  (create a new symlink)  +  spawn zsh Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C. Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack. As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets. REG AD The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. Binance said it’s also working to establish a security research fund and initiatives with AI companies and security shops to focus on AI security in blockchain environments.® supply chain attack north korea binance security cryptocurrency Make us preferred on Google REG AD Threat actor targets Indian fintechs on weekends when defenders aren’t watching CERT-IN warns of ‘significant escalation’ in AI-powered attacks, some after victims tried to improve defences Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up No documented attacks against American supermarkets…yet From expertise to intelligence: NISCO deploys world's first swarm-intelligence steel model at scale PARTNER CONTENT: 300+ AI applications delivering surges in core metrics and annual cost reduction of over CNY100m AWS Kiro aims to solve identity crisis by adding another identity: bot orchestrator The cloud giant refits its agentic dev tools for agent orchestration OPINION Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever. title: Insects don't swarm at LED lights
body_text: Insects Don’t Swarm at LED Lights | Outside My Window Skip to content Outside My Window A Blog of Birds & Nature with Kate St. John Menu Home About Events Peregrine FAQs Search for: Insects Don’t Swarm at LED Lights November 3, 2026 Insects, Spiders , Mexico, Veracruz Kate St. John Insects swarm at gas station light, July 2006 , (photo by cgpgrey , CC BY 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) 3 November 2026 CORRECTION COMING SOON! Many comments remark that I’ve got the Incandescent/LED UV issue backwards. This article is about to change a lot … so don’t waste your time on it yet. Remember when you used to encounter swarms of insects around outdoor electric lights? Their well known attraction to outdoor lights is used by entomologists and moth lovers to conduct insect surveys. All you need is a light and a white sheet to see who’s flying at night. Light trapping for insects at Maui (photo by Forest & Kim Starr , CC BY 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) Nowadays, if you want to attract insects, you have to be picky about the light you use. As everyone changes over to LED lights, we see the color difference but we can’t see the crucial difference in insect attraction between incandescent and LED. Odd one out, LED streetlight by John Goldsmith , CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Our guide Roland Rumm on the WINGS Veracruz trip explained what happens with insects in the switch to LED lights. His family has an outdoor dining space that is well lit with artificial light. As a child he loved to watch the geckos climb to the lights and eat the insects. (This gecko can change to a bland gray color when he needs to.) Bay Island least gecko looking colorful (photo by Laura Gaudette , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) In recent years the family changed over to LED lights and the geckos disappeared. Were the geckos gone? No. But far fewer insects were attracted to the LED lights so the geckos had no reason to show up. In 2024 the BBC wrote about Why insects are drawn to artificial light at night : Flying insects use moonlight to navigate. Since the moon is always above them, they orient themselves so that the light shines on their backs. That’s how they stay upright in flight. Moonlight contains ultraviolet (UV) and infrared wavelengths because it is merely reflected sunlight. Insects cue on UV, believing it to be the moon. When artificial lights transmit UV they look like moonlight so insects orient their backs to it. Consequently they circle the light and even flip upside down when the artificial light is pointing up to the sky! Incandescent lights transmit UV but LEDs do not. Insects are far less attracted to LED. In 2016 scientists at the University of Bristol, UK ran experiments to compare insect attraction to four types of light : Incandescent (tungsten filament), Compact fluorescent, “Cool-white” LED and “Warm-white” LED. We conducted field experiments to compare the relative attractiveness of four commercially available “domestic” lights, one traditional (tungsten filament incandescent) and three modern (compact fluorescent, “cool white” LED and “warm white” LED), to aerial insects, particularly Diptera. We found that LEDs attracted significantly fewer insects than other light sources, but found no significant difference in attraction between the “cool” and “warm white” LEDs. Fewer flies were attracted to LEDs than alternate light sources, including fewer Culicoides midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Use of LEDs has the potential to mitigate disturbances to wildlife and occurrences of insect?borne diseases relative to competing lighting technologies. — Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types? Here’s what they found. NOTES: CFL = Compact fluorescent, FIL = incandescent (the old lightbulb), LEDC = LED cool white, LEDW = LED warm white light. Average insect trap catch in the “evening” sampling periods commencing at sunset (17 sites). Lights were compact fluorescent (CFL), tungsten filament (FIL), light?emitting diode “cool?white” (LEDC), and light?emitting diode “warm?white” (LEDW). Error bars indicate SE. From: Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types? Typically LEDs do not emit UV light and are more energy efficient than traditional technologies. Electrical energy is converted almost entirely into electromagnetic (EM) radiation within the range of the visible light spectrum (400–700 nm) and therefore not wasted on producing wavelengths of light invisible to the human eye, that is, UV and infrared (IR). Thus, LEDs are less attractive to many insects than lights which emit UV light.  — Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types? So that’s why there are very few bugs circling LED lights at night. Street lamp with new multiple LEDs as light source, shines down on a rowan branch with leaves at night, May 2024, Tuntorp, Sweden (photo by W.carter , CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) According to the BBC, this trait of LEDs is a good thing because incandescent (UV) artificial light at night distracts insects so much that they don’t reproduce, don’t feed, etc. Thus artificial light is considered a major reason why insect populations have declined. See: The impact of artificial light at night on nocturnal insects: A review and synthesis . Post navigation ← Who Makes Decisions Twice as Fast as Humans? It’s the Dawn of a New Day → 9 thoughts on “ Insects Don’t Swarm at LED Lights ” Sue Swick says: November 3, 2026 at 9:45 am Thanks again, Kate, for another en”light”enment! Reply Ricky says: November 4, 2026 at 3:41 pm White light LEDs still have a big spike of blue light at 450–465 nanometers, and apparently this part of the spectrum messes up nocturnal animals’ and humans circadian rhythm-related systems. https://www.mariomottamd.com/wp-content/uploads/AmJPrevMed13.pdf Reply Kate St. John says: November 4, 2026 at 5:05 pm Ricky, I agree that LEDs may lessen one problem but cause new ones. I’ve been meaning to write about blue light and our circadian rhythms. Thanks for reminding me. Nihil says: November 4, 2026 at 3:57 pm Worldwide decline of the entomofauna: A review of its drivers https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006320718313636 This may also be having a considerable impact. Reply Kate St. John says: November 4, 2026 at 5:17 pm Nihil, Thanks for the study on causes of the Insect Apocalypse. Ted E Dunning says: November 5, 2026 at 2:41 am I may be a bit mistaken on this topic, but I am pretty sure that normal incandescent light bulbs emit 95% infrared, with essentially all the rest in the visible range and less than 0.01% in the UV range. Halogen bulbs emit a bit more UV, but not a lot more and they weren’t involved in the tests you cited. In fact, in the conclusions, they make the point that FIL lights (incandescent) are essentially UV free and speculate that their attraction may well be based on their thermal emissions. CFL lights also emit more heat than LEDs, so there may well be something to that. In any case, I think your comment that “normal light bulbs emit UV” is just pretty much wrong. Reply Kate St. John says: November 5, 2026 at 8:45 am Ted, yes. Thank you. I’m gonna rewrite this article and in the meantime I’ve put up a CORRECTION COMING notice. Dr Dan Holdsworth says: November 5, 2026 at 8:39 am This reminds me of some work I did on moth attraction to different light sources some thirty-odd years ago. I compared old MV/B mercury vapour lamps, HQL mercry vapour lamps, Actinic 12v lamps and a tungsten filament lamp. As expected here the tungsten was least attractive by quite a way, the actinic more attractive and the two mercury vapour lamps about the same (and much, much more attractive). It is therefore interesting that LED lamps are not very attractive to insects, less so than even tungsten filament lamps. The Rothamsted Insect Survey network uses old-style tungsten filament lamps for their traps, precisely because these were not very attractive. title: Conductor is joining Meta
body_text: Conductor is joining Meta I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta. We launched Conductor a lifetime ago, in the distant past of July 2025. Writing most of your code with agents (let alone a team of coding agents) felt crazy back then. You trusted us to come along for the ride, and we cannot thank you enough! We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface. If you liked Conductor, you’re gonna love what’s coming. We’ll have something new for you to use early next year. Conductor will keep working as normal till then, except for Conductor Cloud, which will shut down over the next few weeks. We’ve built an easy way to transfer Conductor Cloud workspaces to local, and we’re around to help make the transition as easy as possible. Reach out to [email protected] if you need anything. Thank you again for your support! Charlie Timeline Wednesday, Nov 4 No new sign-ups, free for existing users New users can no longer sign up for Conductor or download the app. Existing free users can’t upgrade to a pro plan, but pro users can keep using pro features for free. Friday, Nov 13 Conductor Cloud goes read-only Conductor Cloud workspaces go read-only. You can still read old chats and export data, but you can’t send new messages. Active subscribers will get a refund. Friday, Nov 20 Conductor Cloud shuts down We begin deleting Conductor Cloud user data. Please export your data before this date. Local Conductor will continue to receive new models and critical bug fixes until early 2027. We hope to have something new you can use by then! FAQ When will I have to stop using Conductor? + Conductor Cloud will become read-only on Nov 13, and will fully shut down on Nov 20. We’ve built an easy way to transfer your cloud workspaces to local. To move a cloud workspace and its chats to your Mac, right-click it and choose Transfer to local. To download all your data, go to Settings → Account → Export data. Local Conductor will continue working as normal for now. It will start winding down in early 2027. We hope to have something new you can use by then! Will Conductor still get updates? + Yes, Conductor will still get new models and critical bug fixes until early 2027. How can I export my data? + You can transfer a cloud workspace to local by right-clicking the workspace and selecting Transfer to local. To export an archive of all your Conductor data, go to Settings → Account → Export data. What happens to my data? + We have never sold or trained on Conductor user data, and we still won’t. We’ll delete all Conductor user data when the app shuts down in early 2027. Check our privacy policy here . I just subscribed to Conductor. Can I get a refund? + Yes, active subscribers will get a refund. What are you going to be building? + We can’t share much yet. But if you liked Conductor, you’re gonna like what’s next. I have a different question, where can I get help? + Please email [email protected] . If you do not agree to be bound by the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy, you may not use the 99% Invisible website and services. see recent newsletter Close Article by Kurt Kohlstedt Guerrilla Bike Lanes: San Francisco Makes Illicit Infrastructure Permanent Image via the SFMTrA Click to enlarge image Infrastructure Category Infrastructure Date 11.14.16 Producer Kurt Kohlstedt Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Leave a Comment When two cyclists were tragically  killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such  guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by  making the change official . Image by Nicasio Nakamine The SFMTrA , a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including: Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians. Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists. Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety. Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones , which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive. Image via the SFMTrA “Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement , “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete. Image via the Reasonably Polite Seattleites Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group  Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts. Image via the Reasonably Polite Seattleites City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation  would put the delineators back in place. In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane). 99% Invisible Guerrilla Public Service Redux Episode 288 Guerrilla Public Service Redux Play Pause Add to Queue Remove from Queue Download Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also  jailed or fined  by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress . title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
body_text: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time | nns.ee Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time Nov 02, 2026 Permalink: https://blog.nns.ee/2026/11/02/renault-hack/ The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain. When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it. They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there. Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it. I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much. Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there. That never happened. The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it. I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious . Just RE it Still in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu. Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit ( https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md ). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves. When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont ) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10. After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet. This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me. What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps. I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time. I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying. Fine . I'll just root it and do it myself. Easy wins? I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root. I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins. My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it. While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected. It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls. I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing. Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could. Back to the drawing board I'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved. For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system: rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro) Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard , and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi , which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal , which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec . This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011. Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script , a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time. I reversed ttn , the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed. More wild goose chases I still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector. As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input. I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX / SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver , which launched whatever command line was provided with execve . This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh , which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec . The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful. Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage. Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt ) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root. It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system. However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end. Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes. Borrowing a trick from kernel exploits I had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together. Among other things, I knew I could: Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfs Write ASCII to paths of my own choosing This is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead? Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead ( |/bin/my-coredump-handler ). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there. core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28. Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern . I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh . This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root. Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script. I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect. Putting it together My final master.script turned out to be quite simple: #define LOGFILE .. / .. / proc / sys / kernel / core_pattern LOG |/ bin / sh / media / sdcard / payload.sh SHEX / bin / dbus - monitor I initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the " Execute master.script? " prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution. The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd . With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat , which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, it turned out the unit doesn't really have a concept of timezones at all. It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180. I changed it to 120. That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.
