title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
body_text: Wing Commander Together An 11 year journey to play DOS Wing Commander together By danielrh Watch on YouTube Play it in your browser When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft. In the beginning we were searching for where we were On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman. The actual quote “I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source 1 MB 0000 01A2 WC.EXE root image DS 13D3 data segment, 64K 640K A000 VGA E000 EMS page frame FFFF:F the data segment, dseg:0000 to FFFF 0187 dead string 7728 random seed A9C2 position D248 mission tree 8DF8 comm text CAE2 velocity FFxx stack AEB6 · B1B6 · B4B6 right, up, forward C280 victory points Here is a breakdown of the megabyte of addressable DOS memory and the 64K data segment where Wing Commander puts its game state. This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command. The Hornet cockpit on launch, where the VDU confirms an empty patch of space with nothing to target. Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved. (snapshot origin ⊙ snapshot later ) ∧ (snapshot origin ⊕ snapshot moved ) A stopped stopped5 B stopped again stopped6 C after moving straight4 origin ⊙ later same in origin and later origin ⊕ moved different in origin and moved ∧ candidates 413 bytes 132 with chase view 1,048,323 bytes still 650 bytes moved 253 bytes churn even while stopped 253 bytes churn when stopped, and 650 change during a move. 413 do both. By cross referencing with the chase cam, the total is only 132 bytes. There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be. I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2 . I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location. This technique identified velocity as well at CAE2 , since thre were three 32 bit ints that zeroed out when the craft was stopped. Craft position, camera position, set speed and velocity changes lit up in yellow I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships. Then we searched for what we faced I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November. Diff of two DOSBox memory dumps from turning. The bright band is the data segment. A9C2 position AEB6 right B1B6 up B4B6 forward CAE2 velocity 0 1 2 8 10 18 20 28 30 38 3D 3F slot 0 player · 1 wingman · 2 Tiger's Claw · 3D camera · 3F temporary camera 0x300 apart 64 × 12 bytes contiguous slot 0 → slot 0x3D: 0x2DC bytes (A9C2 → AC9E, CAE2 → CDBE) int32 x int32 y int32 z one slot = 12 bytes In the 64 slot arrays, each slot is 12 bytes. Slot 0 is the player, 0x3D is the camera and 0x3F is a temporary slot. The camera copy caused each value to appear twice 0x2DC bytes apart. To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F . However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D . Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff . Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps. Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code. end of the up table start of the forward table up[0] B1B6 the ship copied every frame up[0x3D] B492 camera copy up[0x3E] B49E empty up[0x3F] B4AA temporary forward[0] B4B6 the ship my write overwritten every frame starfield shifts 00 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 level: (0, 256, 0), 256 = 1.0 82 FF FF FF 34 FF FF FF A5 FF FF FF rolled: (-126, -204, -91), 00 bytes became FF x y z three 4-byte scalars, little-endian The up vector array has the camera copy at offset 0x3D, an empty slot at 0x3E, and the temporary intermediate value at 0x3F. Int32 where 256 means 1.0, thus the nonzero unit vector axis would be 00 01 00 00 in little endian. Yaw from level flight where forward[0] has a 9 byte change and up[0] changed from 00 01 to 7E 00. I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop. BPM 13D3:A9C2 write watch on position[0] vector_add 329A:04DA (stub140) pos[si] += vel[si] physics per ship 2B0F:19E0 (stub141) for si in 0..3C per frame 0560:074C seg001 main loop 0560:20E3 once per frame fires in called by called by called by DOSBox hook: CS:IP == 0560:20E3 run queued calls, exchange a frame neighbours in overlay 140: sub 0568 · zero 047A · cross 09BE normalize 0A7F · orthogonalize 1163 yaw 12B1 · pitch 1280 also seen at 34A5:19E0: same overlay, another load Call stack after memory watchpoint. It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input. Then we searched for how to act December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand. root image (fixed addresses) stub143 = segment 12D7 12D7:0084 EA 99 0A 31 2F jmp far 2F31:0A99 12D7:012E EA 78 29 31 2F jmp far 2F31:2978 12D7:0156 EA 76 2E 31 2F jmp far 2F31:2E76 … one entry per exported function call far 12D7:0084 overlay 143, loaded on demand this run: 2F31 · other runs: 2BBE, 34A5 … 2F31:0A99 do_damage(src, dst, qty, vec) 2F31:2978 fireGunFromShip(ship, gun) 2F31:2E76 fireAllGuns(ship) ships, damage, weapons: ovr143 in IDA via the EMS page frame DOSBox hook, isExecutingFunction(0x12D7, 0x0084) stub bytes 1..4 → live segment:offset reads matches Borland overlays: table of jmp far thunks. Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187 and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline. We would have DOSBox push CS:IP to the stack, then relocate the instruction pointer to the string above. 00 terminates any string pointing here. pushf; pusha the game is mid-frame; leave registers as we found them xor si,si; push si argument: ship 0. Later thunks use mov si,imm16 for each argument call far 12D7:0156 through the stub, so it works wherever the overlay is loaded pop si; popa; popf cdecl: caller cleans the arguments retf back to the CS:IP DOSBox pushed We noted with joy that this caused the laser cannons to activate. DOSBox (host) guest CPU guest memory 1 byte in fire.fifo or a network event 2 push CS, push IP return address: right here 3 write the thunk over the dead string 4 CS:IP = 13D3:0188 resume emulation the game any CS:IP 5 thunk runs pushf pusha … call far 6 fireAllGuns 12D7:0156 → ovr143 13D3:0187 "Loading WING COMMANDER. " ← before 13D3:0187 00 9C 60 33 F6 56 9A 56 01 D7 12 5E 61 9D CB NUL · pushf · pusha · xor si,si · push si · call far 12D7:0156 · pop si · popa · popf · retf pauses here retf from the game function 7 retf → the saved CS:IP DOSBox pushes CS:IP, writes the thunk over the dead string, points CS:IP at it, and the thunk's retf lands back where the game left off. In March of 2017, we found a predictable location in the main loop ( 0560:20E3 ) to hook so we would not need to worry about being in an unpredictable part of the game, and in July we located the do_damage function and prevented the game from calling it as the secondary player. Then we tried to bring together fields from afar In August of 2017, we authored the networking protocol which was a simple TCP client/server architecture with protobuf game messages. Every frame every ship's position would be sent from the leader plus fire events, despawning and damages. The client would reply with its own position, if any lasers were fired or if some cataclysmic event had happened (ejection, landed, died). Each player would have their own craft as entity 0 and the other player as entity 1, which required a swap when receiving packets from the other emulator. TCP · protobuf messages · one exchange per frame leader (server) the mission runs here slot 0: leader · slot 1: wingman client memory writes job queue for this frame slot 0: wingman · slot 1: leader every ship's position, every frame fire events · despawns · damages its own position · lasers fired ejected · landed · died positions → memory writes · events → job queue Positions sent every frame; events go into the per-frame job queue. These packets modified memory directly or were added to a job queue of events that had to happen that frame. We started with a very simple trampoline: pushf pusha nop popa popf retf When Borland's overlay loader swaps a code page in, it walks the chain of saved BP frames on the stack and patches any return address that points into an overlay. The hand-made stub had no frame, so the walk read garbage and the game died at random moments. This was a constant thorn in our side from October to December. The fix was to make the trampoline look like a Borland function: push bp mov bp, sp nop (0x90) ; welcome to the 0x90's pop bp retf frame start 0560:20E3 trampoline stub 55 push bp 8B EC mov bp,sp 90 nop ← hook point 5D pop bp CB retf job queue (DOSBox side) fire(ship 1, gun 2) · damage(src, dst, qty, seed) spawn(situation 3, ship 7) · despawn(12) · chat(…) from the network and local events game function call far stubNNN:xxxx … retf finish(): read AX jump next job? inject the call retf → the nop again queue empty: resume the frame A proper Borland frame around a 0x90 nop, which DOSBox monitors to inject the next queued call. The retf lands directly on the nop again until the queue empties out. We configured DOSBox to notice when the program counter reached the nop and instead inject its call from the job queue of things that should happen. The job queue was based on what was necessary to make the game function correctly in a multiplayer scenario. In October 2017 we noticed that ephemeral objects would be located in different slots for different players. Having the new hook from DOSBox also let us determine when the function had returned, so we could note down which numeric slot a new ship or projectile had been spawned into. Ephemeral objects had their own spawn rules and could occupy shared areas of the 61 entity slots. We modified the location that ephemeral objects were placed in so we could confine them to slots 12 to 15 and keep multiplayer locations consistent. In December we decided to change the client to store a mapping of server ship IDs to local IDs, so we could stop forcing the spawn function return. This allowed packets to translate between local and host IDs. Finally asteroids started to work in multiplayer. server slots client slots 0 leader 1 wingman 2 Tiger's Claw 3 Dralthi 4 Dralthi 12 laser bolt 13 laser bolt 0 wingman 1 leader 2 Tiger's Claw 3 Dralthi 5 Dralthi 14 laser bolt 12 laser bolt server id → local id 0 → 1 1 → 0 2 → 2 3 → 3 4 → 5 12 → 14 13 → 12 packet ship id local slot The same ships can appear in different slots on two machines. In 2018 we focused on animating explosions, missiles, and autopilot. The search continued for both success and defeat In June of 2019 we noted the mission victory calculation was flaky and finicky. We decided to conduct a binary search to find the location of the actual victory point tally. We copied the entire 64K data segment across the network, and slowly cut it in half. After many bisections, we located 80 bytes at 13D3:D248 which held the mission tree. And in October we found the overall victory point counter at 13D3:C280 and mission numbers at 13D3:C255 and C256 , which allowed us to select the mission to play from a dropdown, years later. 0000 8000 FFFF 1 FAIL (0, 32768) 2 OK (32768, 32768) 3 OK (49152, 16384) 4 OK but no landing sprite (53248, 8192) 5 OK (53248, 2048) 6 OK (53760, 256) 7 FAIL (53760, 128) 8 OK (53832, 128) 9 OK (53832, 80) 10 FAIL (53832, 64) dseg:D248, 80 bytes navPointState[]: 25-byte records flag byte ORed at ovr134:122F: or [bx-2DA2],dl Bisection of the data segment down to 80 bytes. And finally the joy of combined words In early 2020, we identified the function that played comm text. This allowed us to send chat over the network and hook typed chat directly into the system so it played using the wingman's VDU. It allowed a very immersive way to chat that reminded us of some of the frenetic sequences in the game. Both pilots typing, sending messages to the other. Some final work in 2020 left the game in a playable state, but we were out of ideas on how to actually share the fun with friends. Expecting people to locate a copy of that old game, compile or download a strange version of DOSBox, share each other's public IPs and punch the firewalls and play together was sadly a bridge too far. We had a few family playthroughs but the game rested on GitHub, mostly idle. finding data and code making the game do things 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 Oct 2015 first dumps, position Sep 2016 snapshot compare tool Nov 2016 right/up/forward, slot 3D, 256 = 1.0 Jul 2017 do_damage Jun–Jul 2019 bisection → D248 Oct 2019 victory points, mission numbers Jan 2020 comm text Dec 2016 – Mar 2017 injected calls, main-loop hook Aug 2017 protobuf over TCP Oct–Dec 2017 trampoline, push bp, slots 12–15, ID map 2018 explosions, missiles, autopilot Mar 2020 chat in the comm panel Oct 2020 playable state Wing Commander Multiplayer discovery timeline. And in 2026, machine assisted development helped us laugh together Until now. With the advent of widespread WebRTC, robust emscripten support, and a new system we put together called lobbylink, the time seemed right to revive the project and share it more widely. lobbylink I built https://github.com/danielrh/lobbylink which is a simple golang lobby system, depending only on a websocket library, that orchestrates peer to peer WebRTC connections. It can run on any small server and simply allows players to connect to one another using WebRTC and a shared room code. The server has a static allowlist of origins and can let browsers or client software in almost any language connect to it with a room code. The room code is used to locate other players with the same room code and they get notified of all joiners in that room. The server also runs coturn and mints TURN credentials in its joined reply, so players behind restrictive firewalls can join. pilot A's browser DOSBox (wasm) WC.EXE + hooks lobbylink client lobbylink server (Go) rooms by room code static allowlist relays WebRTC signaling pilot B's browser DOSBox (wasm) WC.EXE + hooks lobbylink client home router / NAT home router / NAT join: room code joiners in the room offer · answer · ICE join: room code joiners in the room offer · answer · ICE WebRTC data channel: the game's packets · voice TURN relay (fallback) The lobby allows people with the same room code to communicate directly with one another using WebRTC. TURN relay helps establish connections when nothing else is an option. pilot A's browser lobbylink server pilot B's browser join WC1-4821 joined: player 0, ICE servers join WC1-4821 joined: player 1, ICE servers player-joined: 1 offer (from the lower id) answer ICE candidates data channel open · player 0 hosts Room code join steps. I ported over the transport to lobbylink and asked an LLM to configure the build scripts to target emscripten and take a GOG Inno Setup installer package of Wing Commander and unzip it and use it as data files for emscripten. The combination of these makes it possible to download Wing Commander from GOG, drag and drop it into the client-side browser storage, enter a room code, and play. The game is playable at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox/ and the emulator is at https://github.com/danielrh/wcmulti . And as an added bonus I asked an LLM to add voice chat as well for realtime voice in game using a second WebRTC peer connection to carry audio, if people choose. And so we can fly and laugh together.

title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
body_text: Progress on provable inference for large language models \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude 01 Executive summary Progress on provable inference for large language models Read the technical report 01 Executive summary 02 Introduction 03 Trust challenges in AI proliferation 04 Our system: FlashProve 05 Trustworthiness from formal verification 06 Prior work 07 Limitations Published Nov 2, 2026 Team Frontier Red Team Topics Transparency Cybersecurity Global stability Open source Coding See more... Related articles Frontier Red Team Oct 22, 2026 LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale View more Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL) Executive summary When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements. Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows: Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library. Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6 . Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system. Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees. Today we are releasing five artifacts: The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications; A technical report explaining the details of our system; A (Claude-written) protocol specification document; Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing. We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license. 1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it. Introduction When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone. However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford. The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation. One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights. Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference . For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length). The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference. We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development , in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees , in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators , and more. Trust challenges in AI proliferation The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI). Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” ( zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge ). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier , by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation. Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them. Challenge 1: pacing Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used . For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference? How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information. 2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side. Challenge 2: tamper detection As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets . An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses . The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap , Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “ We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights. ” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method. 3 How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API. Challenge 3: text provenance One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version . In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model ? How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response. For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens). Challenge 4: model approval Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe , rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served ? How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request. A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges. Our system: FlashProve FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report ; here we outline the system. FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover ) and a user (the verifier ). It is split into two phases: In the offline phase , the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase. In the online phase , upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement: The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated. Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens. Guarantees A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties: A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness). An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier. A proof file cannot be forged (soundness). It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover. Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial. A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge). The verifier learns nothing about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden. A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness). The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure. Evaluation We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU. Prover. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores. The offline phase runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the technical report , the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The online phase , on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB. Verifier. The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks. Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM , a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried. Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments , which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report. Engineering the system FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report . Here we highlight a few: The prover's work is proportional to the experts that actually ran. In a MoE model a token uses ~17B of the 400B parameters, and the prover's work per token is proportional to those ~17B instead of all parameters (the proof still hides which experts were chosen). Requests are proved in batches, after the fact. The prover reads finished text in one parallel pass (as in prefill), and it opens the commitment to the weights once per batch instead of once per request. The system is designed to fit on a single GPU. The model weights at each layer are split to segments and are proven one segment of layers at a time. The weights are kept in ordinary memory and streamed in, so a single 80 GB GPU, with ~290 GB of host memory beside it, suffices. Post-hoc versus in-line When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report . Trustworthiness from formal verification Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today? The answer is formal verification : we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties: Completeness : if the statement is correct, the resulting proof is accepted by the verifier. Soundness : any fake proof is rejected by the verifier (except with negligible probability). Zero knowledge : the proof reveals no information about the weights of the model, beyond what the verifier can infer from the response itself. 4 These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions. Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this. Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction. For soundness, we only need the verifier code to be correct (the entire value of having “proofs” is that you can fully distrust the prover if you trust the verifier). We provide an executable Lean verifier, alongside the C++ verifier. The Lean verifier runs more slowly, but Lean proves that it accepts only what the verifier in our soundness theorem accepts. Nevertheless, the C++ verifier is the one to use day to day: it carries no formal guarantee, and it agrees with the Lean verifier on every proof in our tests. For completeness, the threat model does not assume adversarial attacks (the prover and verifier are honest). Therefore, a Lean verifier lets us gain confidence through standard software testing that the honest prover produces accepting proofs: run the prover on a correct statement, and then the Lean verifier on the resulting proof. For zero knowledge, we only need the prover to be correct. However, unlike the verifier, the prover is an expensive procedure, and it would be impractical to run a Lean prover. We do not provide facilitations here: we expect that any prover that wants to hide the weights of a model they are serving has access to enough resources for careful agentic and/or human security audits to ensure equivalence to the Lean prover. Prior work Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al . (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet. Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. EZKL (2023) proved a 1M-parameter GPT-style transformer in about 966 s per token (≈0.001 tok/s). Performance progressively improved: zkLLM (2024) proved LLaMA-2-13B on a 2,048-token input in about 15 minutes on GPU, which is ≈0.001 tok/s per new token, or ~2.5 tok/s in the batch. In 2025, zkGPT reduced GPT-2 to 21.8 s (≈0.05 tok/s), zkPyTorch proved Llama-3 8B at ~150 s per token on one CPU core (≈0.007 tok/s), and ZKTorch proved GPT-J (6B) in about 20 minutes (≈0.001 tok/s). VerInf proved Llama 4 Maverick (the same 400B-parameter MoE model we prove) at ≈0.02 tok/s. DeepProve , a current peer-reviewed state of the art, certifies an entire generated sequence with a single forward pass. It reaches about 2.9 tok/s for GPT-2 and 1.4 tok/s for Gemma 3 on one machine, and 31 tok/s distributed. SASH's prover (2026) reached ≈1.25 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B on a single H100. Recently commercial efforts have reached impressive numbers, with Attestable proving Gemma 4 31B at 53–77 tok/s on a single H100; at the time of writing, Attestable has not released a corresponding open source library. The above numbers speak to the precipitous progress of provable inference in the past years. They should update our priors on what it is possible to prove in zero-knowledge. In 2024, zkLLM proved a 13B model at about 2.5 tokens/second on one A100. The only earlier proof of Llama 4 Maverick that we know of, VerInf, reports 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens on a DGX Spark, with a 93.6 GB proof which took almost a day to verify. FlashProve proves the same model at 110 tokens/second on a single H100, with 19 MB proofs that can be verified in seconds. Attestable independently reports 53–77 tokens/second for a dense 31B model. We believe that the progress should transfer to more models and architectures, yielding a flexible and powerful tool with overhead over native computation of roughly 2 orders of magnitude (about 70 to 95 times in our measurements), much less than previously expected. Limitations This release is a research prototype, and has the following technical limitations: No formal guarantees on fast executable code. We provide a Lean implementation of the protocol (including an executable “slow” Lean verifier), along with security properties proved in Lean. The paper and the fast executable code are derived from the Lean protocol, but we do not guarantee that all three (Lean, paper, code) match each other. The proof is about an integer model under greedy decoding. We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position and no longer exactly match the computation proved. The integer version is generally expected and empirically tested to be within some small error rate of true floating-point inference generically (even taking into account non-determinism of floating-point computations), though this does not cover adversarially designed prompts. Architecture hiding. Our system assumes the served model uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, in which each transformer layer’s feed-forward block is replaced by multiple expert sub-networks and a router that activates only a small subset of experts for each token and our system uses the MoE structure for efficiency gains. Other architectures, such as the dense models, are also widely used and its description may contain intellectual-property the model provider would like to keep secret. Indeed, one could also imagine a system that further hides the architecture of the model: the prover commits to both the weights and the architecture (i.e., the “executable code” for inference) via a hiding commitment and the verifier’s claim is about checking the execution of that committed executable on the commitment model. Side channel attacks. The current guarantee of the protocol is that the proof itself reveals nothing about the weights of the committed model. However, “side channel attacks”, such as measuring the time it takes to produce a proof, could potentially reveal information about the weights. We consider this out of scope for this release. Longer contexts. The system currently proves inference over contexts of up to 1,024 tokens. This is quite short in comparison to the contexts accumulated in chat settings. Ideally, this context length could be increased to full context windows for frontier models (which regularly have context windows of 100s of thousands to millions of tokens). Footnotes 01 For our open-source research, we used Llama 4 Maverick (400B parameters), a model by Meta, in a third party’s public 4-bit conversion on Hugging Face. The weights are not in this release: readers download them from Hugging Face themselves, under Meta’s Llama 4 license. In this release we share small things computed from the model, such as commitment IDs, checksums, performance numbers and some parameter settings (THIRD_PARTY.md lists them all), and we encourage readers to verify our results themselves, as well as to adapt this work to other models. Running the full example takes a large GPU machine and access to Meta’s tokenizers. 02 The specific information kept hidden depends on the system design. In our work we hide the weights, but not the architecture. In future work we plan to also hide architecture details. (In principle hiding all model’s details is possible, and the question is how efficiently it can be done.) 03 In the update from October 19, 2026, we also changed the goal name: we now use the term “inference verification” rather than “provable inference”. Our original aim was to achieve high assurance in the integrity of our token stream, which can be achieved in several ways, and “provable inference” suggests a narrower approach than we believe is necessary. Separately from that prototype, we have pushed forward on cryptographic proofs for inference, which are one of those ways to achieve high assurance in our token stream. 04 The model’s architecture is not hidden. Additionally hiding architecture details is left to future work. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Working from above, it reaches floors too cluttered for any wheeled or legged robot. And since the lifting force is shared by all motors, payload capacity scales with their combined torque instead of a single actuator's, peaking near the center of the room where the lines share the load most evenly. What do I need to install Stringman? A room where you can secure the anchors to studs or columns. A computer to run the controller with some NPU or GPU (macs work great!) A handheld drill A step ladder that lets you reach the ceiling. 1 Secure the cleats 2 Hang the anchors 3 Run calibration Secure the cleats to wall studs near the ceiling with wood screws, or to columns with ratchet straps. Hang the anchors and connect the lines to the gripper. Run calibration. This hands off process takes about five minutes and adapts Stringman to your room. Step-by-step: picture guide or video guide Have a ceiling fan? That's fine. The original prototype was built in a room with a ceiling fan, and it still runs there today. Mount the anchors at or below the level of the blades and the lines can't physically reach it. Training new models Several methods are available for control with default models for automatic grasping, target, and destination selection to make it easy to quickly build new behaviors. Stringman is fully capable of LeRobot control using including Pi.05, JEPA, Multitask DiT, and others. Collecting training data for new behaviors can be done from the UI, and as few as 50 episodes can be enough for certain models like DiT to learn a behavior. However, when parked, they are up near the ceiling and out of the way. Clutter on the ceiling is preferable to clutter on the floor in our opinion. If you need to remove the anchors, they can be detached from their mounts without tools, leaving a relatively small white cleat on the wall. Can it be used in rooms with ceiling fans? Yes, it's just a matter of mounting the anchors at or below the level of the fan, making it physically impossible for the lines or marker tag to touch it. Similarly, the work area can be shrunk to exclude low hanging light fixtures if they are off to the side, but if the center of the room does contain low hanging objects, Stringman cannot be installed in that room. What happens if someone is caught in the wires? When reaching a tension limit of 28 newtons (about the weight of a backpack), all motors relax and the lines can be pulled loose. Since they are overhead most of the time, it's uncommon for people to collide with them. Can it be controlled remotely? Not by default, but if you bind it with neufangled.com/playroom then you or anyone you share access with can operate it from anywhere, and access can be revoked at any time. Neufangled Robotics does not store any of the information from your robot that is forwarded through its servers. Remote Management For those who prefer to make the trade-off by binding their robot to an account, our web-based console allows you to monitor and control Stringman from anywhere. Think of it as a security camera with a hand. If you do decide that you would like to make use of our cloud telemetry relay, You can use it, and still go back to a completely lan only mode whenever you want. Your data is never collected. Set Your Drop Bins Organizing your home is a physical process, not a coding task. Use our clip-on fiducial tags to designate your laundry bin, toy box, and trash can. Stringman maps these locations visually. You don't need to tag individual pieces of clutter—just the destination. If there's something you never want it to pick up, you can mark that item as off-limits. Networks trained to control stringman have learned that the word "toybox" refers to that tag, so you can use it to mark anything even if it doesn't look like the toyboxes from our training set. You can also use the tags as arbitrary source and destination markers for ferry jobs, such as carrying items from one robot arm to another. or carrying laundry from the ground to a robotic folding station For Educators A classroom with a Stringman robot gives your students a chance to become familiar with robotics fundamentals such as inverse kinematics, telemetry, and imitation learning while controlling an exotic and capable flying gripper. If you have walls and a MacBook, you're more than halfway there. Cross embodiment is one of the biggest challenges in robotics, and showing that a model can operate a vastly different body type is a stronger result than moving it from one bimanual robot to another. Our datasets are public on Hugging Face , there's a controller-in-the-loop MuJoCo sim, and Stringman works with LeRobot, making it one of the most inexpensive robots to test on and a natural capstone project. No Charging Downtime Mobile robots spend a significant portion of their time charging. Because Stringman is a powered from the wall, it's always ready for work. Furthermore, by removing the heavy battery pack, we've increased the payload capacity per dollar compared to mobile platforms that must waste energy carrying their own power supply. The gripper's power is delivered via one of the support cables. A two-conductor FEP jacketed twisted pair cable with a tensile strength of 50N. Swing Cancellation What's that pole for? Stringman's gripper hangs below the pivot point so it can reach the floor next to beds and tables. This additional linkage could allow unconstrained motion so Stringman employs active swing cancellation algorithms to counteract momentum, without adding the cost of any additional motors. This ensures the gripper remains steady and predictable even during rapid cross-room traversals. There's a whole video about swing cancellation if you're curious about how it works! Wrist and Fingers Often, a simple solution that gets the job done has more value than a complex one. Stringman uses a two fingered gripper with a wrist. This is enough dexterity for the clutter it is designed to pick up, keeping weight and cost low and reliability high. In our household tests we have determined that more layers of grip tape is simply a better return on investment than more articulated fingers. The gripper can rotate it's wrist to better place the fingers around flat sided or long objects. Blends In Like the fishing line, the anchors themselves are not trying to be seen. The cover can be painted or re-printed to match your room. Customize Your Look The Stringman faceplate is easily swappable. Grab the STL or bambu 3MF files to print your faceplate in any color. ¶ kitty is a feature-rich, cross-platform, fast , GPU based terminal. To update kitty , follow the instructions . Recent major new features ¶ Docked windows [0.50] ¶ kitty windows can now be docked to an edge of another window or of the tab. Docked windows are placed outside the layout, making them perfect for status bars, file trees or a shell kept next to your editor. A dock attached to a window follows it around, moving with it to other tabs and closing when it closes. Create docks with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock . Docks are saved in sessions too. Restore after logout [0.50] ¶ Like other applications, kitty can now save its state when you log out, restart or shut down your computer, and restore it the next time it starts. Simply set restore_session_after_logout and every kitty instance comes back with all its OS Windows, tabs and windows in place, including their scrollback. On macOS, the saved state is encrypted using a key stored in your keychain. See Restoring kitty after logging out for details. Custom shaders [0.49] ¶ kitty now has official support for Custom Shaders . These can be used for all manner of graphical effects, from animated backgrounds to focus highlighting to animations that change how cursor movements or mouse clicks are visualised. See the documentation for a video gallery showcasing various custom shaders that ship with kitty. Performance improvements [0.49] ¶ This release saw tons of performance work focused on improving throughput making kitty even faster than it already is. Real world effective throughput should see a 15-35% improvement depending on workload. Some details: Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text with a scrollback buffer much larger than the CPU cache by ~35% by prefetching scrollback memory before it is written to Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text by ~50% for ASCII and ~15% for Unicode by writing runs of plain ASCII chars to the screen in batches and skipping unnecessary bookkeeping in the scrolling and tab handling hot paths Speed up SIMD UTF-8 decoding: ~20% faster for ASCII and ~50% faster for multi-byte text on both x86 and ARM, by processing pairs of vectors of plain ASCII text at a time and compacting decoded codepoints within 128-bit lanes, avoiding expensive cross-lane operations. Also add an AVX-512 based decoder, another ~75% faster for multi-byte text, used automatically on CPUs that support it (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+). Improve throughput when processing escape code heavy input by ~30% by taking the input buffer lock once per buffer of input rather than once per escape code and using cheaper arithmetic to parse CSI parameters Improve throughput when processing large amounts of plain text by another ~10% by finding runs of printable ASCII chars with SIMD , filling cells using wide stores and skipping unnecessary work in the scrolling hot path when there are no images Speed up pixel compositing with SIMD vectorization: alpha blending of graphics protocol images and animation frames is 2-3.5x faster and glyph alpha masks are composited onto canvases using the same vectorized primitives. Cache HarfBuzz results for repeated short runs (≤32 cells) so redraws of the same on-screen text are not reshaped Vertical tabs [0.48] ¶ kitty now has support for vertical tabs along the left or right edge of the OS Window. Useful for people that have wide aspect ratio windows. Drag and drop for terminal programs [0.47] ¶ kitty now has a new Drag and Drop kitten that allows you to seamlessly drag and drop files between kitty and any GUI program like the OS file manager or a webapp. It even works over SSH! It is powered by a new protocol allowing the use of drag and drop from any TUI program. Mousing [0.46] ¶ kitty already had excellent mouse support, but now it is taking it to the next level. The kitty scrollback buffer grew support for smooth scrolling and momentum based scrolling for a natural, smooth and kinetic scrolling experience. Additionally, you can now drag kitty tabs around with the mouse to re-order them, move them to another kitty OS Window or even detach them into their own OS Window. Finally, a long requested feature, the ability to resize kitty windows (aka splits) with the mouse was implemented. Choose files, fast [0.45] ¶ A new kitten to select files at the speed of thought with a keyboard first interface and support for content previews of text files with syntax highlighting, images, videos, e-books and more. Allows you to select files for use at the shell prompt or other terminal workflows with just a few keystrokes, similar to how fuzzy finders like fzf operate, but designed for files in particular, leveraging the various innovations of kitty such as image display and variable sized text. On Linux, it can even be used as a drop in replacement for the File Open/Save dialog boxes in GUI programs. Sessions [0.43] ¶ kitty has long had support for Sessions , aka simple text files where you can define what tabs, windows and programs you wish to run in kitty. Now in addition to that kitty has the ability to create and switch between sessions with a single keypress and also to manually setup some tabs/windows in kitty and save it as a session file , for seamless and intuitive session file creation. A scrollbar for the kitty scrollback [0.43] ¶ A long requested feature, kitty has finally gotten a scrollbar that can be used with the mouse for browsing its scrollback. The bar appear automatically when you start scrolling backwards and is extensively configurable in kitty.conf. Note that the old scrollback_indicator_opacity option is deprecated. Multiple cursors [0.43] ¶ kitty has pioneered a new escape code protocol that allows terminal applications to use multiple cursors, rendered natively. These are typically used in editors to make the same edit at multiple locations. Now terminal based editors can use properly rendered native cursors, just like their GUI cousins, at last. Access kitty with a single keypress [0.42] ¶ Screenshots macOS ¶ Linux ¶ A sample panel on Linux ¶ How the screenshots were generated . kitty now has a Quake like floating, translucent terminal window, so you can access all that kitty goodness instantly with a single keypress. See the screenshots on the side and head over to the kitten page for details on how to set it up . Multiple sized text [0.40] ¶ kitty is the first major terminal to introduce the concept of multiple sized text. Terminal programs running in kitty can now opt-in to use and display text in multiple font sizes both larger and smaller than the base font size. This is done in a backwards compatible, opt-in way that does not affect how traditional terminal programs work at all. For details on the new feature and how to use it, see The text sizing protocol . Cursor trails [0.37] ¶ Show an animated trail when the text cursor makes large jumps making it easy to follow cursor movements. Inspired by the similar feature in neovide, but works with terminal multiplexers and kitty windows as well. See the pull request for a demonstration video. This feature is optional and must be turned on by the cursor_trail option in kitty.conf . Variable font support [0.36] ¶ Terminal aficionados spend all day staring at text, so getting text rendering just right is very important. In that spirit, kitty now supports OpenType Variable fonts . These allow precise customisation of font characteristics, such as weight and spacing. Not only that, kitty now has a new choose-fonts kitten that provides a UI for choosing fonts with support for font features, variable fonts and previews of how the font will look. This is in addition to its existing best-in-class font customization abilities, such as: symbol_map , text_composition_strategy , font_features and modify_font . kitty knows text rendering is important, and goes the extra mile for it. Desktop notifications [0.36] ¶ kitty now has a notify kitten that can be used to display desktop notifications from the command line, even over SSH. It has support for icons, buttons, updating notifications, waiting till the notification is closed, etc. The underlying Desktop notifications protocol has been expanded to support all these features. Wayland goodies [0.34] ¶ Wayland users should rejoice as kitty now comes with major Wayland quality-of-life improvements: Draw GPU accelerated desktop panels and background running arbitrary terminal programs. For example, run btop as your desktop background Background blur for transparent windows is now supported under KDE using a custom KDE specific protocol The kitty window decorations in GNOME are now fully functional with buttons and they follow system dark/light mode automatically kitty now supports fractional scaling in Wayland which means pixel perfect rendering when you use a fractional scale with no wasted performance on resizing an overdrawn pixmap in the compositor With this release kitty’s Wayland support is now on par with X11, provided you use a decent Wayland compositor. Detailed list of changes ¶ 0.50.0 [2026-11-03] ¶ Allow docking kitty windows to the edges of other windows or of the tab, for status bars, file trees, etc. Create them with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock , see Docked windows A new option restore_session_after_logout to save the state of every kitty instance, including scrollback, when logging out, restarting or shutting down and restore it the next time kitty starts. On macOS, the state is encrypted with a key in the keychain. On Linux, it requires the Inhibit desktop portal. See Restoring kitty after logging out ( #1197 , #10659 ) Allow using tabs like named workspaces: A new launch --focus-existing option to focus an existing window or tab instead of creating a new one, a new by-title value for launch --location to keep tabs in alphabetical order and new options for kitten @ detach-window and the detach_window action to send windows to a named tab, creating it if needed ( #10627 ) Wayland: The client side window decorations used on compositors such as GNOME now look like native GNOME decorations and follow the desktop titlebar font, text scaling, button layout and titlebar click action settings ( #10766 ) Wayland: Support touchscreens. A tap is a click, a finger that moves scrolls with momentum, and a finger held still before it moves selects text ( #5432 , #10551 ) Custom shaders: New cursor-trail-railgun , cursor-trail-torpedo and cursor-trail-pixiedust shaders that make particles fly off the cursor as it moves, in the style of neovide. Shaders can now be controlled with key presses via the new shader_event action (see Controlling shaders with key presses ), can be faded in and out, reversed and looped with new animation_* pipeline directives and can define a pointer_map() function so that clicks and selections land on the text shown under the mouse, which the crt shader now uses, see Shaders that move content . Also fix animations becoming jerky after kitty has been running for a few hours, shaders specified by path not being found and various pipeline bugs ( #10587 , #10667 , #10693 , #10595 , #10694 , #10639 ) Graphics protocol: Add two new indexed color image formats whose pixels are indices into the terminal color palette, so that images change color along with the color scheme, and allow clients to detect support for individual protocol features, such as animation and Unicode placeholders, via the new e query key, see Querying support for protocol features ( #9379 , #10732 ) Support the Program Status Protocol (OSC 7501) that lets programs report whether they are working, finished, failed or blocked waiting on the user.
