See tab_bar_style and tab_fade for details. The old look can be restored by setting tab_bar_style to separator . Pre-compiled binaries with all bundled dependencies for Linux ( #595 ) A new kitten to create dock panels on X11 desktops showing the output from arbitrary terminal programs. Reduce data sent to the GPU per render by 30% ( commit: 8dea5b3e3 ) Implement changing the font size for individual top level (OS) windows ( #408 ) When viewing the scrollback in less using ctrl+shift+h and kitty is currently scrolled, position the scrollback in less to match kitty’s scroll position. ( #148 ) ssh kitten: Support all SSH options. It can now be aliased directly to ssh for convenience. ( #591 ) icat kitten: Add kitty +kitten icat --print-window-size to easily detect the window size in pixels from scripting languages ( #581 ) hints kitten: Allow selecting hashes from the terminal with ctrl+shift+p>h useful for git commits. ( #604 ) Allow specifying initial window size in number of cells in addition to pixels ( #436 ) Add a setting to control the margins to the left and right of the tab-bar ( #584 ) When closing a tab switch to the last active tab instead of the right-most tab ( #585 ) Wayland: Fix kitty not starting when using wl_roots based compositors ( #157 ) Wayland: Fix mouse wheel/touchpad scrolling in opposite direction to other apps ( #594 ) macOS: Fix the new OS window keyboard shortcut ( ctrl+shift+n ) not working if no kitty window currently has focus. ( #524 ) macOS: Keep kitty running even when the last window is closed. This is in line with how applications are supposed to behave on macOS ( #543 ). There is a new option ( macos_quit_when_last_window_closed ) to control this. macOS: Add macOS standard shortcuts for copy, paste and new OS window (⌘+C, ⌘+V, ⌘+N) Add a config option ( editor ) to set the EDITOR kitty uses ( #580 ) Add a config option ( x11_hide_window_decorations ) to hide window decorations under X11/Wayland ( #607 ) Add an option to @set-window-title to make the title change non-permanent ( #592 ) Add support for the CSI t escape code to query window and cell sizes ( #581 ) Linux: When using layouts that map the keys to non-ascii characters, map shortcuts using the ascii equivalents, from the default layout. ( #606 ) Linux: Fix fonts not being correctly read from TrueType Collection (.ttc) files ( #577 ) Fix inactive_text_alpha also applying to the tab bar ( #612 ) hints kitten : Fix a regression that caused some blank lines to be not be displayed. Linux: Include a man page and the HTML docs when building the linux-package Remote control: Fix kitty @ sometimes failing to read the response from kitty. ( #614 ) Fix kitty @ set-colors not working with the window border colors. ( #623 ) Fix a regression in 0.10 that caused incorrect rendering of the status bar in irssi when used inside screen. ( #621 ) 0.10.1 [2018-05-24] ¶ Add a kitten to easily ssh into servers that automatically copies the terminfo files over. kitty +kitten ssh myserver . diff kitten: Make the keyboard shortcuts configurable ( #563 ) Allow controlling background_opacity via either keyboard shortcuts or remote control. Note that you must set dynamic_background_opacity yes in kitty.conf first. ( #569 ) diff kitten: Add keybindings to scroll by page diff kitten: Fix incorrect syntax highlighting for a few file formats such as yaml macOS: Fix regression that caused the macos_option_as_alt setting to always be disabled for all OS windows in a kitty instance after the first window ( #571 ) Fix Ctrl+Alt+Space not working in normal and application keyboard modes ( #562 ) 0.10.0 [2018-05-21] ¶ A diff kitten to show side-by-side diffs with syntax highlighting and support for images. See diff kitten . Make windows in the various kitty layouts manually resizable. See Layouts for details. Implement support for the SGR faint escape code to make text blend into the background ( #446 ). Make the hints kitten a little smarter ( commit: ad1109b6f ) so that URLs that stretch over multiple lines are detected. Also improve detection of surrounding brackets/quotes. Make the kitty window id available as the environment variable KITTY_WINDOW_ID ( #532 ). Add a “fat” layout that is similar to the “tall” layout but vertically oriented. Expand environment variables in config file include directives Allow programs running in kitty to read/write from the clipboard ( commit: 889ca7791 ). By default only writing is allowed. This feature is supported in many terminals, search for OSC 52 clipboard to find out more about using it. Fix moving cursor outside a defined page area incorrectly causing the cursor to be placed inside the page area. Caused incorrect rendering in neovim, in some situations ( #542 ). Render a couple more powerline symbols directly, bypassing the font ( #550 ). Fix ctrl+alt+<special> not working in normal and application keyboard ( #548 ). Partial fix for rendering Right-to-left languages like Arabic. Rendering of Arabic is never going to be perfect, but now it is at least readable. Fix Ctrl+backspace acting as plain backspace in normal and application keyboard modes ( #538 ). Have the paste_from_selection action paste from the clipboard on platforms that do not have a primary selection such as Wayland and macOS ( #529 ) Fix cursor_stop_blinking_after=0 not working ( #530 ) 0.9.1 [2018-05-05] ¶ Show a bell symbol on the tab if a bell occurs in one of the windows in the tab and the window is not the currently focused window Change the window border color if a bell occurs in an unfocused window. Can be disabled by setting the bell_border_color to be the same as the inactive_border_color. macOS: Add support for dead keys Unicode input: When searching by name search for prefix matches as well as whole word matches Dynamically allocate the memory used for the scrollback history buffer. Reduces startup memory consumption when using very large scrollback buffer sizes. Add an option to not request window attention on bell. Remote control: Allow matching windows by number (visible position). macOS: Fix changing tab title and kitty shell not working When triple-clicking select all wrapped lines belonging to a single logical line. hints kitten: Detect bracketed URLs and don’t include the closing bracket in the URL. When calling pass_selection_to_program use the current directory of the child process as the cwd of the program. Add macos_hide_from_tasks option to hide kitty from the macOS task switcher macOS: When the macos_titlebar_color is set to background change the titlebar colors to match the current background color of the active kitty window Add a setting to clear all shortcuts defined up to that point in the config file(s) Add a setting (kitty_mod) to change the modifier used by all the default kitty shortcuts, globally Fix Shift+function key not working Support the F13 to F25 function keys Don’t fail to start if the user deletes the hintstyle key from their fontconfig configuration. When rendering a private use unicode codepoint and a space as a two cell ligature, set the foreground colors of the space cell to match the colors of the first cell. Works around applications like powerline that use different colors for the two cells. Fix passing @text to other programs such as when viewing the scrollback buffer not working correctly if kitty is itself scrolled up. Fix window focus gained/lost events not being reported to child programs when switching windows/tabs using the various keyboard shortcuts. Fix tab title not changing to reflect the window title when switching between different windows in a tab Ignore -e if it is specified on the command line. This is for compatibility with broken software that assumes terminals should run with an -e option to execute commands instead of just passing the commands as arguments. 0.9.0 [2018-04-15] ¶ A new kitty command shell to allow controlling kitty via commands. Press ctrl+shift+escape to run the shell. The hints kitten has become much more powerful. Now in addition to URLs you can use it to select word, paths, filenames, lines, etc. from the screen. These can be inserted into the terminal, copied to clipboard or sent to external programs. Linux: Switch to libxkbcommon for keyboard handling. It allows kitty to support XCompose and dead keys and also react to keyboard remapping/layout change without needing a restart. Add support for multiple-key-sequence shortcuts A new remote control command set-colors to change the current and/or configured colors. When double-clicking to select a word, select words that continue onto the next/prev line as well. Add an include directive for the config files to read multiple config files Improve mouse selection for windows with padding. Moving the mouse into the padding area now acts as if the mouse is over the nearest cell. Allow setting all 256 terminal colors in the config file Fix using kitty --single-instance to open a new window in a running kitty instance, not respecting the --directory flag URL hints: Exclude trailing punctuation from URLs URL hints: Launch the browser from the kitty parent process rather than the hints kitten. Fixes launching on some systems where xdg-open doesn’t like being run from a kitten. Allow using rectangle select mode by pressing shift in addition to the rectangle select modifiers even when the terminal program has grabbed the mouse. 0.8.4 [2018-03-31] ¶ Fix presence of XDG_CONFIG_DIRS and absence of XDG_CONFIG_HOME preventing kitty from starting Revert change in last release to cell width calculation. Instead just clip the right edges of characters that overflow the cell by at most two pixels 0.8.3 [2018-03-29] ¶ Fix a regression that broke the visual bell and invert screen colors escape code Allow double-click and triple-click + drag to extend selections word at a time or line at a time Add a keyboard shortcut to set the tab title Fix setting window title to empty via OSC escape code not working correctly Linux: Fix cell width calculation incorrect for some fonts (cell widths are now calculated by actually rendering bitmaps, which is slower but more accurate) Allow specifying a system wide kitty config file, for all users Add a --debug-config command line flag to output data about the system and kitty configuration. Wayland: Fix auto-repeat of keys not working 0.8.2 [2018-03-17] ¶ Allow extending existing selections by right clicking Add a configurable keyboard shortcut and remote command to set the font size to a specific value Add an option to have kitty close the window when the main processes running in it exits, even if there are still background processes writing to that terminal Add configurable keyboard shortcuts to switch to a specific layout Add a keyboard shortcut to edit the kitty config file easily macOS: Fix restoring of window size not correct on Retina screens macOS: Add a facility to specify command line arguments when running kitty from the GUI Add a focus-tab remote command Fix screen not being refreshed immediately after moving a window. Fix a crash when getting the contents of the scrollback buffer as text 0.8.1 [2018-03-09] ¶ Extend kitty’s remote control feature to work over both UNIX and TCP sockets, so now you can control kitty from across the internet, if you want to. Render private use unicode characters that are followed by a space as a two character ligature. This fixes rendering for applications that misuse private-use characters to display square symbols. Fix Unicode emoji presentation variant selector causing new a fallback font instance to be created Fix a rare error that prevented the Unicode input kitten from working sometimes Allow using Ctrl+Alt+letter in legacy keyboard modes by outputting them as Ctrl+letter and Alt+letter. This matches other terminals’ behavior. Fix cursor position off-by-one on horizontal axis when resizing the terminal Wayland: Fix auto-repeat of keys not working Wayland: Add support for window decorations provided by the Wayland shell macOS: Fix URL hints not working macOS: Fix shell not starting in login mode on some computers macOS: Output errors into console.app when running as a bundle 0.8.0 [2018-02-24] ¶ A framework for kittens, that is, small terminal programs designed to run inside kitty and extend its capabilities. Examples include unicode input and selecting URLs with the keyboard. Input arbitrary unicode characters by pressing Ctrl+Shift+u. You can choose characters by name, by hex code, by recently used, etc. There is even and editable Favorites list. Open URLs using only the keyboard. kitty has a new “hints mode”. Press Ctrl+Shift+e and all detected URLs on the screen are highlighted with a key to press to open them. The facility is customizable so you can change what is detected as a URL and which program is used to open it. Add an option to change the titlebar color of kitty windows on macOS Only consider Emoji characters with default Emoji presentation to be two cells wide. This matches the standard. Also add support for the Unicode Emoji variation presentation selector. Prevent video tearing during high speed scrolling by syncing draws to the monitor’s refresh rate. There is a new configuration option to control this sync_to_monitor . When displaying only a single window, use the default background color of the window (which can be changed via escape codes) as the color for the margin and padding of the window. Add some non standard terminfo capabilities used by neovim and tmux. Fix large drop in performance when using multiple top-level windows on macOS Fix save/restore of window sizes not working correctly. Remove option to use system wcwidth(). Now always use a wcwidth() based on the Unicode standard. Only sane way. Fix a regression that caused a few ligature glyphs to not render correctly in rare circumstances. Browsing the scrollback buffer now happens in an overlay window instead of a new window/tab. 0.7.1 [2018-01-31] ¶ Add an option to adjust the width of character cells Fix selecting text with the mouse in the scrollback buffer selecting text from the line above the actually selected line Fix some italic fonts having the right edge of characters cut-off, unnecessarily 0.7.0 [2018-01-24] ¶ Allow controlling kitty from the shell prompt/scripts. You can open/close/rename windows and tabs and even send input to specific windows. See the README for details. Add option to put tab bar at the top instead of the bottom Add option to override the default shell Add “Horizontal” and “Vertical” window layouts Sessions: Allow setting titles and working directories for individual windows Option to copy to clipboard on mouse select Fix incorrect reporting of mouse move events when using the SGR protocol Make alt+backspace delete the previous word Take the mouse wheel multiplier option in to account when generating fake key scroll events macOS: Fix closing top-level window does not transfer focus to other top-level windows. macOS: Fix alt+arrow keys not working when disabling the macos_option_as_alt config option. kitty icat: Workaround for bug in ImageMagick that would cause some images to fail to display at certain sizes. Fix rendering of text with ligature fonts that do not use dummy glyphs Fix a regression that caused copying of the selection to clipboard to only copy the visible part of the selection Fix incorrect handling of some unicode combining marks that are not re-ordered Fix handling on non-BMP combining characters Drop the dependency on libunistring 0.6.1 [2017-12-28] ¶ Add an option to fade the text in inactive windows Add new actions to open windows/tabs/etc. with the working directory set to the working directory of the current window. Automatically adjust cell size when DPI changes, for example when kitty is moved from one monitor to another with a different DPI Ensure underlines are rendered even for fonts with very poor metrics Fix some emoji glyphs not colored on Linux Internal wcwidth() implementation is now auto-generated from the unicode standard database Allow configuring the modifiers to use for rectangular selection with the mouse. Fix incorrect minimum wayland version in the build script Fix a crash when detecting a URL that ends at the end of the line Fix regression that broke drawing of hollow cursor when window loses focus 0.6.0 [2017-12-18] ¶ Support background transparency via the background_opacity option. Provided that your OS/window manager supports transparency, you can now have kitty render pixels that have only the default background color as semi-transparent. Support multiple top level (OS) windows. These windows all share the sprite texture cache on the GPU, further reducing overall resource usage. Use the shortcut ctrl+shift+n to open a new top-level window. Add support for a daemon mode using the --single-instance command line option. With this option you can have only a single kitty instance running. All future invocations simply open new top-level windows in the existing instance. Support colored emoji Use CoreText instead of FreeType to render text on macOS Support running on the “low power” GPU on dual GPU macOS machines Add a new “grid” window layout Drop the dependency on glfw (kitty now uses a modified, bundled copy of glfw) Add an option to control the audio bell volume on X11 systems Add a command line switch to set the name part of the WM_CLASS window property independently. Add a command line switch to set the window title. Add more options to customize the tab-bar’s appearance (font styles and separator) Allow drag and drop of files into kitty. On drop kitty will paste the file path to the running program. Add an option to control the underline style for URL highlighting on hover X11: Set the WINDOWID environment variable Fix middle and right buttons swapped when sending mouse events to child processes Allow selecting in a rectangle by holding down Ctrl+Alt while dragging with the mouse. 0.5.1 [2017-12-01] ¶ Add an option to control the thickness of lines in box drawing characters Increase max. allowed ligature length to nine characters Fix text not vertically centered when adjusting line height Fix unicode block characters not being rendered properly Fix shift+up/down not generating correct escape codes Image display: Fix displaying images taller than two screen heights not scrolling properly 0.5.0 [2017-11-19] ¶ Add support for ligature fonts such as Fira Code, Hasklig, etc. kitty now uses harfbuzz for text shaping which allow it to support advanced OpenType features such as contextual alternates/ligatures/combining glyphs/etc. Make it easy to select fonts by allowing listing of monospace fonts using: kitty list-fonts Add an option to have window focus follow mouse Add a keyboard shortcut (ctrl+shift+f11) to toggle fullscreen mode macOS: Fix handling of option key. It now behaves just like the alt key on Linux. There is an option to make it type unicode characters instead. Linux: Add support for startup notification on X11 desktops. kitty will now inform the window manager when its startup is complete. Fix shell prompt being duplicated when window is resized Fix crash when displaying more than 64 images in the same session Add support for colons in SGR color codes. These are generated by some applications such as neovim when they mistakenly identify kitty as a libvte based terminal. Fix mouse interaction not working in apps using obsolete mouse interaction protocols Linux: no longer require glew as a dependency 0.4.2 [2017-10-23] ¶ Fix a regression in 0.4.0 that broke custom key mappings Fix a regression in 0.4.0 that broke support for non-QWERTY keyboard layouts Avoid using threads to reap zombie child processes. Also prevent kitty from hanging if the open program hangs when clicking on a URL. 0.4.0 [2017-10-22] ¶ Support for drawing arbitrary raster graphics (images) in the terminal via a new graphics protocol. kitty can draw images with full 32-bit color using both ssh connections and files/shared memory (when available) for better performance. The drawing primitives support alpha blending and z-index. Images can be drawn both above and below text. See Terminal graphics protocol . for details. Refactor kitty’s internals to make it even faster and more efficient. The CPU usage of kitty + X server while doing intensive tasks such as scrolling a file continuously in less has been reduced by 50%. There are now two configuration options repaint_delay and input_delay you can use to fine tune kitty’s performance vs CPU usage profile. The CPU usage of kitty + X when scrolling in less is now significantly better than most (all?) other terminals. See Performance . Hovering over URLs with the mouse now underlines them to indicate they can be clicked. Hold down Ctrl+Shift while clicking to open the URL. Selection using the mouse is now more intelligent. It does not add blank cells (i.e. cells that have no content) after the end of text in a line to the selection. The block cursor in now fully opaque but renders the character under it in the background color, for enhanced visibility. Allow combining multiple independent actions into a single shortcut Add a new shortcut to pass the current selection to an external program Allow creating shortcuts to open new windows running arbitrary commands. You can also pass the current selection to the command as an arguments and the contents of the screen + scrollback buffer as stdin to the command. title: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers
body_text: Verification Is Not Knowledge Cosmos Institute Subscribe Sign in Verification Is Not Knowledge Science needs more than answers Cosmos Institute and Jessica Hullman Oct 30, 2026 60 7 15 Share This is a guest essay by Jessica Hullman , Ginni Rometty Professor of Computer Science and Policy Fellow at Northwestern University. Diego Velázquez, The Fable of Arachne (c.1657) In his essay on the role that rigorous proofs play in mathematical advances, Bill Thurston writes that the measure of success in math research is “whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics.” Many recent discussions of AI for science hinge on a tension between understanding and answers. Is science about humans achieving insight, or the archiving of verifiable solutions? One side prioritizes outputs. Progress is implied to be evident in verifiable proofs of longstanding conjectures and cures for diseases, whether humans were involved in their making or not. The other side argues that human understanding is paramount, because it drives integration of new findings into the canon, because it shapes and inspires the next generation, and so on. But the first side, those who emphasize correct outputs, dismisses this as gatekeeping or nostalgia. When Terry Tao posed a thought experiment in a recent talk , asking how comfortable people would be taking a cancer treatment produced by AI, complete with a formal certificate of correctness and a passed phase 3 trial, but without any human understanding how it was found, critics suggested that Tao’s reasoning missed the point. Of course a patient with stage 4 cancer would welcome the treatment. Other examples concern ambiguity in authorship. Tom Dietterich wrote about arXiv’s growing problem with papers submitted by human authors who seem unlikely to have the expertise to understand the claims. Many questioned in response why accountability – by which I mean being answerable for a claim, able to describe what it rests on and respond when it’s challenged – should matter if verification has been solved. I suggested peer reviewers reserve their expert judgment for texts that don’t get flagged as heavily AI-written, so as to prioritize review as human exchange, but some see this as an obstruction to truth-seeking rather than an attempt to preserve it. The problem is that if we all agree that outputs matter–that we do care about the solutions to longstanding conjectures, that we do ultimately want to know how to cure diseases–then understanding appears as something separate. It’s cast as a mental state that looks optional next to the cure or the proof itself, and becomes easy to dismiss as a second-order constraint that we tack on because historically we’ve required it to arrive at the solutions in the first place. When defenders of understanding don’t dispute this separation, they immediately lose the argument. It becomes easy for the side that prioritizes output to peg them as simply not trying hard enough to envision a new future. But the superficial framing of understanding that we keep falling back on obscures deeper concerns that these examples share. They are less about anyone’s mental state than about what happens when something goes wrong. Tao’s scenario turns on the possibility that the AI passed the trial by exploiting a weakness in the trial itself. A paper whose authors can’t explain its claims leaves no one to consult if those claims fail. Where along the way did we come to believe that scientific value lies in correctness alone? This intuition is ultimately less about AI than it appears. The inclination to let AI drive science is less a sign of how forward-thinking one is about our future with AI, and more a symptom of a “value-free ideal” that has shaped our thinking since the Cold War era: a view that only epistemic criteria (not ethical and social values) deserve a place in judging what the evidence shows. That it pervades our debates about AI for science is not so surprising; it’s only in the last few decades or so that rejecting the value-free ideal became the philosophical mainstream. This ideal feeds unrealistic expectations and keeps us from seeing that pushback against the rapid infiltration of AI output into the scientific record is neither anti-AI nor anti-science. The stakes are bigger than any one debate or field. The value-free ideal distorts how we go about seeking truth, causing us to mistake verified results for knowledge. It threatens the human capacities that sustain science, causing us to see criticism and accountability as inconvenient overhead rather than the mechanics of knowledge production. It leaves us confused about what understanding is, and consequently why it matters. Subscribe Is science “naturally aligned”? The social contract for science represents an idealized relationship between science and society that arose after World War II in the US: scientists receive public funding and autonomy , and in return society receives the benefits of their inquiry. Built on a distinction between pure and applied science and a “linear model” in which basic research feeds applied work, the social contract replaces abstract arguments about the value of understanding with practical societal benefits, reshaping how we see science. Drawing on arguments made by concerned scientists in the late 1800s, who worried public celebration of new inventions like electric lights and the steam engine would crowd out respect for what they viewed as their more essential contributions, it also helped to forge a value-free ideal that says that at its core, science must be removed from “contextual values” like ethical or social concerns. For the social contract to gain broad societal buy-in as a model of scientific progress (and consequently shore up government investment in scientific research), we needed to imagine truth-seeking as the impersonal application of methods, immune to political or social pressures. Philosophers of science aspired to inquiry based only on “epistemic” (or “cognitive”) values. Any influence from the scientist’s intentions or values came to be seen as a risk that the right methods should minimize, laying the groundwork for today’s questions about why it should matter who asserted the claim so long as it’s correct. Many debates about AI’s role in science come down to disagreements about whether the scientific truth can be realized purely through use of the right procedures. Over the course of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there was almost a moralizing drive to eliminate as much of the scientist’s self as possible from the scientific process, so that trust in individuals could be replaced with trust in the system. AI agents set loose on the scientific literature, able to verify and intervene experimentally themselves, look like the long-awaited fulfillment of nineteenth century scientific ethics. Much of the “AI for science” rhetoric inherits what I call the “science is naturally aligned” premise: by enacting the scientific method at scale, with its various justification procedures, we can reach a place where we no longer need human judgment to produce truth. Is what is true really so separable from understanding or accountability? Math has become a centerpiece in recent debates because it gives us a case where correctness can be separated cleanly; a proof can be verified by AI without any human understanding how it works. What mathematicians still want after verification is a clue to what mechanical objectivity can’t provide. Truth as a value-driven practice Philosophers of science now predominantly reject the value-free ideal as being appropriate or helpful. Values enter because whether we reject or accept hypotheses is contingent on how we weigh consequences. Even in abstract realms like math, there are often simply too many possible truths for values not to be brought to bear in sifting through them. Mathematicians accepted long ago that in principle a machine can enumerate the set of theorems that can be proved from a given set of axioms. Yet the scale of this space is immense, motivating people to seek clever shortcuts for exploring it. But even with automated theorem-proving at scale, not all theorems are equally interesting to people. Values are inherent in the choices that lead to certain open problems gaining widespread appeal, and in the processes by which the community comes to accept and internalize the results. Fermat’s Last Theorem initially got attention not because it was an inherently important conjecture, but because Fermat claimed to have a proof but never provided it, enticing others to try their hand. It became central when it was shown that it would follow from the modularity conjecture, which proposed a previously unanticipated link between disparate areas of math. It was considered solved after peer review exposed an error that led to a corrected version of the original proof, even though formal verification didn’t come until recently. Epistemic taste develops because without it, we face an undifferentiated flood of facts. Taste is a capacity we develop over time as we choose problems, pursue some of them, and see which yield new understanding or ideas. If AI takes over choosing, we risk losing the personal fulfillment and community cooperation that motivates many to want to develop a capacity for scientific judgment in the first place. Tao makes a similar point by framing open problems as lighthouses rather than destinations. Reaching them prematurely with AI may sterilize the field around them. If, as fields are transformed by AI, we stop producing people who can judge what’s interesting and aligned with human aspirations, we may end up with a science that fails to serve basic human interests. Its results will consume attention from those to whom it is targeted, while providing neither fodder for subsequent discoveries nor contributing to the processes that help shape the next generation. This starts to sound like motivation for a new kind of linear model for science, which ensures that human reflection and inquiry are sustained despite AI becoming better than the average mathematician. The risk of proceeding without human intervention is drift, as anyone who relies heavily on agents to carry out their work knows. Even when you think you’re providing a well-specified pipeline for implementing and verifying an idea, it’s easy to end up mired in nuance in some branch you never expected to traverse. When you don’t assert epistemic agency, you can easily end up with a “view from nowhere” – not a form of pure objectivity, but an answer without a corresponding question. Maintaining alignment is not a problem you solve once and move on from. It requires a supply of humans who can articulate and adjudicate between values. Mechanical objectivity attempted to replace trust in individuals with trust in procedures, but that substitution has never happened as intended. To understand why, we need to look at the interactions that truth-seeking depends on. Sociality is not contamination of rationality There’s a tendency to see the social aspects of science as opposed to rationality. The social side of science can produce pathologies, like bad conventions, herd behavior, or deference to prestige. But scientific knowledge as we know it has always been the product of many epistemic agents bringing values and expertise to bear, and revising their views in response to challenge, not from some external verifying engine. As the philosopher Helen Longino argues , the basis for objective public knowledge is a shared language and a belief that things we describe exist independently of how we perceive them. If we can agree on descriptions of the world, then two things become possible: we can defer to others’ experiences to obtain knowledge, and meaningfully criticize scientific claims. Scientific communities develop shared standards and vocabulary that allow us to build on one another’s findings. We don’t need to verify everything firsthand, and sometimes relying on others’ findings can give us better grounds for believing something than investigating it ourselves, particularly when they possess evidence or expertise that we lack. Without criticism, we cannot have objectivity; it is, as Longino puts it “dependent upon the depth and scope of the transformative interrogation that occurs in any given scientific community.” For criticism to be transformative requires someone who is obliged to take it up. Practices like peer review and post-publication critique are not just fact-checks for sifting out false positives – they are about members of the community holding one another to the commitments that their assertions imply, and negotiating where to draw the line on the influence of personal preference. As Longino explains, “[t]he function of peer review is not just to check that the data seem right and the conclusions well-reasoned, but to bring to bear another point of view on the phenomena, whose expression might lead the original author(s) to revise the way they think about and present their observations and conclusions.” Method itself is best understood as a social process, where progress depends on how well a community sustains critical dialogue. This dialogue builds the people in it, shaping what it means for them to understand and exercise judgment along with the knowledge it produces. If criticism and an ability to trust others’ assertions are integral to the production of knowledge, we might ask whether AI can fulfill these same functions. Can models realize transformative criticism without human involvement? Can we trust the assertions of AI agents without obtaining direct understanding ourselves? And if we do, what happens to our own capacity to question, criticize, and stand behind results? What does it mean to assert something is true? The view that it shouldn’t matter who asserted some result as long as it’s correct corresponds to reliabilist epistemologies in philosophy. Classical epistemology insisted that true beliefs are only knowledge if the believer is able to produce reasons for their belief. In contrast, reliabilist epistemologies argue that true beliefs can, at least in some cases, represent genuine knowledge even when the believer can’t produce justifying reasons, provided they arrived at those beliefs by exercising capacities that are reliable producers of true beliefs in those circumstances. But there are limits to what reliability can provide. The philosopher Robert Brandom imagines a community where the members hold true beliefs, which they have acquired through reliable means, but cannot offer reasons for any of them. Because attributing reliability to the source of their beliefs would itself provide a form of justification based on inference, the community can’t know that they are reliable. They are reliable as instruments indicating something about their surroundings, but unable to recognize themselves as such. Unable to even possess the concept of reliability, Brandom concludes, they cannot have knowledge. If reliability alone can’t produce knowledge, what can? Brandom’s response is that calling something knowledge is a social act. To call what someone has “knowledge,” we have to attribute to them a commitment (that they believe that thing) along with an entitlement to that belief (that it is justified). But we also have to undertake that commitment ourselves, in the sense that we endorse the belief. The scientist who first asserted the claim allows us to repeat the claim (and draw conclusions from it) while leaving them responsible for justifying it if challenged. We do this relatively easily in human science because if it turns out there was something wrong with the original assertion, there is an answerable source we can consult to resolve it. Assertions have social significance because we can hold the original author accountable for what was said. This is the sense of understanding that matters most for science, that mathematicians want after the proof has been verified, and that Tao’s patient wants too: results that can be interrogated and reconceptualized where needed, to avoid the perception of progress that fails to serve our goals. But when we rely on AI results we don’t understand, there is only the person whose name is on the result to turn to. This is the problem arXiv is concerned with: no author can take responsibility for what they cannot understand, and hence they cannot respond to criticism by saying what it rests on, or whether it should be withdrawn. In other words, formal authorship survives while substantive authorship weakens . And so we lose the potential for transformative criticism, which is what sustains our notions of “objective” results in the first place. Could AI act as an accountable epistemic agent? A natural question is whether we could put the criticism to the AI agent itself, letting it decide whether to defend the result or concede and revise. What would it mean for AI to be an epistemic agent capable of committing to its assertions? There are a few challenges with today’s agents that would need to be overcome. One is their lack of persistence and identity in the sense that we attribute it to people. An agent that retracts something it asserted in one session is not bound to maintain its correction or the reasoning behind it in the next. If each new result is produced by a new bespoke multi-agent infrastructure, it becomes hard to “keep score” in the way that naturally happens within networks of human scientists. Scientific knowledge production depends on epistemic agents who have something at stake. Making bad claims changes the scientist’s standing in the community, which is how trust in individuals can remain calibrated. It’s not clear what comparable loss an AI agent faces in retracting its assertions, particularly given its lack of persistence. To overcome such limitations would require a considerable shift in how we develop AI: away from being maximally helpful in each exchange and toward being accountable across them, as human scientists tend to be. This may well be possible. But I don’t think accountable AI will be enough to sustain meaningful science from our human perspective. Let’s say we succeed in developing agents that can answer for claims. This is half of what accountability demands, but we also need others capable of holding them accountable, by asking for evidence, questioning assumptions, recognizing when an answer is evasive. Endorsements of others’ assertions are only as good as our capacity to engage with what we are endorsing. These are capacities that get built by exercising them, by choosing problems, defending our work, reviewing papers, challenging others’ results. When we don’t exercise our capacities, we lose them. It’s not clear what we gain from a perfectly accountable AI if no one can judge how good its answers are. We’d have truth-seeking in theory, but no one who is able to do it. Thurston’s notion of mathematical success points to this shared capacity to interrogate, extend, and repair a field’s knowledge that he’s hinting at. As he puts it, “As long as people in the field are comfortable that the idea works, it doesn’t need to have a formal written source.” Verification can tell us a result checks out in a technical sense, but only a community of people prepared to stand behind it can turn it into knowledge. If we continue to appeal to value-free ideals that frame correctness as all that matters, we will keep building tools that prioritize answers while neglecting the truth-seeking and understanding of the people who can make them count. Cosmos Institute is the Academy for Philosopher-Builders, technologists building AI for human flourishing. We run fellowships, fund fast prototypes, and host seminars with institutions like Oxford, Aspen Institute, and Liberty Fund. Subscribe 60 7 15 Share Previous Next Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Daniel Dal Monte 6d Liked by Jessica Hullman Powerful article! Reply Share JEFF TSAO 1d Liked by Jessica Hullman Verification vs knowledge reminds me of the distinction engineers draw between verification and validation. Verification asks whether we built the product right, meaning whether it meets its specification. Validation asks whether we built the right product, meaning whether it actually serves the people it’s meant to serve. AI can be extraordinarily good at verification--checking a result against a well-posed specification. Validation is harder, because it requires an intimate understanding of the human user: what they need, what they value. There's knowledge in both verification and validation, but verification lives more on the "is this a good answer" side while validation lives more on the "is this a good question" side. title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
body_text: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading · honnibal.dev honnibal.dev The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading 2026-11-03 · 5 minute read Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways. One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc. When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it must be working. This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. If you read that, would you assume that the Qwen experiment worked ‘just by looking at the raw weights’? Well it doesn’t. There’s experiments that look at raw weights, and experiments that improve a game-playing network, and an experiment that improves Qwen at maths. But those latter two aren’t just working with raw weights, they write Python programs. Here’s a summary of what the post actually does and how the techniques work. # Experiment Size Reads raw weights? Writes weights? Python? Runs network? Result 1 Name the game a PPO MLP was trained on 17K Yes No No No 4/4 correct 2 Name the shape a diffusion MLP generates 24K Yes No No No 3/3 correct 3 Name a char transformer’s language and copying heads 7.2M No No Yes No 3/3 correct 4 Fix a stuck Kinetix car policy 172K Yes Yes No No¹ 0% → 100%² 5 Write MinAtar game MLPs from scratch 20K No³ Yes No No Beats PPO-100M⁴ 6 Write a 9×9 Go network 1.5M No Yes Yes Yes (0–50 passes) Beats PPO 7a Spot the sycophantic Gemma 3 270M No No Yes No Failed 7b Same, seeing attention patterns 270M No No Yes Yes⁵ 3/3 correct 8 Fix Qwen3.5’s maths 800M No Yes Yes Yes (50 passes) 7.9% → 48.1% 8b Same, on Gemma 3 270M No Yes Yes Yes (50 passes) Failed ¹ Given one recorded episode of the failure. ² In one try, changing 3.5% of the weights. ³ Weights start at zero, so there’s nothing to read. ⁴ Beats PPO-500M only on Breakout (517 vs. 25); loses to it on Seaquest (53 vs. 89) and Asterix (53 vs. 55). ⁵ Runs up to 16 texts and sees only the attention patterns, not the outputs. The “just by looking at the raw weights” setting (raw floats in context, no tools, no running the network) only appears in experiments 1, 2 and 4, on networks of 17K–172K weights. Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python, and the Qwen result, which is the headline one, also gets to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems. What the Qwen result actually shows is that Astra can be prompted to devise and perform tasks that a human ML engineer could do. Human ML engineers write snippets of code that analyse or even modify network weights “directly” all the time. Figuring out how to do this productively is not nothing, and AI models of a year or two ago would have failed at all these tasks. But to me the Qwen result and the other experiments that use Python don’t belong in the same post or paper as the experiments that read the weights directly. A single technique that could achieve both, “Author weights for a small game from scratch” and “Improve the performance of a large model on a sample task” would imply a deep capability. If you test a single technique that way you’ve demonstrated a sort of ‘gestalt’ of the weights (it can write them out from scratch) and also that it understands a large existing network. But that’s not at all true here, because it’s not a single technique. Matthew Honnibal Computational linguist from Sydney based in Berlin, Germany. I'm the author of the spaCy Natural Language Processing library and the co-founder of Explosion , where we're building Ellf : a platform that helps your team and coding agents build custom, fully private AI solutions in-house. honnibal.dev

Sign in Tape Revival Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand Low costs and offline security mean magnetic tape still has a job. Nick Indge – Oct 30, 2026 1:38 pm | 110 ... ... ... Credit: iStock / Getty Images Plus Credit: iStock / Getty Images Plus Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels. The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape. Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data. Fujifilm’s work with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000, the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011, the company was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls “fine hybrid magnetic particles” by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech. Each generation of tape (currently Gen 10) has seen meaningful increases in both compressed and uncompressed storage limits. LTO capacity by generation. Gen 10 is the current tech; Gen 11-14 figures are consortium projections for the future. Credit: LTO.org LTO capacity by generation. Gen 10 is the current tech; Gen 11-14 figures are consortium projections for the future. Credit: LTO.org According to Fujifilm, “major cloud service and data center operators” have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: “Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.” Nick Indge Senior Technology Reporter Nick Indge Senior Technology Reporter Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now. Namespace @ namespacelabs Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks. 4:27 PM · Aug 24, 2026 · 25M Views 1K 964 5K 1.8K So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them . So why MacBooks? Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option. Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version. xtool xtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac. But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage. But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born. Our beautiful Mac racks Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down. Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI. Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers. And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential. Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines. Not the problems we expected: HDMI, FileVault, and USB NICs Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared. I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected. And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections. The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf. Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon. Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case! Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time. Mac reboot While on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart . And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life. What about Mac Minis and Studios? At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in the DC: they have a built-in 10 Gb network card, they boot up automatically after a power cycle and the OS can be configured entirely automatically via MDM. But Namespace has some special sauce for the Minis too. We design custom-made shelves that hold the machines with focus on efficient cooling. We have tested a few designs using airflow simulation to arrive at what we are deploying now. In the end installing Mac Minis is a breeze: unpack them, throw 10 pieces into the holder, connect power and network and press the power button once (famously inconveniently located). From there on automation takes care of them. Virtualizing Macs Under the hood a Namespace instance is backed by a virtual machine. We have multiple virtual machine engines integrated into a unified platform to run Linux, Windows, and Mac instances in the most efficient way. This way we can provide the same features that make Namespace special, like cache volumes , telemetry, or VPC connections. Unsurprisingly, our Mac solution is based on Apple’s excellent Virtualization framework . It is an embeddable and flexible virtual machine engine. It’s easiest to compare it to Firecracker in how it fits the system architecture: it implements generic VM operations end-to-end as well as typical peripherals. macOS on Apple Virtualization Namespace VM host process Virtualization framework · like Firecracker QEMU VMM Hypervisor framework Apple · like KVM The Namespace VM host starts macOS guests through the Virtualization framework, which fits the system the way Firecracker does. Underneath is the Hypervisor framework, comparable to KVM. QEMU uses the Hypervisor framework too, but it can't run macOS. For completeness, Apple also provides a lower-level Hypervisor framework , which is comparable to the KVM API of Linux. For instance QEMU uses it on macOS under the hood. Hypervisor provides a way to execute machine code in isolation, but requires the application developer to implement the bulk of machine architecture and peripherals. It could give us a lot of control, but unfortunately it cannot run macOS (it requires an Apple proprietary environment that third parties cannot, or shouldn’t, try to recreate). In fact, most competing platforms are built on the same foundation. But the details matter: Apple gives us a few primitives that need to be arranged in just the right way to work fast and be secure. The more interesting thing is to watch how different people solve similar problems with different constraints. Limitations of Apple Virtualization A well-known limitation is that Apple only allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. It can be a Mac Pro with 24 cores and 192 GB memory, yet it is limited to running only two guest VMs. This limitation leaks into our product offering: we can only slice Mac resources in two halves. So we run instances with 6 or 12 cores on 14-core Mac Minis and 8/16-core instances on 18-core MacBooks (we reserve a couple cores for management overhead). MacBook · 18 cores IPC roundtrips 0 2 host · 8 + 8 VMs process boundary Namespace VM host process · 2 cores Virtualization framework VM 1 · VMM process not started VM 2 · VMM process not started VM 3 Hypervisor framework Two cores stay with the Namespace VM host, and the rest split in half between the only two macOS VMs Apple allows per Mac. Each VM runs in its own VMM process, so hooking VM behavior or a custom virtual device costs an IPC roundtrip across the process boundary. On a 14-core Mac mini, the split is 2, 6 and 6. An important consideration of Virtualization VMs is that the virtual CPU is executed by a separate OS process (VMM process in the diagram) from the software integrating Virtualization (here Namespace VM host). If we want to hook some VM behavior or implement custom virtual devices, every interaction with them requires an IPC roundtrip between the VM process and the “host” process. Such context switches are unavoidable and need to be taken into account when designing the system. Virtual networking Virtualization framework offers a few ways to connect a virtual machine to the network. For instance, bridged and NAT networking modes route traffic directly from the VMM process to the host network interfaces. These are suitable for VMs running on a local computer where the workload is trusted. Namespace instances run untrusted code and we need to enforce policies on what a VM can or cannot access (these policies can also be customer-defined! ). Also we provide a few additional services to the instances that should appear “as if” they were on the local network for the guest system. This requires us to take full control of guest networking in the mode where we process every packet that comes out and into the VM in software. We based our guest networking on a userspace TCP/IP stack from Google gVisor project and use it to implement an IP gateway/firewall for the instances. This way we minimize exposure of the host OS to unprocessed packets controlled by the guest. Network packet handling needs to be very efficient, but as outlined above the path involves IPC. The VMM process needs first to pass the packets to the “VM host” process, which then processes and passes them to the network interface. It takes careful implementation and batch processing wherever possible to minimize the number of IPC roundtrips. The above approach allows Namespace MacOS instances to reach 4 Gbps upstream bandwidth (per Fast.com ). This is unfortunately still lower than the line rate. We have been exploring alternative approaches, including ideas on how to avoid IPC for network processing entirely. But productionizing the new setup is still left for the future. After all, 4 Gbps is still quite respectable. VM images Creating your first VM using Apple Virtualization is very easy: download a macOS IPSW restore image, use UTM/Tart/any of the dozens of open-source Virtualization wrappers to start a machine, click through Setup Assistant, install Xcode and you are good to go. Now you have a VM image that you can fork and run any workload locally. But you need to test on multiple versions of iOS, so you install a few iOS runtimes. And then you install the upcoming Xcode beta version (and new runtimes too). And before you know it your VM image has grown to 500 GB (iOS runtime packages are huge). You also want to have the previous version of macOS for testing that one little thing. Another 500 GB right here. Apple releases the new macOS developer preview, one more image. And then you realize that the Xcode beta version subtly breaks the non-beta Xcodes on the same system (true story!). After all, Xcode installation bumps the “global” versions of CoreDevice and CoreSimulator. Hence any bugs in the beta Xcode simulator are visible when you’re using ostensibly stable Xcode versions. So now you are maintaining image versions with and without the pre-release Xcodes. And now you have 2 TB of VM images. On what? A 2 TB MacBook hard drive? That’s the challenge we faced: we need to build, distribute, and store huge images across the fleet of hundreds of machines. Build process Building images is a repeatable process so that we can reliably produce new images when Apple releases new software versions. Building is driven by a script that replicates installation and configuration as a human user would do it (e.g. the build script can run shell commands, click UI buttons or reboot the VM). Wherever possible we stick to using controls designed by Apple to configure the VMs in order to avoid surprising behaviours inconsistent with what a typical local user would be seeing. Naturally, building images is an automated and repeatable process. It is driven by a workflow expressed as a sequence of operations in a YAML file. Operations can be VM control (e.g. reboot), running a shell script or programmatic interaction with the system or setup UI over VNC. Resulting VM images are handed over to Namespace internal Image Registry , in fact the same one that handles Linux and Windows image storage, replication and distribution (covered in the excellent article by Matteo ). Disk images are of course quite different from normal container images: OCI layers are simple tarballs of files, while disks are generally flat arrays of bytes. Very large arrays in fact. And to a large extent they contain empty space: that’s the disk space that would be available to users as free space. Naturally, it would be very wasteful to transfer and store the “empty” data in the registry. So we developed a simple format that allows us to preserve the “sparse-ness” of the images when stored in the registry. Unallocated spans of the image take just a few bytes. And there is another important optimization. Remember the example scenario mentioned in the VM Images section: we have an image of the same system that differs only in addition of an extra Xcode installation. Obviously the latter image is built using the former as a base and most of the bytes are unchanged. Our storage format preserves the “shallow copy” relationship and stores such images as multiple layers: the base layer is shared between them, while subsequent layers only contain the modified blocks. image A image B base layer offset=0 len=3 A B C offset=5 len=1 D BASE LAYER SHARE DELTA LAYER STORED ◀ Back Pause Next ▶ Image A is stored as a base layer of block extents, and its holes take no space. Image B shares that base and stores only a delta: the blocks it changed and a hole where D used to be. Distribution At this point we have the images in an OCI registry now. But of course Virtualization framework cannot start a VM directly using a disk residing in the registry. It needs to have something on the node itself: a VM disk can be backed by either an image file on the local host SSD, or it can route disk I/O requests to a server using Network Block Device (NBD) protocol. The latter would allow us to intelligently serve highly demanded data from a local cache, while conserving on-device space by not storing unneeded blocks. But NBD has the same drawback as userspace networking from above: every I/O operation would incur an IPC roundtrip at minimum, including buffer copying and context switches. You see the same pattern as with networking: a very direct hardwired and fast option and an indirect “software-defined” but disappointingly slow option. At Namespace we value performance a lot, so the choice is clear: we’ll serve the images from the local disk. We need to materialize them from OCI images in the registry on the SSD of every node in the fleet. 500 gig images to hundreds and thousands of nodes. And we need to do it fast. Obviously, every node naively downloading from the central registry was not going to work. With the example numbers we are talking about half a petabyte of traffic transferred within, conservatively, tens of minutes. The registry (and the network fabric) would need to serve terabits per second! The bytes that we are distributing are the same going to every node so the obvious solution is to organize a peer-to-peer delivery of these blobs. Each block only needs to be downloaded from the registry once by some node. Then another node that is close by (by certain metric) can download the block directly from the peer and we have two copies. So two more nodes can pull these bytes and so on. The fleet is exponentially flooded. BitTorrent Obviously, BitTorrent was a heavy inspiration for this design. But unlike BitTorrent, which works in a public network of untrusted peers, we could make different tradeoffs leading to better efficiency and predictability. But that’s a topic for another post. copies 0/8 · registry reads 0 nodes Registry block 0x6ed2 N1 N2 N3 N4 N5 N6 N7 N8 Each block is read from the registry once. Every node that has it passes it to another node, so the number of copies doubles each round. Storage Now the bytes are on the node disk. But remember the storage optimizations we did in the Build Process? With the naive approach of storing the images on disk there are a lot of bytes that are useless: they are either holes or could be shared with another image. Some of you probably know that these are exactly the types of storage optimization techniques that are possible with modern file systems, namely APFS. ZFS Linux users have seen the same features in ZFS. Using these cool features is also pretty easy: open a new file for writing, seek to offset 100G, write a block. And there you just made a file with a large hole in it. Only the block you wrote is allocated on disk, the rest is 100 GB of imaginary zeroes. When reading the file you won’t even notice the holes. The OS will return actual zeros. Creating a sparse file on APFS % truncate -s 1g hole.bin % dd if=/dev/random of=hole.bin bs=4k seek=256k count=256 % ls -lh hole.bin -rw-r--r-- 1 kirill staff 1.0G Sep 29 05:36 hole.bin % du -h hole.bin 1M hole.bin Sharing the blocks is similarly transparent: just use the cp -c mode or clonefile syscall. The new file will share the same disk blocks and essentially not take any space. /dev/disk1 disk usage 0 blocks hole.bin du 0 WRITE CP -C OVERWRITE WRITE B ◀ Back Pause Next ▶ hole.bin allocates only the blocks that were written. cp -c makes clone.bin share those blocks, and writing to the clone allocates only the blocks that change. Writing to the cloned file is also transparent: as soon as you try to overwrite some blocks, these particular blocks will be allocated on the disk, while the shared portion will remain shared. What’s next? The pace at which we are expanding our fleet is increasing and the experience from all the above has transformed into a repeatable process. We know exactly how long it takes to bring a MacBook rack into prod. The rack assembly line is dialed in. DCOps people are trained. Disk images are built and distributed. We can bring whatever number of machines our customers need into the fleet when we need to (well, as long as we can purchase them at all). We can still do better! What if there was a “holy-grail” device to host a shelf of MacBooks, providing power, ethernet and KVM connections over a single USB-C cable? It should be possible, yet there is currently no hardware on the open market that satisfies our requirements. So we are working on something very custom. Or maybe we’ll do another crazy thing? What if we deploy phones to the datacenter? See what the future brings on our X soon! name logo The dev platform for the next 100 billion commits. title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
body_text: Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode | WebKit WebKit Downloads Feature Status CSS Features Standards Positions Documentation Web Inspector Tracking Prevention Policies Project Goals Bug Prioritization Bug Report Guidelines Code Style Guidelines Commit and Review Policy Feature Policy Security Policy Tracking Prevention Policy WebKit AI Tool Use Policy Contribute Getting Started Contributing Code Testing Contributions How to Report Bugs GitHub Repository Blog News Posts CSS Posts Contributing Posts Privacy Posts Performance Posts JavaScript Posts Standards Posts Web Inspector Posts Safari Technology Preview Posts Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode Nov 3, 2026 by Simon Fraser, Luming Yin, Lily Spiniolas, Joanne Pan, Veda Periwal and Jen Simmons We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark. In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright . Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web. You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’. For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark. How does Adaptive Dark Mode work? At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged. While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio . Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark. Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear. It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos. Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict. It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy. Making your site work even better In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices. If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding. Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles. Building your own dark mode For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier. Here’s an example of a website in light mode (left) and with Adaptive Dark Mode applied (center). If the site creates a custom dark mode, it could look like the third version (right). All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including: <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> :root { color-scheme: light dark } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { } <picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"> light-dark() Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color() , plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility. Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible. Using the “light only” color scheme If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme . The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { } . (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.) Protecting user privacy Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers. As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form. Feedback If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com . If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant . (Learn more about filing Feedback ). body_text: Hironobu SUZUKI @ InterDB The Internals of PostgreSQL I am officially open to new international opportunities! ð After a temporary stay in Japan to focus on my health and personal responsibilities, I am fully recovered, ready, and excited to work abroad again. The Internals of PostgreSQL PostgreSQL is a well-designed, open-source multi-purpose relational database system which is widely used throughout the world. It is one huge system with the integrated subsystems, each of which has a particular complex feature and works cooperatively with each other. Although understanding of the internal mechanism is crucial for both administration and integration using PostgreSQL, its hugeness and complexity make it difficult. The main purposes of this documentation are to explain how each subsystem works, and to provide the whole picture of PostgreSQL. This documentation covers versions 19-beta (excluding the new buffer page lock mechanism) and earlier. Some academic papers have referred to this documentation. The Chinese version of this documentation was published in June 2019. This documentation was first published on 26 September 2015. Contents Chapter 1 .
