Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the ontology SQL evaluation repository . Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the Apache License 2.0 . Third-party open-source components bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . This project is currently not accepting external contributions. Key Features Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM. Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes. Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth . Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings. Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack. Software Components Component Technology Role Default port Frontend Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma Web UI, authentication, API gateway 3000 Backend FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs 3001 Ingestion worker FastAPI (Python 3.12+) Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings 3002 Postgres + pgvector Relational Database App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store 5432 HashiCorp Vault Optional Secure storage of connection credentials — NVIDIA NIM Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted NVIDIA API catalog ( integrate.api.nvidia.com ) or self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are: LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2 The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT , DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL , EMBED_ENDPOINT , and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY . Model triplets Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables — <PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY , and <PREFIX>_MODEL : Prefix Role DEFAULT_MODELS Shared default; every field below falls back to it. REASONING Main chat / NL-to-SQL model. NON_REASONING Lighter model used for entity extraction. EMBED Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). RERANK Reranker used by the retrieval flow. You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD> . So the simplest setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL , NON_REASONING_MODEL ). *_API_KEY also falls back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility. Quickstart This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers, Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2, uv , and an NVIDIA API key ( nvapi-... ) from build.nvidia.com . Clone the repository and create .env : git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env Then set these values in .env : DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-... AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32> APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password> CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY . Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop) Build and start the rest of the stack: docker compose up -d --build Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env . Go to Settings → Semantic Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes. Ask a question in Chat : What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015? The agent resolves revenue , product , and state to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source: Answer: Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines. SQL: SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines FROM sales.invoicelines il JOIN sales.invoices i ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid JOIN warehouse.stockitems si ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid JOIN sales.customers c ON i.customerid = c.customerid JOIN application.cities ct ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll' AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania' AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01' Steps: Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province Validated the filter values against the data, then executed Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability first and asks you to clarify: You: What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015? Agent: check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend" Agent: I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another source I should connect? If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for localhost:3000 and sign in again. For other setup failures, see the setup skill's troubleshooting guide . How it works Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it. The ontology holds three kinds of definition: Terms. Business concepts such as Customer or Invoice Line , each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them. SQL attributes. Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way. Relationships. How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data. Generate. The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases: Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog. Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns. Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history. Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval. The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting Order shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes: Certify. People make the draft trustworthy: Test with real questions in Chat, or with check_answerable and ask_question over MCP. Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API. Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct. Answer. For each question, the agent: Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names. Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search. Writes SQL from those candidates. Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the SQL when a check fails. Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took. When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's configured (see Predictions ). In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as CSV, or read them as a chart: Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie , the open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a converter for Auto-Ontology , which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML. Use Settings → Import / Export , or POST /api/model/import and POST /api/model/export . Component Technology Role Port Frontend Next.js, Better Auth, Prisma Web UI, authentication, public API gateway 3000 Backend FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain Text-to-SQL agent, catalog, ontology APIs 3001 Ingestion service FastAPI (Python 3.12+) Ingestion and semantic compilation 3002 MCP server FastMCP Read-only agent tools over the public API 3003 Postgres + pgvector PostgreSQL 17 Catalog, ontology, app data, vector store 5432 HashiCorp Vault Optional Connection credential storage n/a Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity the frontend forwards in the x-auto-ontology-user-id header, and the ingestion service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000. Use it from your agent MCP server The MCP server gives any MCP client read-only tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every call runs with that user's permissions. Job Tools Readiness check_readiness : can this deployment answer anything at all Terms search_terms , get_term , get_term_columns , get_term_sql_attributes , get_sql_attribute , describe_table Answerability check_answerable : does the ontology cover this question Questions ask_question : the answer, the SQL, and the rows Run the server against your deployment: AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \ uvx --from "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp" auto-ontology-mcp Cursor ( ~/.cursor/mcp.json ): { "mcpServers": { "auto-ontology": { "url": "http://localhost:3003/mcp" } } } Claude Desktop ( claude_desktop_config.json ), bridged with mcp-remote : { "mcpServers": { "auto-ontology": { "command": "npx", "args": ["mcp-remote", "http://localhost:3003/mcp"] } } } Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts. Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in docs/mcp.md . Agent skills Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at AGENTS.md . Skill Covers nvidia-ontology-setup Install, connect sources, compile, prove readiness nvidia-ontology-management Inspect, model, certify, import/export, and publish nvidia-ontology-query Ask questions and validate the SQL, rows, and answer REST API Ask a question with POST /api/chat/completions on the web app's origin. Mint an API token under the user menu → API Tokens . The response is a server-sent event stream: a result event carries the answer, and data: [DONE] ends the stream. curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \ -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}' import json import os import requests response = requests.post( "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions", headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]}, json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}, stream=True, timeout=900, ) response.raise_for_status() for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True): if not line or not line.startswith("data:"): continue payload = line.removeprefix("data:").strip() if payload == "[DONE]": break event = json.loads(payload) if event["type"] == "result": print(event["answer"]["response"]) print(event["answer"]["sql_code"]) elif event["type"] == "error": raise RuntimeError(event["message"]) Event types, multi-turn conversations, and the gateway trust boundary are in docs/conversation-api.md . Every other operation is in the OpenAPI spec . Connectors, models, and predictions Sources Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines: PostgreSQL MySQL Databricks Snowflake ClickHouse Trino Apache Kyuubi HeavyDB DuckDB SQLite Add connections under Settings → Connections , or list them in CONNECTION_STRINGS . DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See docs/connections.md for URL schemes, scoping, and credential storage. Models Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an nvapi- key, each defaults to an NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com : Role Default model What it does REASONING nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b Builds the ontology (terms, relationships, SQL attributes), writes each answer's SQL and explanation, and grades answerability NON_REASONING nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b Runs the agent's faster steps: question intent, entity extraction, candidate selection, and SQL checks and repair EMBED nvidia/nemotron-3.5-embed-1b Indexes tables, columns, terms, and SQL attributes in pgvector, and matches each question to them RERANK nvidia/nemotron-3.5-rerank-8b Ranks candidate tables when compilation builds bridge-table SQL attributes To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set <ROLE>_ENDPOINT , <ROLE>_API_KEY , and <ROLE>_MODEL . Any field you leave unset falls back to DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD> , so the simplest setup fills in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and overrides only what differs. Use models that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for ingestion and queries. .env.example documents every variable. Predictions Set KUMO_RFM_API_KEY and the agent routes predictive questions to KumoRFM. KumoRFM is a hosted service: to answer, the agent uploads the connected tables to it, capped by KUMO_MAX_TABLES (20 by default) and KUMO_MAX_ROWS_PER_TABLE (unlimited unless set). Review what that sends, and complete your organization's data review, before you enable it. Integrate with us To integrate an agent platform, application, or storage provider with Auto-Ontology, open an integration request . The Auto-Ontology team maintains the code and doesn't accept external pull requests. Integration requests and bug reports are welcome as issues. Report security vulnerabilities through SECURITY.md . Maintainer workflow is in CONTRIBUTING.md . title: Synaptics Appears to Use Legal Threats to Block Open-Source DisplayLink Driver
body_text: Synaptics Appears To Use Legal Threats To Block Open-Source DisplayLink Driver - Phoronix Articles & Reviews News Archive Forums Premium Ad-Free Contact Popular Categories Close Articles & Reviews News Archive Forums Premium Contact Categories Computers Display Drivers Graphics Cards Linux Gaming Memory Motherboards Processors Software Storage Operating Systems Peripherals Synaptics Appears To Use Legal Threats To Block Open-Source DisplayLink Driver Written by Michael Larabel in Hardware on 4 November 2026 at 06:03 AM EST. 61 Comments From earlier in the year you may recall a new experimental open-source Linux driver for modern DisplayLink hardware . That "Vino" driver for DisplayLink driver was a clean-room reverse-engineered DisplayLink driver that was developed in part by AI and written in Rust. Unfortunately, that open-source driver has disappeared following legal threats by Synaptics. I hadn't heard anything more on this in-development Rust kernel driver in a while until this morning when a Phoronix reader pointed out a troubling post on the mailing list that I missed. It appears Synaptics resorted to using their legal team to block this independent, community-developed driver on the basis of violating their patents. A cease and desist notice was sent to the Vino driver developer of this open-source driver. Those curious can find the various correspondence via attachments on this LKML thread . The Vino driver repository on GitHub is no longer publicly available. So don't look for an open-source, upstream DisplayLink driver in Linux anytime soon... The original USB2-era DisplayLink hardware worked well on Linux and even had open-source driver support, but looks now like Synaptics will ensure that no open-source driver exists for their latest IP around USB graphics. 61 Comments Tweet Related News Linux's RAID6 Check Tool Sees 3x Performance Via Batching AMD Ryzen Zen 6 Looks Like It Will Be In Good Shape With Linux 7.4, Laptop Improvements I3C Hub & HDR-DDR Support Merged For Linux 7.4 System76 Introducing AMD-Powered Linux Small PC Linux 7.4 Expands Sensor Monitoring For More ASUS & MSI Motherboards, New Minisforum Driver Initial Support For The Apple M4 & Apple A18 Pro Make It Into Linux 7.4 About The Author Michael Larabel is the principal author of Phoronix.com and founded the site in 2004 with a focus on enriching the Linux hardware experience. title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
body_text: [2605.29713] The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2605.29713 (cs) [Submitted on 28 May 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 8 Sep 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer Authors: Tianhua Chen View a PDF of the paper titled The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer, by Tianhua Chen View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students. Comments: Revised preprint version, 195 pages. Added visual explanations throughout. title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
body_text: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?       Main Papers Talks Code Writing Writing Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996? by Nicholas Carlini 2026-11-01 On February 10th, 1996, a computer program (IBM's Deep Blue) defeated the reigning chess champion (Garry Kasparov) in a game of chess for the first time. Deep Blue would go on to lose the match, but a year later, would get its revenge in a 3.5-2.5 rematch. In order to achieve this feat, IBM spent several million dollars on research and development building a special-purpose computer specifically for this purpose. Deep Blue itself (the victorious, upgraded version) was powered by 30 P2SC processors each running at roughly 120 MHz, and (most importantly) 480 custom VLSI chess co-processors used to perform chess-specific operations like move generation and position evaluation. When it was built, Deep Blue was the 259th most powerful supercomputer in the world, and could analyze over 200 million chess positions per second. But was Deep Blue necessary to beat Kasparov? Or could we have gotten away with an off-the-shelf 1996 desktop running a smarter chess engine? As it turns out, we could easily have beaten Kasparov without building Deep Blue, using only commodity hardware, and it (almost certainly) wouldn't have even been close. I know this because, as I write this very sentence, I have sitting next to me a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro (released exactly 31 years ago---November 1st, 1995) with 64MB of RAM running a custom port of Stockfish that plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 ± 87 at classical time controls---far beyond the strength of any human, or indeed Kasparov's Elo of just under 2800. But wait, there's more! I've hooked this machine up to the internet with a Realtek RTL8139C Ethernet card, so you can play it below! copy link Analyze on lichess â All games Connecting to the Pentiumâ¦ Resign Other games in progress Play vs. the Pentium The Pentium Pro's monitor, live (its VGA text screen, refreshed every second) wait, what?! how?? There are three ways to get stronger at chess: you can analyze more moves, analyze better moves, or analyze moves better . Famously, humans improve by doing the latter two: the average chess grandmaster during a classical game will analyze roughly the same number of moves as an amateur player, but they analyze only the most critical moves and do a better job with that analysis. Chess engines like Stockfish , running on silicon instead of our human brains, dominate us at the first of these and analyze millions of positions per second. And because there's not that much room for micro-optimizations on modern engines that will let a given CPU process more positions per second, most progress in chess AI also tends to follow how humans improve and finds better methods for selecting moves and analyzing boards. Skill in chess is measured by an Elo score. A difference of 200 Elo means that you should expect the stronger player to win three out of every four games, and multiplicatively from there: a 400 Elo gap corresponds to a 90% expected score and a 1000 Elo gap gives a 99.7% expected score. The best chess engines that you could run on commodity 1996 hardware were rated roughly 2300 Elo. Deep Blue was rated 2700. In contrast, modern Stockfish is rated closer to 3700. This raises the question: how much of the advantage of a modern chess engine comes down to the fact that a modern desktop computer is extremely fast, and how much of the advantage comes down to the fact that we've just gotten better at programming chess engines? As it turns out, the majority of the Elo gains (+720 of the +1335 gained) can be attributed to better programming, and not better hardware. To test this, I ran two experiments. The first experiment uses Crafty , a competitive engine from 1996 whose source code is now available. On my Pentium Pro, the 1996 build of Crafty version 11.13 has an Elo of 1999 ± 90 at 1 second per move, and 2383 ± 77 at 10 seconds per move. On modern hardware (a Ryzen 7) this engine's Elo jumps massively to 2614 ± 97 at the same 1 second per move. But if I take this engine and slowly start to add all the knowledge we have about how to design better chess engines---adding modern search algorithms like fail-soft, LMR, correction history; adding better quiescence methods; and adding neural-net evals (NNUE)---then you can increase the Elo up to 2718 ± 34 on the Pentium Pro at 1 second per move, and 2974 ± 74 at 10 seconds per move. In the second experiment I go somewhat further: instead of trying to update Crafty, let's just try to get Stockfish---the best chess engine today---running on 1996 hardware and see how it does. This takes some work and is mainly a matter of rewriting the code so that it uses 32-bit arithmetic (a PPro is a 32-bit machine) and doesn't use more than 64MB of RAM. This naive port has an Elo of roughly 2496 ± 64 at 1 second per move (2940 ± 76 at 10 seconds per move). But we can do better! A modern Stockfish engine is designed to run on a modern CPU. By making a number of adjustments to the algorithm and tuning it to the Pentium, we can increase its Elo to 2846 ± 35 at 1 second per move, 3109 ± 79 at 10 seconds per move, and 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move. The most concise way to summarize all of the above is just to have them play a match of 100 games against each other. And when I do this, I find that a modern chess engine running on a 1996 Pentium Pro wins 78, draws 17, and loses 5 games against the 1996 Crafty engine running on modern hardware. The remainder of this article provides the details. Technical details: Hardware & OS There's not much to say about the hardware, to be honest. I bought a used ( "vintage" said the listing; I feel old.) desktop PC with standard period-appropriate hardware. The desktop is running a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro connected to an Intel VS440FX motherboard with 64MB of SIMM RAM clocked at 66 MHz. The operating system boot off of a 1.44MB 3.5 inch floppy disk, and connect to the Internet via a Realtek RTL8139C. I also have a 1MB Trio64V+ graphics card connected over VGA to my monitor, with input coming from a PS/2 keyboard---but I don't much use either of those and instead communicate with it over a serial port connected to my modern desktop. For those readers who may not be able to appropriately contextualize this hardware, a 200 MHz Pentium Pro sold for $1,325 at launch in November 1995, and four 16 MB SIMMs would have cost about $2,000. Add on the other peripherals, and this machine would likely have gone for about four or five thousand dollars. So it's a nice workstation, but by no means a supercomputer. However, given the rate of depreciation and the exponential rate of improvements to hardware, this same machine in 1997, when the second match occurred, would likely go for just a thousand dollars (because who would want to buy a Pentium Pro when the better-in-almost-every-way Pentium MMX was now available for just $400?) The interface between the chess engine and the internet is a custom-built "operating system" whose sole job is to spin up the chess engine and connect it directly to the networking card. (Throughout this article, when I say "I wrote", what I really mean is "I asked an LLM to write". I used a combination of Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 to implement the code here. (This article, though, is human text.).) It's designed to be as compact as possible: the operating system (which, in fact, is more like a hypervisor, or something) is sitting on a bootable floppy disk. Its sole job is to boot the Pentium Pro into 32-bit protected mode, initialize the networking card, and await further instructions. I can then send it any arbitrary "userspace" guest program that I want into RAM and it'll boot that up and start running it. The chess program I wrote starts up a custom-built HTTP server which waits for incoming HTTP requests with a given position (as a FEN string) and maximum run time, and on each request runs the engine until the timer expires, and returns a response. Technical details: Software As mentioned earlier I (again: a language model) actually modified two engines. The stronger of the two is powered by Stockfish adapted to run efficiently on a thirty-year-old processor. It plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 at classical time controls [a] Because I can't run nearly enough games at classical time controls on my single machine to get this number, I've extrapolated it from shorter time controls. I measured 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move, and it gained +70 Elo per tripling of the time between 1 second to 10 seconds and 10 seconds to 30 seconds. Because a classical game gives about six minutes per move (including thinking on the opponent's turn) we should expect an Elo of 3350. Allowing for some diminishing returns, a safe estimate is an Elo of 3300. , high enough above Kasparov's 2800 Elo that we should expect Stockfish-1996 to come out ahead with a score of roughly 9/10. The (only slightly) weaker engine starts with the source code to Crafty 11.13, and is brought forward in time by adding all the lessons we've learned about how to write a better chess engine over the past thirty years. Updating Crafty 11.13 (1996) with modern tricks The first engine I (read: my LLM) worked on was Crafty 11.13, its 1996 release. On this engine the LLM had to do the most work to backport ideas we've learned over the last 30 years. Below is a breakdown of where the Elo gains come from, when evaluating either at 1 second per move or 10 seconds per move. [b] Sometimes you'll find the 1s vs 10s improvements disagree. Part of this clearly could be noise---I only ran a few hundred games which leaves a relatively large margin of error---but there is also quite a lot of signal here. Because the 1996 computer is so much slower, at 1s/move it has a very low search depth and so how fast the evaluation runs matters more than how good it is. But at larger search depths, once you stop making tactical blunders, the position evaluation becomes much more important. 1 s/move 10 s/move Change 1999 ± 90 2383 ± 77 Crafty 11.13, released December 1996, as shipped. The initial alpha-beta engine as written. It has a custom evaluation function, with standard 90's-era search algorithms. 2063 ± 73 (+64 ± 116) 2323 ± 75 (−60 ± 107) The first improvement is mostly micro-optimizations. It replaces two 64K-entry lookup tables with calls to the bsf / bsr instructions; and sliding-piece attacks are migrated away from the older rotated-bitboard function call. In total these changes make the engine 15% faster, but it uses the same algorithms. 2022 ± 73 (−41 ± 103) 2420 ± 76 (+97 ± 106) The next improvement goes for the search algorithms. This includes techniques like fail-soft (which returns the real score instead of clipping), futility and late-move pruning (which skips quiet moves near the leaves), late move reduction (which searches later moves one ply shallower), and orders moves by counter-move and history tables. 2224 ± 72 (+202 ± 103) 2520 ± 74 (+100 ± 106) The next change tunes the search and the evaluation function. It first runs SPSA to tune all search constants based on several thousand games of self-play. It then gives evaluation terms separate middlegame and endgame values (blended by remaining material) and re-fits all the evaluation weights (Texel tuning). Finally the evaluation function introduces mobility terms rewarding the safe squares that pieces attack. 2192 ± 72 (−32 ± 102) 2565 ± 74 (+45 ± 104) From here, the evaluation function is rewritten and replaced with a neural network evaluation with a small network trained on 11 million positions of self-play, labeled by its own searches. This step doesn't do much by itself but it prepares the next step... 2420 ± 82 (+228 ± 109) 2712 ± 74 (+147 ± 104) Updates the NNUE that was just generated with a stronger teacher instead of self-play. In principle, I could have used the same engine itself as the teacher, but just to save on wall clock time I used Stockfish. This reduced the wall-clock time from ~4000 1996-core-years (something entirely doable in 1996---but sadly not something I can do with my single lonely desktop) to just a few days on a modern desktop running a modern engine. 2630 ± 82 (+210 ± 116) 2810 ± 75 (+98 ± 105) With a much stronger evaluation function, the search can now actually rely on it. It adds reverse futility pruning to early-return when the evaluation says the position is already won. It also adds some performance improvements to the evaluator (with an evaluation cache, and accumulators shared with null moves). This lets it widen the network 6x. It also cleans up some code, for example by getting rid of some of Crafty's special cases that mattered with weaker evaluation functions but don't matter any more with the NNUE. 2720 ± 82 (+90 ± 116) 2938 ± 74 (+128 ± 105) The parameters are again re-tuned with SPSA given the new evaluation function. It also fixes some bugs in the code, amusingly. And finally it adds some changes to the NNUE: it adds more output heads and picks based on the number of pieces on the board, adds some hidden units, and doubles the training data with more self-play. Porting Stockfish 17 onto a Pentium Pro On the second engine, as mentioned above, I did the inverse. I (again, read: my LLM) ported Stockfish to run on 1996 hardware, and then tweaked the parameters so that it would be better suited to lower search depth. The gains here are thus somewhat more modest, because there are no large algorithm wins that remain. 1 s/move 10 s/move Change 2496 ± 64 2940 ± 76 Stockfish 17 squeezed onto the machine. The first naive port rewrites Stockfish 17 for a 1996 machine: single core, no SIMD, no 64-bit registers and no C++ standard library. It removes the threading, the endgame tablebases, and the 71 MB NNUE replacing it with a much smaller one. It rewrites bitboards as a pair of 32-bit ints, and it evaluates the small NNUE with plain integer arithmetic. 2590 ± 67 (+94 ± 93) 2961 ± 74 (+21 ± 106) Faster accumulator upkeep. The second fix makes sure the NNUE running sums are better kept up to date, and improves the performance of the evaluator. 2752 ± 68 (+162 ± 95) 3006 ± 74 (+45 ± 105) Cheaper evaluation function, use a PeSTO blend, change the compiler flags. Next it again changes the NNUE and reduces the size and tunes it to run faster on the Pentium Pro, reducing the evaluation time by 3x. Combined with a few more optimization changes this pass gains the most of any step at 1 second per move, where raw speed matters most, and much less at 10 seconds per move. 2780 ± 67 (+28 ± 95) 3070 ± 72 (+64 ± 103) Fine-tune the NNUE on-policy. Basically repeats the prior work but on Stockfish, scoring several million positions with Stockfish to re-derive the NNUE weights. 2784 ± 65 (+4 ± 93) 3070 ± 72 (+0 ± 101) SPSA to re-tune the search, remove PeSTO given the improved NNUE. The original Stockfish assumed that it would run at several million nodes per second, so on the slower CPU it's necessary to re-tune the parameters with another pass of SPSA. These changes also make it so the PeSTO pass is no longer needed. 2819 ± 65 (+35 ± 92) 3074 ± 72 (+4 ± 101) Add correction history, jointly tune other parameters and the NNUE. The next pass brings back Stockfish's non-pawn correction history, jointly optimizes (again via SPSA) the parameters, and re-fits the NNUE. 2846 ± 35 (+27 ± 74) 3109 ± 79 (+35 ± 107) The final step changes no code and just changes the compiler, adds some link-time optimization, and adds 32-byte code alignment. So would this have beaten Kasparov? I think it's overwhelmingly likely to be the case, but it's actually a little bit more tricky of a situation than you might hope. You see, I've done a bit of sleight of hand throughout this article. The problem is that Elo scores are relative, and I've been comparing my engine's Elo to that of various Stockfish engines that have known strengths on the Computer Chess Rating Lists (CCRL). But because humans don't play against engines very frequently, there can be some small divergences between scores on the FIDE Elo ladder and the CCRL ladder, in the same way a player's FIDE Elo doesn't directly translate to their Elo on online chess. Fortunately, because I've gotten these engines to play at an Elo rating of 3200-3300, and Kasparov was rated just under 2800, there should be more than sufficient buffer to absorb any discrepancy. But if you happen to know a 2700+ Super GM who wants to try and defeat a 2026 chess engine playing on 1996 hardware, I'd be happy to accept the challenge! Conclusion The first time we humans do anything, we rarely do it efficiently. Once we see a path that would clearly work if only we scaled it up, we do just that. Only later, after we've had the time to better understand the problem at hand, do we come to recognize that we could have achieved the same feat much more efficiently by being clever. I mostly did this for fun, because whether I could have beaten Kasparov with commodity hardware sounded like a fun question to answer, but I also hoped it would provide a tiny bit of insight into the rate of algorithmic progress in "AI". Chess engines in 1997 were already quite advanced; after all, Alan Turing helped write the first chess program nearly fifty years earlier. So I suppose at the time it seemed plausible that maybe there weren't that many more ideas left to find. And with hindsight it's easy to see that's wrong. Which leads to the question: just how much are we leaving on the table with modern-day "AI"---that is to say, language models. Will the advances we accrue over the next few years from software outpace the advances in hardware scale? Clearly this toy experiment doesn't answer that question definitively, but it does gesture at a potential future. (There's also probably some kind of meta-lesson about using LLMs---"AI"---to speed up our ability to answer weird research questions like this.) (Also, uh, if anyone has any ideas for projects I could do with a Pentium Pro in a few weeks once I no longer need it to host this chess engine ... do let me know!) If you want to be notified the next time I write something (maybe like this, maybe not) enter your email address here. There's also an RSS Feed if that's more of your thing. -->

title: European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative
body_text: ERICI — European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative ERICI Why now The gap Reference stack Join European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative RISC-V Industrial Computers. Open, partitioned, built to last. RVA23 silicon has arrived. The industrial computer built on it has not. ERICI coordinates a reference stack, from firmware to real-time and general-purpose operating systems: it fixes the interfaces between the layers and verifies that they boot together on real RVA23 hardware. A box that boots it is ERICI-compatible . Non-commercial RVA23 Based in Europe, open worldwide Join the initiative ▶ Demonstration Linux operator GUI, HMI QSOE real-time control gRouvr partitioning hypervisor mr-bml boot loader, OS selection HFI BIOS firmware, Set-Up, boot control RVA23 RISC-V SoC cores, memory, devices, IOMMU The ERICI reference stack, tested together layer by layer. See how it boots Why now Industrial computing is ready for RISC-V Today's industrial computers run on x86 and Arm: two instruction sets, each owned and licensed by a single company. RISC-V is open, governed by a non-profit, and implemented by many vendors. Until recently it lacked what industrial systems need. That has changed. 1 An open ISA No license for the instruction set, no single owner, no single country. A machine expected to run for 15 years should not depend on one company's roadmap, or one government's decisions. 2 RVA23: a real baseline The RVA23 profile, ratified in October 2024, makes the hypervisor and vector extensions mandatory. Software can rely on them on every compliant chip. 3 Silicon is shipping The first RVA23 SoCs and boards are available in 2026, with eight 64-bit cores and an IOMMU. Developers can buy them today. 4 One box instead of two A partitioning hypervisor runs real-time control and the operator's Linux side by side, isolated from each other, on one SoC. From a university project to industrial computing 2010 RISC-V starts at UC Berkeley 2015 RISC-V Foundation founded 2020 RISC-V International, based in Switzerland 2021 Hypervisor and vector extensions ratified 2024 RVA23 profile ratified 2026 First RVA23 boards. ERICI starts. So why are there no RISC-V industrial computers yet? Board makers wait for software, software waits for boards, and customers wait for both. ERICI breaks that loop with an open reference stack running on real hardware. The gap The silicon is here. The industrial computer isn't yet. The first RVA23 machines are on the market: eight 64-bit RISC-V cores, the hypervisor extension, an IOMMU. They are excellent development and edge platforms. An industrial computer has to do more: survive the control cabinet, talk to the field, and stay available for a decade or longer. Firefly AIBOX-K3 T-Chip Intelligent Technology · edge mini PC SpacemiT K3, 8× X100 RISC-V cores up to 2.4 GHz, RVA23 Up to 32 GB LPDDR5, UFS, M.2 NVMe 2× Gigabit Ethernet, 9–20 V DC input −20 to 60 °C operating temperature Image © T-Chip Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd. · product page Milk-V Jupiter2 Milk-V · single-board computer, metal case SpacemiT K3, 8× X100 RISC-V cores up to 2.4 GHz, RVA23 Up to 32 GB LPDDR5, UFS, M.2 NVMe Gigabit and 10 GbE SFP+, Wi-Fi 6 Real-time I/O expansion for EtherCAT and CAN-FD modules Image © Milk-V · product page What a RISC-V Industrial Computer needs Requirement AIBOX-K3 Jupiter2 RVA23 SoC with hypervisor extension and IOMMU Yes Yes 24 V DC supply, wide input range 9–20 V 12 V / USB-PD Extended temperature, −40 to 85 °C −20 to 60 °C Not stated Fieldbus and real-time I/O (EtherCAT, CAN, TSN) Not stated Via modules DIN-rail or panel mounting Not stated Not stated Hardware watchdog, isolated digital I/O Not stated Not stated Industrial EMC and safety certification Not stated Not stated Long-term availability, 10–15 years Not stated Not stated Partitioned software stack: real-time next to Linux Not yet Not yet Partitioned stack: demonstrated on the SpacemiT K3 PicoITX board, not yet on these products. See the video . Specifications as published by the manufacturers, October 2026. Both products are shown as examples of RVA23 hardware available today. No affiliation with ERICI or endorsement by the manufacturers is implied. The missing pieces are not the cores. They are the industrial hardware around them and an open, partitioned software stack on top. That is where ERICI starts. Reference stack Defined together, verified together A RISC-V Industrial Computer is built in layers. ERICI defines a reference stack, documents the interface between each pair of layers, and verifies the whole stack on real RVA23 hardware. The reference components are developed by QSOE Systems; Linux by its community. Each layer depends only on what the layer below hands over. Layer In the reference stack Interface below Operator partition GUI, HMI, networking Linux a general-purpose OS for everything that is not time-critical devicetree kernel + initrd Real-time partition control loops, machine I/O QSOE a QNX-style environment: /N on its own Skimmer microkernel, /L on seL4, same userspace devicetree kernel + initrd Multiboot3 for /L, next gRouvr Partitioning CPUs, memory, devices, IOMMU gRouvr --> gRouvr RVA23 resource-partitioning hypervisor; every available means of isolation, IOMMU included kernel + initrd, like Linux Loading boot menu, OS images mr-bml menu-driven boot loader: the operator selects which systems to start UEFI application Firmware initialization, boot control HFI BIOS U-Boot-based, with POST and a BIOS-style Set-Up for industrial boards RVA23 profile Hardware RVA23 SoC with IOMMU SpacemiT K3 8× X100 cores, hypervisor extension, IOMMU the silicon itself How it boots The firmware initializes the system, runs POST and offers its Set-Up . Then it starts a UEFI boot loader, and its job is done. The loader starts operating systems, or a hypervisor together with them. gRouvr is loaded just like a Linux kernel with its initrd. Its boot package is a CPIO archive that holds the kernel and initramfs image of every partition. So mr-bml loads it, and so does GRUB. gRouvr then gives each partition its own CPUs, memory and devices, and a devicetree that describes them. Real-time and Linux partitions start side by side. ▶ Watch the demonstration gRouvr booting Linux and QSOE/N on the SpacemiT K3. Opens on YouTube. Built to outlast Not tied to one chip The first RVA23 SoCs come from Chinese vendors; more will follow from other vendors and other regions. The reference stack depends on the RVA23 profile and on open interfaces, not on a particular SoC. Moving a box to another RVA23 chip means porting the firmware, adapting the hypervisor and the board's drivers. The real-time application and the operator's Linux move with it. Not tied to one developer The reference stack is open source: HFI BIOS under GPL-2.0, like the U-Boot it is based on; mr-bml under GPL-3.0; gRouvr and QSOE under Apache 2.0. Anyone can build, audit and maintain it, with or without its original developers. A machine that runs for 15 years needs software that can be maintained for 15 years. Join Build the RISC-V industrial computer with us ERICI is in its founding phase. Companies and institutions that see RVA23 as the future of industrial computing are welcome to join now and shape the initiative from the start. Who we invite, and what they bring Industrial hardware makers the box itself: an RVA23 board in a real enclosure, with I/O and a datasheet Silicon vendors RVA23 SoCs with an IOMMU and long-term availability Machine builders and plant operators requirements from the field, and a first machine to put a box in OS and driver vendors your RTOS, Linux distribution or drivers, brought up on a named RVA23 box Universities and research teaching and theses on real ERICI systems How ERICI works Non-commercial. ERICI sells nothing and charges no membership fees. Open interfaces. How each layer hands over to the next is public: UEFI, kernel + initrd, devicetree. Closed-source components are welcome, as long as they keep to these interfaces. Bring a real system. Contributions are RISC-V industrial computers: a named SoC in a real box, with a datasheet and a date. Software counts when it serves such a system, such as the driver that lets the real-time partition on box X run its machine. Concrete, not abstract. No road maps without silicon, no specs without a system that boots them. Interested? Let's talk. contact@erici.eu Initiated by Yuri Zaporozhets · Ravensburg, Germany ERICI · European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative · non-commercial QSOE HFI BIOS gRouvr --> Impressum Privacy

It’s that wonderful time of year when our favorite Japanese festival, Jimi Halloween, is on full display. Mundane Halloween, as we coined it back in 2018, is when people dress up in costumes so mundane they have to be explained. The tradition was started in 2014 by a group of adults at  Daily Portal Z  who kind of wanted to participate in the festivities of Halloween, but were too embarrassed to go all out in witch or zombie costumes. title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
body_text: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise 836 points by aarushyadav 3 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 393 comments Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) ( https://subvocal.company/ ). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech. Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI (Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.) Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV... We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology. We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work: - Signal changes due to sweat - Electrical interference - Placement variability - Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!! So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text. Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc... Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C... This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas. That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data. So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration). We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well. Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases. For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder !   help vessenes 3 days ago | next [–] Just preordered -- glasses request: there's no way to say it nicely, I have a big nose. With a high bridge. Many glasses are really tough to get properly placed; may I request you not give up on the pads w/metal adjusters that you have in the product photos? Don't let a designer take them away from you, us folks not one standard deviation from 'normal' noses will thank you. Second, how tough is this signal processing? Will it be done on-glasses, or through an app? Third, what's the equivalent of a wake word for these? I'm reminded of the Apple Vision Pro radar to see if your fingers are clicking. I could imagine a lot of modalities where I want to just start talking and have things happen, and a lot where I don't want the glasses to pick it up. Fourth, I think a cool voice change demo would be rad -- not sure what latency is like, but if you could get it end to end under like 250ms you could probably have someone exaggerate the mouth movements and pipe out audio of them talking like someone else. Which would be another really cool demo. Super cool. You're going to be working 80 hour weeks for the next year, I'm excited to see what you put out! reply jdelfuego 2 days ago | parent | next [–] > there's no way to say it nicely, I have a big nose. But there is! "Érase un hombre a una nariz pegado, érase una nariz superlativa, érase una nariz sayón y escriba, érase un peje espada muy barbado" (Francisco de Quevedo, 1580-1645) Or, as translated by Timothy Adès ( https://timothyades.com/francisco-de-quevedo-1580-1645-a-una... ): "There was a nose, which had a man appended. It was a nose superb, superlative, it was a nose, a hangman and a scribe, it was a swordfish, sharp and hairy-ended" reply Eddonarth 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Is that considered nice? I thought Quevedo was making fun of Góngora. Some more of their poetic battles (in Spanish): https://lclcarmen1bac.wordpress.com/2026/05/07/quevedo-vs-go... reply aarushyadav 3 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] Yep, we have been quite set on nose pads to keep them comfortable. I will keep you updated with the designs! The decoding is done via a companion app on your laptop or phone in the cloud, but end to end latency is still quite fast, under 500ms usually. To begin with we don't plan to have a wake word, but rather a trigger key on your connected device that you're entering text into (pressing Alt for example), similar to Wispr Flow. We're doing some R&D into the silent speech equivalent of voice activity detection, so we have a low power basic RF detection always-on, not enough to decode speech from but enough to detect rough movement, and when it detects speech-like activity beginning to start we can trigger full sensing within tens of ms. This would likely ship as a software update a few months after shipping, though. The voice change demo is something I've thought about actually, but we never got around to doing. Might film it soon :) reply vessenes 3 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Also I note from your comments here you don’t plan on local inference - that seems like a huge self own, provided the model is less than like 2b params. I’m not saying people won’t in practice prefer your cloud version, but you have this huge uphill battle ahead of you on privacy which can be wiped at the stroke of a pen with “yep it will run on your Mac.” You can get both markets (ease of use and technical) by allowing it. Also i would bet that you gain almost no product security locking off local inference - the hardware is the hard bit. Once someone has your hardware in hand it will not take them long to reverse and build their own processing layer; you’ll need to fight those people on patents and product quality. Heck for a v1 just allowing local sensor data would probably be enough for the tech enthusiasts. But please don’t lock this off from the get go - it makes the sale harder and I don’t think it gives you much in return. reply joshspankit 3 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Agreed. Cloud processing can be tempting as the primary revenue stream, but it entirely cuts off those users who cannot send arbitrary PII over the internet (regardless of encryption promises). It also invites the (especially now-LLM-empowered) enthusiasts to reverse engineer it. Instead, consider selling the glasses with >20% profit, and give local users a cheaper subscription to something else (maybe the model updates?) so they can also help keep the company sustainable. reply pipe01 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] They did say they hoped to support local models in the future https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50346346 reply nolroz 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I will happily pre order once a local option is available at launch reply vessenes 3 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Super cool. For a cool voice change demo we'll allow a gb200 over low latency wifi :) elevenlabs has deals with a number of professional actors and voice actors for licensed uses, seems like you could probably find an ethical and cool co-brand opportunity in there. Have fun building this! It's worth doing. reply IHLayman 3 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Wait. You are taking the RF response, sending it up to the cloud to interpret, and then sending the result back? Hard pass from me, sorry. Cool tech, but I don’t want my internal thoughts anywhere near the cloud. Also, this would mean I couldn’t use something like this on the subway when the phone signal goes out intermittently, right? reply kaonwarb 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] The commercial reality I’m sure they’re dealing with is that the percentage of users who care enough to deal with everything required for local inference is nowhere close to large enough to make it into an initial launch. reply aarushyadav 3 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Fair enough! We take data security and privacy very seriously and have built many safeguards to prevent even us from accessing the raw data in the cloud. At some point in the future we hope to launch local inference models too! reply snackbroken 3 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Respectfully, talk is cheap. Every company says they take security and privacy seriously even after their database has been breached and their customers' plaintext passwords and credit card details have become public information. If you were actually serious about prioritizing privacy above securing an ongoing service relationship you would ship local inference as the default and only (possibly later) offer a cloud service as an optional add-on for those who want/need it. reply johnhtodd 3 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] This is the gate for me. I've put a deposit down, but need to see how this is going to be run locally before I'll actually pay for them. There is absolutely zero chance of me sending everything that goes to my "keyboard" to my system via a cloud, no matter how many assurances are provided. Maybe I can see that being necessary on mobile (maybe?) but on a laptop it is a full-stop "no" - I have lots of horsepower, this needs to work 100% locally. I might be OK with doing a cloud-assisted "training" interval, but once complete, there should be no requirement for network connectivity for production use. reply coldspoon95 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Same for me. I put the deposit down but will pull out if it doesn’t come with local inference. Makes no sense for my thoughts to go to the internet. I’m ok with having slightly poor local inference quality compared to the cloud one. And one can encrypt the local inference to prevent reverse engineering the weights etc. reply beanaroo 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Echoing others on privacy and security while also concerned about service availability and reliability. Offline capability would be really meaningful for a variety of reasons. reply ComputerGuru 3 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I just want to say 500ms isn’t fast. reply aarushyadav 3 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Yes, this is the unoptimized speed while we are in development. We are working hard to make it much faster for production! reply nextaccountic 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > The decoding is done via a companion app on your laptop or phone in the cloud, but end to end latency is still quite fast, under 500ms usually. Why don't you do this on the phone? You don't want to have your proprietary tech on the user device? Or maybe you wanted to save the recording on your cloud anyway so you can train on it later or otherwise use the data? reply eptcyka 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Is there a way to not have someone inspect me uttering profanities under my nose in the cloud? title: C++26 Disapproved
body_text: C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive? - Andreas Fertig's Blog Courses From C to C++ Modern C++ - When Efficiency Matters Programming with C++11 to C++17 Programming with C++20 Safe and Efficient C++ for Embedded Environments Self-Study Courses A day with C++20s coroutines C++17 & C++20 Course and Coaching Bundle Essential C++ for Safe and Efficient Embedded Systems Mastering C++ Templates Safely Programming with C++17 and C++20 Books Notebook C++: About move semantics Notebook C++: Tips and Tricks with Templates Programming with C++20 - Concepts, Coroutines, Ranges, and more Code Review Blog Talks Get In Touch C++ C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive? Nov 03, 2026 On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved ! I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views. The Current Status As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote. In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures , there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved. The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release. The Process Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree. However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently. The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026. It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me. The History of Contracts in C++ The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote. In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes. And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached. Planning your team's C++ training for 2027? I'm available for in-house C++ classes worldwide, on-site or remote. Popular topics: From C to C++ Programming with C++11 to C++26 C++ in embedded environments All classes can be customized to what you and your colleagues actually work on. Find the right class Not sure what fits? Just get in touch. What happens next? The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options: Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote. Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase). Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification. Cancel the project. All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue. The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed. Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time. Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken. Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken. The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse. The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project. My Personal Opinion Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust. title: If you love a website, back it up
body_text: If you love a website, back it up - The Future Is Now The Future Is Now RSS Blog Archives If you love a website, back it up Oct 29 th , 2026 4:21 pm This story starts with a little tragedy. See, Iâve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. Thereâs websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and thereâs something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes. There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken . Itâs about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea. 1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads. I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didnât. This post is here to beg you to do what I didnât think to, and to teach you how. You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe itâs something they couldnât do. Itâs something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But thatâs not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can , but should ! Donât just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you donât want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up! All of the tools Iâll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC 2 . You donât have to worry about any of the technical details 3 , but Iâm telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post: You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. Itâs an entire website right in a post! (And if you donât trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose âdownload archiveâ, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!) By the way, for disclosure: the tools Iâm going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but thatâs not because theyâll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving. Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesnât take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is: Install the browser extension . Visit the first page you want to archive. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click âStart Archivingâ. If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads. Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click âStop Archivingâ. Youâre done! You just archived a web page! Now that itâs all saved, you can preview it and see how it went by clicking the extensionâs icon and then the home icon to open the extension dashboard. From there, you can click on your archiving session to preview the pages you archived, load them in browser, and see if they work. (Iâll go into more details on how you can look at web archives and share them with others later in this post.) Option 2 - archiveweb.page app If you donât want to install a browser extension, or you donât have Chrome installed, you can also grab the standalone archiveweb.page app . This is basically the same thing as the browser extension above, it just has its own web browser built in. It also opens straight to the menu that lets you browse your web archives, so itâs a handy way to look at your web archives locally. Pretty much everything else I described above applies. Option 3 - Browsertrix The above options are great for single pages or sites that are small enough for you to browse manually. But if youâve got a webpage thatâs big enough that itâs going to be annoying visiting all of the pages by hand, you probably want to look at a web crawler tool for web archiving. There are a bunch of options out there, but the easiest to use as an individual is probably Browsertrix . A web crawler is basically an automation tool built around a web browser; you provide instructions on what page to start from and what pages it should visit, and it will go ahead and click links to automatically find pages so that it can archive the page as completely as possible. The web archive I embedded above was done using Browsertrix on pretty close to its default settings: I just told it I wanted to do a site crawl for the entire domain https://teapuppies.mistys-internet.website , and it worked it out from there: But, depending, on what youâre looking for, it has options which can be customized to narrow down what content it archives. For example, if you decided you only want pages for the episodes, you could tell it to only capture anything at the /episodes/ section of the website: Or even just a single page and anything that page links to: There are a lot more options than I can go into in a quick overview - itâs a comprehensive tool with a lot of options. But if youâre looking to archive a whole website, or a complete social media profile, Iâd recommend giving it a try. Unlike the other tools, which you mainly run on your own computer, Browsertrix is primarily a web app. Itâs also the only paid tool in this post - thereâs a seven day trial, but after that you do have to pay per use. Since itâs open source, though, technically inclined users can run their own copies on their computer or deploy a copy somewhere if they like. Viewing your archived webpage Once youâve actually backed the site up, you can replay it to use it in your browser just like a live webpage. Itâs kind of like having your own private version of the wayback machine. You can test it out yourself for your own private use using the interface built into the version of archiveweb.page you used, but if you want to share it with someone else you have a few options. If you want to share it with someone privately, you can send them the WARC/WACZ file and let them load it into the ArchiveWeb.page app or the ReplayWeb.page website. If you want to share it with the world, though, you can set up a website with your web archive on it. This post is using the ReplayWeb.page embedded viewer, which is open source and can be embedded inside any other web page you want. You donât have run any kind of app on your server to do this; as long as you have the ability to upload the archive and a little bit of JavaScript, you can easily add a copy of the replay interface into any web page or blog post. Preserving the data once you have it Since everything you backed up is bundled inside a single WACZ file, itâs really easy to keep safe - or share with someone else. Lots of copies keeps stuff safe, after all; if you think you have friends whoâd like to hold on to a copy of whatever site youâve backed it up, pass it along and share the duty of preserving it! If any of this sounds interesting to you, Iâd encourage you to at least give it a try. Iâd love for the world to be filled with thousands upon thousands of little web archives, with people and community groups archiving and sharing the things that matter to them for themselves. If youâre finding any of this overwhelming, and youâre not sure where to get started, please reach out to me - Iâm very happy to give you a hand. The appeal to me is, I hope, obvious.Â ↩ Most of the tools Iâm mentioning also use the WACZ format, which packages up WARC files along with extra metadata.Â ↩ For those who want a little extra technical detail, though: one of the things that makes WARC special is that it records complete information about requests and responses, including all headers. This gives WARC a much more complete view of the whole process of visiting a website, and makes it possible to archive even complicated sites with client-side JavaScript that make a ton of requests.Â ↩ Posted by Misty De Meo Oct 29 th , 2026 4:21 pm archives « Performing digital surgery to fix MIDIs for my hardware (and then discovering the entire premise of my post was wrong) Recent Posts If you love a website, back it up Performing digital surgery to fix MIDIs for my hardware (and then discovering the entire premise of my post was wrong) What's up with that song from the duck game on Amiga CD32 anyway?
